A **printing press** is a machine that applies pressure to transfer ink onto a surface made of paper, cloth, or a similar material. Its workers are known as **printing press operators**.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-1) It marked a significant improvement on earlier methods, in which the paper was rubbed by hand to transfer applied ink to the printing surface.

The printing press was invented by the German goldsmith [Johannes Gutenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Gutenberg "Johannes Gutenberg") around 1440, and [its subsequent global spread](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_spread_of_the_printing_press "Global spread of the printing press") revolutionized literary production and communication during the early modern period. The spread of printing brought about an era of [mass communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_communication "Mass communication") in European society, allowing information to quickly spread across Europe and contributing to the [Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation#Printing "Reformation") and the [Scientific Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_Revolution#Printing "Scientific Revolution"). The cost of printed texts declined and their availability increased, facilitating higher adult literacy rates across Europe. Books increasingly appeared in [vernacular languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernacular_language "Vernacular language") rather than [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin"), and national languages were standardized.

The basic design of the wooden handpress was largely consistent for over three centuries, until the [Industrial Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution"). By 1800 [Lord Stanhope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Stanhope,_3rd_Earl_Stanhope "Charles Stanhope, 3rd Earl Stanhope") had built a new [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cast_iron "Cast iron") printing press printing a sheet at one pull. In 1814, _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times "The Times")_ adopted [Friedrich Koenig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Koenig "Friedrich Koenig")'s new presses, which incorporated [steam power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_power "Steam power") and rotary motion. [Richard M. Hoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_M._Hoe "Richard M. Hoe")'s [rotary printing press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotary_printing_press "Rotary printing press"), introduced in 1843, enabled much higher output; later rotary presses could produce millions of page impressions in a day. During the twentieth century, the letterpress was largely replaced by [offset printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offset_printing "Offset printing"), [phototypesetting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phototypesetting "Phototypesetting"), and [digital printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_printing "Digital printing") in commercial work.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Printing_press&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 9: Medieval manuscript illustration of a lecturer addressing rows of students in a vaulted hall](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Laurentius_de_Voltolina_Vorlesung_vor_Studenten_-_Min_1233_-_Kupferstichkabinett_Berlin.jpg/250px-Laurentius_de_Voltolina_Vorlesung_vor_Studenten_-_Min_1233_-_Kupferstichkabinett_Berlin.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Laurentius_de_Voltolina_Vorlesung_vor_Studenten_-_Min_1233_-_Kupferstichkabinett_Berlin.jpg)

A [medieval university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_university "Medieval university") class, 1350s

Main article: [History of printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_printing "History of printing")

[Johannes Gutenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Gutenberg "Johannes Gutenberg") invented the movable-type printing press around 1440, utilizing four existing technologies: the [screw press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screw_press "Screw press"), [movable type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movable_type "Movable type"), the [codex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codex "Codex") book format, and mechanized paper production.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMan200226,_115,_136-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChildress200851%E2%80%9355-3) The economic and cultural changes of [late medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Middle_Ages "Late Middle Ages") Europe brought about viable commercial conditions for his press. The urban [middle class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_class "Middle class") grew alongside [trade and commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_capitalism "History of capitalism"), while the growing number of [universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_university "Medieval university") since the twelfth century had increased demand for books. Hand-copying was slow and expensive, and by the fifteenth century, the supply of manuscripts was much less than the demand.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-5)

### Technological factors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Printing_press&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Technological factors")]

[![Image 10: Large wooden screw press with vertical timbers and central screw](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Holzspindelkelter_von_1702.jpg/250px-Holzspindelkelter_von_1702.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Holzspindelkelter_von_1702.jpg)

Early modern [wine press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wine_press "Wine press"). Such screw presses, used in Europe for a wide range of uses, provided Gutenberg with the model for his printing press.

Gutenberg integrated these four technologies into a single working system and added a number of innovations of his own, including a [hand mold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hand_mould "Hand mould") for casting type and an oil-based ink suited to metal type.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChildress200851%E2%80%9355-3)

The first factor, the screw press, permitted direct pressure to be applied on a flat plane. Used for a variety of tasks[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWolf197421%E2%80%9335-6) and [introduced by the Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_agriculture "Roman agriculture") in the 1st century AD, it was often used by farmers for [pressing grapes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressing_grapes "Pressing grapes") to make wine and [olives to make oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olive_oil "Olive oil").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-7) Gutenberg may also have been inspired by the paper presses which operated similarly to the screw press and were used across the [German lands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") from the late 14th century.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchulte193956-8) He adopted the basic design of the screw press, thereby mechanizing the printing process.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWolf197439ff.-9) Printing brought the machine different demands, and Gutenberg adapted the construction so that the [platen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platen "Platen") (a flat surface) exerted even pressure across the paper with minimal smearing. Gutenberg introduced a movable undertable with a level surface on which the sheets could be swiftly changed.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWolf197439%E2%80%9346-10)

[![Image 11: Rows of small metal letter blocks arranged in a wooden compartmented case](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Metal_movable_type.jpg/250px-Metal_movable_type.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Metal_movable_type.jpg)

Movable type sorted in a letter case and loaded in a [composing stick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composing_stick "Composing stick") on top

[![Image 12: Open book showing two columns of dense black printed text on a cream page](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Gutenberg_Bible%2C_Lenox_Copy%2C_New_York_Public_Library%2C_2009._Pic_01.jpg/250px-Gutenberg_Bible%2C_Lenox_Copy%2C_New_York_Public_Library%2C_2009._Pic_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gutenberg_Bible,_Lenox_Copy,_New_York_Public_Library,_2009._Pic_01.jpg)

A paper codex of the 42-line Bible, Gutenberg's major work

Movable type is the [typographical principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typographical_principle "Typographical principle") of writing a text from individual reusable characters. The Chinese artisan [Bi Sheng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bi_Sheng "Bi Sheng") invented the first movable type in the 11th century during the [Song dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_dynasty "Song dynasty"), using characters made of baked clay.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilkinson2012911-11) Around 1300, [Wang Zhen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Zhen_(inventor) "Wang Zhen (inventor)") developed a set of movable wooden type, arranged on revolving tables, which he used to print a local gazetteer. Wang wrote about his invention in his agricultural treatise.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilkinson2012911-11) Woodblock printing remained the primary method in East Asia. The oldest surviving book incorporating [metal movable type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_case "Type case") is the _[Jikji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jikji "Jikji")_ dating to 1377, produced under the Korean state of [Goryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goryeo "Goryeo").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilkinson2012911-11) However, none of the various East Asian methods gained widespread usage, largely due to their relative inefficiency. The [logographic script](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logographic_script "Logographic script") used in China included thousands of distinct characters, resulting in high production costs for a full set of type.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilkinson2012911-11) The Gutenberg press benefited from its use of the [Latin alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_alphabet "Latin alphabet") with a relatively small set of characters.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-12)

The codex book format also dated to the [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire"),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobertsSkeat198324%E2%80%9330-13) and was of utmost significance in the history of the book. By 500 AD, Christian and Muslim scribes had shifted from using [scrolls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scroll "Scroll") to using codices.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-14) The codex proved more convenient than the scroll format because of its greater legibility, compact arrangement, lower costs, and the availability of both [left and right pages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left_and_right_pages "Left and right pages").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-15)

Medieval papermakers had successfully mechanized the production of paper. Water-powered [paper mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paper_mill "Paper mill") were in usage by 1282,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurns1996418-16) resulting in much greater production and replacing the tedious processes associated with Chinese[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-17) and Muslim papermaking.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-18) The number of papermaking centers grew rapidly in late 13th-century Italy, causing paper to become much cheaper than [parchment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parchment "Parchment"). These centers became more common in Germany a century later.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurns1996417-19)

However, the increased usage of paper was just as dependent on the rise of movable-type printing.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-20) Codices of parchment are superior in quality to any other [writing material](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writing_material "Writing material"),[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-21) and Gutenberg still made great use of them in his edition of the [42-line Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/42-line_Bible "42-line Bible").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-22) After much experimentation, he concluded that the formula for an oil-based ink worked best for printing with metal type.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChildress200860-23)

### Gutenberg's press

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Printing_press&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Gutenberg's press")]

See also: [Letterpress printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letterpress_printing "Letterpress printing")

[![Image 13: Drawing of Johannes Gutenberg standing beside a printing press, holding a printed sheet](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/Printing_and_writing_materials_-_their_evolution_%281904%29_%2814777458662%29.jpg/250px-Printing_and_writing_materials_-_their_evolution_%281904%29_%2814777458662%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Printing_and_writing_materials_-_their_evolution_(1904)_(14777458662).jpg)

Johannes Gutenberg, 1904 reconstruction

Gutenberg began working on the printing press around 1436, when he partnered with the [gemcutter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemcutter "Gemcutter") Andreas Dritzehn and the paper miller Andreas Heilmann.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeggs199858%E2%80%9369-24) The first known mention of Gutenberg's work is in a 1439 [lawsuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawsuit "Lawsuit") against him which describes his types, type molds, and collection of metals.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeggs199858%E2%80%9369-24) Gutenberg had formerly worked as a professional goldsmith, and had obtained knowledge of metals from that craft. He was the first to produce type from an alloy of [lead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead "Lead"), [tin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tin "Tin"), and [antimony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antimony "Antimony"). This alloy produced a particularly durable type suitable for high-quality printing. To create these lead types, Gutenberg used a special matrix that allowed him to rapidly and precisely mold new type blocks from a uniform template.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeggs199858%E2%80%9369-24) His type case is estimated to have contained 290 separate letter boxes including special characters, [ligatures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typographic_ligature "Typographic ligature"), and [punctuation marks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punctuation_marks "Punctuation marks").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMahnke2009290-25)

Gutenberg is also credited with introducing an oil-based ink, which was more durable than the previously used water-based inks. He used both paper and [vellum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vellum "Vellum") (high-quality parchment) in his printing. He created a trial of color printing for a few of the page headings in the [Gutenberg Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible "Gutenberg Bible"), present only in some copies.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKapr1996172-26) The [Mainz Psalter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainz_Psalter "Mainz Psalter") of 1453, likely designed by Gutenberg, featured elaborate red and blue printed initials and was published by his successors [Johann Fust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Fust "Johann Fust") and [Peter Schöffer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Sch%C3%B6ffer "Peter Schöffer").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKapr1996203-27)

### Operation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Printing_press&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Operation")]

[![Image 15: Technical engraving showing the side view of a printing press with its screw, platen, and frame](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/Printing_press.jpg/250px-Printing_press.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Printing_press.jpg)

Printing press, engraving by W Lowry after [John Farey Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Farey_Jr. "John Farey Jr."), 1819

[![Image 16: Woodcut showing two printers at work: one removes a printed sheet while the other inks type with leather balls](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Printer_in_1568-ce.png/250px-Printer_in_1568-ce.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Printer_in_1568-ce.png)

This [woodcut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodcut "Woodcut") from 1568 shows the printer on the left removing a printed sheet while the printer on the right inks the type. Working together, they could perform 14,000 hand movements and produce c.3,600 impressions in a working day.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-Wolf_1974,_67f.-28)

A classical printing press is a stationary machine about 5 to 7 feet (1.5 to 2.1 m) long, 3 feet (0.91 m) wide, and 7 feet (2.1 m) tall.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChildress200856-29) A compositor set the type, the small individual metal letters, into the desired lines of text. Several lines were arranged at once and inserted into a wooden frame, the galley. Once the correct number of pages was composed, the galleys were laid face up in another frame called a forme, which rested on a flat stone, the bed.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTELyons201159-30)

The type was inked using two pads of leather called [ink balls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ink_ball "Ink ball") and mounted on wooden handles. The ink balls were stuffed with wool or horsehair, and the leather was usually sheepskin, but sometimes also calfskin and dogskin. The compositor pressed the ink balls together to distribute the ink evenly, and then applied the balls to the type. A sheet of dampened paper was held together by various small pins and two thin frames, the [tympan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tympan "Tympan") and the [frisket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frisket "Frisket"). The paper was placed on the tympan, and the frisket, which contained cut-out openings matching the type, was folded over the sheet to protect the margins from ink.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTELyons201159-30)

The tympan and frisket were then folded down so that the paper rested on the inked type. The rounce (a small handle) and the [windlass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windlass "Windlass") (a winch) were used to wind the bed under the platen. The compositor pulled a long lever, the bar, which drove a screw that pressed the platen onto the paper, and the elastic nature of the machine caused the bar to spring back after each pull. The rounce was then rotated in the opposite direction to move the bed away from the platen, the tympan and frisket were lifted, and the printed sheet was removed.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTELyons201159-30) Human hand worked the entire process until the development in the early 19th century of iron presses, some of which could be operated by [steam power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_power "Steam power").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeggs1998130%E2%80%93133-31)

### Mass production and spread in Europe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Printing_press&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mass production and spread in Europe")]

See also: [List of early modern newspapers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_early_modern_newspapers "List of early modern newspapers")

[![Image 17: Map of Europe with dots marking cities where printing presses were established by the end of the fifteenth century](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/Printing_towns_incunabula.svg/250px-Printing_towns_incunabula.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Printing_towns_incunabula.svg)

The spread of printing in the 15th century from [Mainz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainz "Mainz"), Germany

[![Image 18: Line graph showing European printed book output rising from near zero around 1450 to approximately one billion by 1800](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/European_Output_of_Printed_Books_ca._1450%E2%80%931800.svg/250px-European_Output_of_Printed_Books_ca._1450%E2%80%931800.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:European_Output_of_Printed_Books_ca._1450%E2%80%931800.svg)

European book output rose from a few million to around one billion copies within a span of less than four centuries[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuringhvan_Zanden2009p._417,_table_2-32)

Gutenberg's mechanical movable-type printing press, alongside consumer demand for printed copies of Bibles and other religious works, precipitated the widespread growth of the printing industry across Europe.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFebvreMartin1997248%E2%80%93261-33) Gutenberg's print shop in [Mainz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainz "Mainz") was originally the only one in Europe, but by the end of the 15th century around 270 European cities were involved in printing.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-ISTC-34) As early as 1480, there were printers active in 110 different places in Germany, Italy, France, Spain, the Netherlands, Belgium, Switzerland, England, Bohemia and Poland.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFebvreMartin1997182%E2%80%93183-35) The historians [Lucien Febvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucien_Febvre "Lucien Febvre") and [Henri-Jean Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri-Jean_Martin "Henri-Jean Martin") conclude that by this date, the printed book was used throughout Europe.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFebvreMartin1997182-36)

In Italy, a center of early printing, print shops existed in 77 cities and towns by 1500, while 151 locations in Italy had hosted printing at some point by 1600. In 1600, nearly 3,000 printers are known to have been active in Italy. However, printing centers soon emerged, and one third of the Italian printers published in [Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice "Venice").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-37)

By 1500, printing presses throughout Western Europe had produced over 20 million copies.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuringhvan_Zanden2009417-38) Their output grew to an estimated 150–200 million copies by 1600.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuringhvan_Zanden2009417-38) European printing presses c.1600 could produce between 1,500[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollak1972-39) and 3,600 impressions per workday.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-Wolf_1974,_67f.-28) By comparison, with manual [woodblock printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodblock_printing "Woodblock printing"),[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-40) a skilled printer could print 1,500 to 2,000 double sheets per day. A printing block could be used for up to 25,000 prints with repairs.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-41) The Korean _Kabin_ font metal movable type developed in 1434 could print 40 sheets per day.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOh2013108-42) At least 750,000 copies of [Erasmus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erasmus "Erasmus")'s works were sold during his lifetime (1469–1536),[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIssawi1980492-43) while [Martin Luther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther "Martin Luther") became Europe's most published author c.1520, at the start of the [Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation "Reformation"). Printers across Germany reprinted 291 editions of Luther's 45 original works, and between 1518 and 1520 they distributed 300,000 printed copies of his works, with the widespread printing surprising both [the pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Leo_X "Pope Leo X") and secular rulers.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettegree2015104-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDuchesne200683-45)

Newspapers arose due to faster typographical production and falling costs (see _[Relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relation\_(journal) "Relation (journal)")_), and provided a new means of conveying current information to the public.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeber2006387f.-46) The historian [Andrew Pettegree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Pettegree "Andrew Pettegree") argues that the Reformation directly contributed to the market for printed news. Printers who had gained readers from Luther's pamphlets kept them by producing news sheets discussing current events. These news pamphlets closely resembled the Reformation _[Flugschriften](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flugschriften "Flugschriften")_ (printed pamphlets) in format, typically running to four or eight pages in [quarto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quarto "Quarto"). In the early seventeenth century, a German publisher issued news bulletins on a regular schedule, creating the first weekly newspaper, and after the format spread it remained the principal news medium in northern Europe for over a century.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettegree2015336%E2%80%93337-47) Many libraries in Europe and North America contain works printed before 1501, known as [incunabula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incunable "Incunable").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-ISTC-34)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-48)

### Global spread

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Printing_press&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Global spread")]

Main article: [Global spread of the printing press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_spread_of_the_printing_press "Global spread of the printing press")

The printing press spread rapidly across Europe largely because the equipment was portable, making censorship efforts difficult. When [religious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theocracy "Theocracy") or government entities attempted to curtail the technology in one city, the printers would relocate to neighboring cities, further accelerating the press's spread across Europe.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-49) Colonial and missionary networks spread the European-style printing press even farther, as [Jesuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuit "Jesuit") missionaries established a press at [Goa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Goa "Old Goa") in 1556 with João de Bustamante as its first printer.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTELent1980129%E2%80%93130-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-51) The Portuguese Jesuit [Diogo de Mesquita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_de_Mesquita?action=edit&redlink=1 "Diogo de Mesquita (page does not exist)") acquired a press during a visit to Europe in 1586 and maintained it at [Nagasaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagasaki "Nagasaki"), producing religious works in Japanese until his death in 1614.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTELent1980119-52) The [Dominicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominican_Order "Dominican Order") set up the first press in the Philippines, publishing the _[Doctrina Christiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctrina\_Christiana "Doctrina Christiana")_.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTELent1980120-53) In the [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire"), [Sephardi Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sephardi_Jews "Sephardi Jews") quickly established a Hebrew press in [Constantinople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople "Constantinople") in 1493, an Armenian press was established in 1567, and a Greek press in 1627, but [İbrahim Müteferrika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C4%B0brahim_M%C3%BCteferrika "İbrahim Müteferrika") established the first Arabic-script press for a Muslim readership in 1727. [Esad of Ioannina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esad_of_Ioannina "Esad of Ioannina") assisted Müteferrika in the development of his press, which produced seventeen works before 1742.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-54) In the Americas, [Juan Pablos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Pablos "Juan Pablos") established the first press in [Mexico City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City "Mexico City") in 1539, working on behalf of the Seville-based publisher Juan Cromberger, while British colonists established another press at [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts"), in 1638.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-55)

### Industrial printing presses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Printing_press&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Industrial printing presses")]

The overall design of the wooden handpress was largely consistent throughout its long history, but its construction and performance improved considerably over three centuries, with metal screws replacing wooden ones c.1550 and the tympan and frisket becoming standard fittings.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollak1972227%E2%80%93228-56) Around 1620, the Dutch cartographer [Willem Blaeu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willem_Blaeu "Willem Blaeu") introduced a press with a more advanced hose arrangement and a more reliable mechanism for moving the type form into position beneath the platen,[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollak1972228-57) and printers introduced further changes over the next two centuries. As new metal components were introduced, the straight lever bar was curved to facilitate its movement, and screw dimensions were adjusted to suit particular press sizes. By the closing years of the wooden-press era, the Ramage press enhanced the speed of printing by incorporating a mechanism that returned the platen automatically after each impression.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollak1972228%E2%80%93229-58) According to one estimate, these improvements raised press productivity by a factor of three or four between the mid-15th and late-16th centuries.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollak1972228-57)

Several more innovations and improvements followed before the start of the Industrial Revolution. By 1800, [Lord Stanhope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Stanhope,_3rd_Earl_Stanhope "Charles Stanhope, 3rd Earl Stanhope") had built the first iron printing press, which maintained the screw of the wooden hand press but increased the pressure from a single pull through a new arrangement of bar and spindle. To allow greater force on the frame, Stanhope cast the structure in iron.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoran197346%E2%80%9347-59) The Stanhope press could print a whole sheet in one pull, its chief advantage over the wooden press, and did so with far less effort on the lever.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoran197353-60) It could print 480 pages per hour, double the output of the old press.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBolza196780-61)

The use of steam power for running the machinery and the rotary motion of cylinders also drastically altered the design of the printing press, and the German printer [Friedrich Koenig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Koenig "Friedrich Koenig") successfully introduced both elements in his press designs developed between 1802 and 1818.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBolza196788-62) Koenig moved to London in 1806, where the printers [Thomas Bensley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Bensley "Thomas Bensley"), [George Woodfall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Woodfall "George Woodfall"), and [Richard Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Taylor_(editor) "Richard Taylor (editor)") financed his experiments.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoran1973105-63) In 1810, Koenig patented a press in 1810 that operated on both a [steam engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_engine "Steam engine") and the old platen. A machine made to this design entered operation in Bensley's office in April 1811, with the engineer [Andreas Friedrich Bauer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Friedrich_Bauer "Andreas Friedrich Bauer") assisting.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoran1973105-63) He patented his first cylinder machine in October 1811.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoran1973105%E2%80%93106-64)[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_][John Walter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Walter_(editor,_born_1776) "John Walter (editor, born 1776)") of _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times "The Times")_ ordered two steam-driven double machines built under Koenig's patent of 1813, with _The Times_ printing 1,100 sheets an hour on them from 29 November 1814.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoran1973107%E2%80%93108-65) A further patent of 1814 covered a perfecting machine that printed both sides of a sheet in one operation; the first example was completed in 1816.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoran1973109%E2%80%93110-66)

#### Rotary press

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Printing_press&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Rotary press")]

In the United States, [Richard M. Hoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_M._Hoe "Richard M. Hoe") invented the steam-powered [rotary printing press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotary_printing_press "Rotary printing press") in 1843,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeggs1998147-67) which could produce millions of copies of a page in a single day. The transition to rolled paper, with continuous feed, greatly increased the rate of the presses. [[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-68)Hoe's original design produced up to 8,000 pages per, with 2,000 revolutions per hour each printing four page images.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-69) By 1891, _[The New York World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_World "The New York World")_ and the _Philadelphia Item_ were operating presses that produced either 90,000 four-page sheets per hour or 48,000 eight-page sheets.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-70)

In the mid-19th century, a separate class of [jobbing presses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jobbing_presses "Jobbing presses") emerged for small-format commercial work such as cards, [billheads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billhead "Billhead"), and leaflets. [Stephen P. Ruggles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_P._Ruggles?action=edit&redlink=1 "Stephen P. Ruggles (page does not exist)") pioneered the platen jobber in Boston from the 1830s, and [George Phineas Gordon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Phineas_Gordon "George Phineas Gordon") refined it. Gordon's Franklin press was so influential that by 1894 at least eleven firms were manufacturing Gordon-type presses, and James Moran estimates that between 1840 and 1940, no fewer than 123 different kinds of treadle-driven jobbers were made in the United States alone. The quick pace of the platen jobber made it a significant force in reshaping the printing trade during the 19th century.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoran1973148%E2%80%93153-71)

#### Machine composition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Printing_press&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Machine composition")]

Type continued to be set by hand long after the press itself had been mechanized. Two hot-metal systems automated composition toward the end of the nineteenth century.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-72)[Ottmar Mergenthaler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottmar_Mergenthaler "Ottmar Mergenthaler")'s [Linotype](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linotype_machine "Linotype machine") operated on a keyboard and assembled matrices to cast a whole line of type at once, and it became widely used, while [Tolbert Lanston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolbert_Lanston "Tolbert Lanston")'s 1887 [Monotype](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monotype_System "Monotype System") cast single characters from hot metal. As most text was now machine set, hand-set foundry type went into decline, and machine composition remained standard until [phototypesetting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phototypesetting "Phototypesetting") and [digital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_printing "Digital printing") methods displaced it in the later 20th century.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeggs1998134-73)

### Later developments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Printing_press&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Later developments")]

Main articles: [Offset printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offset_printing "Offset printing"), [Phototypesetting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phototypesetting "Phototypesetting"), and [Digital printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_printing "Digital printing")

During the 20th century, printing technology moved beyond the letterpress principle. [Offset printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offset_printing "Offset printing"), developed in the early 1900s, transfers an image from a plate to a rubber blanket and then to paper, and its speed and high quality made it the dominant commercial printing method by mid-century.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-74) The introduction of phototypesetting in the 1960s and 1970s replaced hot-metal type composition with photographic methods, and the spread of [desktop publishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desktop_publishing "Desktop publishing") software from the mid-1980s shifted much of the typesetting process to personal computers.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-75) By the early 21st century, digital printing had made short-run and on-demand production commercially viable, while offset remained the standard for high-volume work.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-76)

## Impact

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Printing_press&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Impact")]

See also: [Scientific Revolution §Printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_Revolution#Printing "Scientific Revolution"), and [The Gutenberg Galaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gutenberg_Galaxy "The Gutenberg Galaxy")

The wide circulation of information and ideas due to the printing press has been called the "printing revolution", and the historian [Elizabeth Eisenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Eisenstein "Elizabeth Eisenstein") described the press as an "agent of change" across various societies. After its invention, books were produced and sold in greater numbers, authors were more closely associated with their works, reading became a more individualistic affair, and Latin declined as a scholarly language.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEisenstein1980xv%E2%80%93xvi-77) In 1997, [Time Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Life "Time Life") selected Gutenberg's invention of the printing press as the most important event of the second millennium.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-78)

### Authorship and reading

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Printing_press&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Authorship and reading")]

The printing press resulted in a greater association between authors and their texts, and the production of identical copies allowed for the precise citation of references and attached greater importance to individual authors and their exact words. For many works produced before the printing press, the name of the author has been entirely lost.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEisenstein198080%E2%80%9388-79) The consistency of the printed page gave authors new encouragement to number pages and include [tables of contents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_of_contents "Table of contents") and [indices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Index_(publishing) "Index (publishing)") in their books.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEisenstein198088%E2%80%9392-80)

Reading habits also shifted, due to the lower cost and wider availability of printed texts compared to manuscripts. Individuals shifted away from communal oral recitation toward silent and private reading, marking what Eisenstein describes as a transition "from a hearing public to a reading public".[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEisenstein1980129%E2%80%93131-81) A sermon or speech had required listeners to gather in one place at one time, whereas people scattered across a continent could read a printed text. The reading public was therefore highly individualistic, and its members often did not know each other.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEisenstein1980131%E2%80%93133-82) After the printing press was invented, wider availability of texts contributed to increasing adult literacy rates across Europe in the next two centuries, although the growth of literacy differed regionally.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFebvreMartin1997262%E2%80%93265-83)

By the end of the 15th century, printers had circulated editions of major classical works across Europe, and the printed book had come to play a central role in the diffusion of classical literature.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFebvreMartin1997262,_265-84) Many Greek scholars came to Italy after the collapse of the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire"), and between 1495 and 1515 the Venetian printer [Aldus Manutius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aldus_Manutius "Aldus Manutius") drew on their knowledge and published many Greek works in printed editions. Without the press, the equivalent recovery of Latin texts had taken over a century.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarker197874-85) Book production became increasingly commercial, and the first [copyright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright "Copyright") laws were passed.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFebvreMartin1997160%E2%80%93164-86)

### Science

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Printing_press&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Science")]

The press also changed how [natural philosophers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_philosophers "Natural philosophers") worked. Although Latin scientific treatises rarely became bestsellers, the shift from script to print preceded the conceptual revolutions of the sixteenth century rather than following them. [Ptolemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemy "Ptolemy")'s _[Almagest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almagest "Almagest")_, published in the 2nd century AD, remained authoritative as an astronomical text for some 1400 years before [Copernicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copernicus "Copernicus")'s _[De revolutionibus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De\_revolutionibus "De revolutionibus")_ surpassed it in 1543, but _De revolutionibus_ was surpassed in less than 100 years.[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] According to Eisenstein, the shift emerged largely not due to the genius of the later investigators but the introduction of printing. Scholars had previously circulated discoveries individually through manuscript letters, but could now circulate them with printing to more people,[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-87) communicate faster with each other,[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-88) and reach a wider geographical range.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEisenstein1980453%E2%80%93455,_462%E2%80%93466-89)

Printing also encouraged the gradual emergence of scientific communities whose members, scattered across Europe, could work on shared questions using shared methods and compare their results. Such communities had begun to take shape in the era of [incunabula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incunabula "Incunabula"), well before the first learned journals of the late seventeenth century. Their features included the serial publication of new findings, the preservation of data across generations, a shift from professional secrecy toward public disclosure, and an exchange between informed readers and responsive authors and editors.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEisenstein1980462-90) Hand-copied medical and botanical illustrations had degenerated over time, and classical authorities had warned against trusting pictures and counseled direct inspection of nature. Printed anatomical plates, herbal woodcuts, and star charts could be reproduced without further loss of detail. Observers such as [Andreas Vesalius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Vesalius "Andreas Vesalius") could therefore disseminate carefully drawn figures alongside their texts, making cumulative correction of the visual record possible for the first time.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEisenstein1980469%E2%80%93470,_484%E2%80%93486-91)

### Politics, state and church

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Printing_press&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Politics, state and church")]

Rulers and governments adapted quickly to the new medium. Princes who had previously relied on manuscript proclamations turned to print to publish declarations of war, treaties, and disputed points of policy in pamphlet form.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEisenstein1980135-92) According to Eisenstein, citing the historian [Geoffrey Elton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Elton "Geoffrey Elton"), [Thomas Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Cromwell "Thomas Cromwell")'s campaign in the 1530s supporting [Henry VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII "Henry VIII")'s break with Rome was the first European government effort to exploit the press for propaganda. Cromwell coordinated printers and publicists who issued vernacular tracts defending royal supremacy, while Parliament formalized the breach.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEisenstein1980312-93) The French monarchy used printed bulletins on similar lines to evoke the [patrie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeland "Homeland") as the realm of France and to represent the king as its personification. This gave early modern states a means of conducting a "psychological war" alongside military operations.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEisenstein1980135-92)

The political reach of print provoked sustained efforts at control. A series of pre-Reformation papal and episcopal censorship measures began with the Mainz archbishop's licensing edict of 1485. It culminated in the [Leo X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Leo_X "Pope Leo X") decree of 1515, which required all translations to be vetted by bishops or inquisitors. The Counter-Reformation papacy went further: the first [Papal Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Index_Librorum_Prohibitorum "Index Librorum Prohibitorum") under [Paul IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Paul_IV "Pope Paul IV") in 1559 forbade lay Catholics to read certain books, and the 1564 Index of [Pius IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Pius_IV "Pope Pius IV") reiterated the prohibition on vernacular Bibles. Secular governments introduced licensing systems requiring printers to obtain authorization before issuing new works, and some jurisdictions banned imported books outright.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEisenstein1980347%E2%80%93350-94) These measures had only partial success. Printed material crossed borders easily, and clandestine presses operated in many cities. The contest between authorities seeking to regulate the press and those seeking to circulate forbidden material became a recurring feature of European political life for the next three centuries.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEisenstein1980347%E2%80%93350-94) Pettegree argues that print was particularly important in the confessional conflicts of the later sixteenth century, including the [French Wars of Religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Wars_of_Religion "French Wars of Religion") and the [Dutch Revolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Revolt "Dutch Revolt"). In territories where open Protestant preaching was suppressed, pamphlets, broadsheets and clandestine printing became the main means by which Reformed ideas reached a wider public, and Catholic polemic responded in kind.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPettegree2005-95) Printed literature later played a major role in rallying support, and opposition, during the lead-up to the [English Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War "English Civil War"), and later the [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution "American Revolution") and [French Revolutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution "French Revolution"), through newspapers, pamphlets and bulletins.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBailynHench19811%E2%80%933-96)

Quantitative work in economics has tested some of these claims. [Jeremiah Dittmar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremiah_Dittmar?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jeremiah Dittmar (page does not exist)") has shown that cities where printing was established in the fifteenth century grew around 60 percent faster than comparable cities without presses between 1500 and 1600. Separate regressions using distance from Mainz as an instrument for press adoption support that finding.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDittmar20111133-97) Jared Rubin, using the same instrument, estimates that cities with at least one press by 1500 were 52 percentage points more likely to have adopted Protestantism by 1530, 42 by 1560, and 29 by 1600. The declining effect suggests that the press mattered most in the early phase of the Reformation, before politics and the wider diffusion of printing took over.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTERubin2014270%E2%80%93271,_281-98)

In a survey of the literature, Sascha Becker, Steven Pfaff, and Jared Rubin distinguish between supply-side and demand-side accounts of the Reformation. Supply-side accounts emphasize institutional or technological factors such as the press; demand-side accounts emphasize the religious, political, and economic grievances that drew populations and rulers toward reform.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeckerPfaffRubin20161%E2%80%934-99) Subsequent work has refined the picture. Davide Cantoni finds that German princes were much more likely to adopt the Reformation if their immediate neighbors had done so. He attributes the apparent effect of distance from Wittenberg to strategic neighborhood interactions rather than print exposure alone.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTECantoni2012502-100) Becker, Yuan Hsiao, Pfaff and Rubin reconstruct Luther's personal network from correspondence, recorded visits, and University of Wittenberg enrollments before 1523. They report that 36 percent of cities with documented contact had adopted the Reformation by 1530, compared with 6 percent of cities without contact. The authors argue that personal ties and trade-route diffusion explain the spatial pattern more fully than printing alone.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeckerHsiaoPfaffRubin2020861-101) The press is now generally treated as one channel among several rather than the single decisive cause.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeckerPfaffRubin201616%E2%80%9318-102)

[Benedict Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedict_Anderson "Benedict Anderson") places printing in a longer arc of political change. He identifies the gradual erosion of three older "axiomatic" cultural conceptions as a precondition for national consciousness in the late eighteenth century. These were that a sacred script offered privileged access to truth, that society was naturally organized under monarchs ruling by divine dispensation, and that time was indistinguishable from cosmology. For Anderson, print-capitalism was a central mechanism in this displacement. It replaced sacred languages with vernaculars, accustomed readers to news organized in homogeneous calendrical time, and contributed to the long decline of the doctrine of the [divine right of kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divine_right_of_kings "Divine right of kings").[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAnderson200636,_39%E2%80%9346-103)

### Contemporary criticism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Printing_press&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Contemporary criticism")]

Not all contemporaries welcomed these developments. The Dominican friar Filippo de Strata, writing c.1473, characterized the press as a "whore" (_meretrix_) compared to the "virgin" pen, and argued that printers valued profit over accuracy and classical scholarship.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee2022-104) The Benedictine abbot [Johannes Trithemius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Trithemius "Johannes Trithemius") argued in his 1492 treatise _De laude scriptorum manualium_ that printing would make monks intellectually lazy and that paper books were less durable than parchment manuscripts. He also presented hand-copying sacred text as a spiritual discipline that mechanical reproduction could not replace.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrithemiusBehrendt1974-105) The Florentine humanist Niccolò Perotti argued in 1470 that many printed books in circulation were inaccurate. Gerolamo Squarzafico claimed in 1481 that most printers were illiterate, and Giorgio Merula voiced concern that printing could damage classical scholarship. The Swiss physician [Paracelsus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paracelsus "Paracelsus") and his followers urged practitioners to reject inherited textual authority, repeating the Galenic slogan that "the sick should be the doctor's books" and promoting direct observation over book learning. Paracelsus himself made full use of print to broadcast his views. The slogan made better sense in scribal culture, where hand-copied medical illustrations had been prone to degeneration, than in print culture, where repeatable woodblock images preserved observations from nature more reliably.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEisenstein1980474,_484%E2%80%93486-106) Some critics also feared that religious heterodoxy would spread as biblical texts became accessible to readers without formal training.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee2022-104)

### Language

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Printing_press&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Language")]

The spread of printing also contributed to the decline of Latin as the dominant language of publication. As works were increasingly issued in the [vernacular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernacular "Vernacular") language of each region, printed texts helped to standardize the spelling and syntax of these languages, reducing their variability. Febvre and Martin argue that printing exercised a greater influence on the development of national languages than any other single factor. They identify the process as one of several forces contributing to the rise of nationalism in Europe.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFebvreMartin1997319%E2%80%93332-107)

# One Printing Press and Three Museums

## **Deaccessioning as an essential part of museum practice**

**A Collections Chronicles Blog**by Martina Caruso, Director of Collections and Rob Wilson, Art Director and Operations Manager, Bowne & Co.  
June 10, 2021

* * *

The story we’re about to tell you came out of the process of inventory, research, and investigation of the history of collecting items related to printing history, often displayed, interpreted and used at [Bowne & Co.](https://southstreetseaportmuseum.org/visit/bowne/) It follows the life of one printing press and its connection to three different museums on two coasts. When we thought of telling a larger audience about this adventure we had a few points that we wanted to highlight: first, how impactful long-term loans can be; second, how important and healthy it is to refine a collection; and third, how critical it is to build a network of peers and professionals in our field(s).

The South Street Seaport Museum as a whole celebrates the community and economy that grew up around the port of New York. Throughout the 19th century, every business and transaction needed receipts, bills, advertisements, and certificates; printing offices like the historic Bowne & Co. filled that need. The Seaport Museum holds over [28,000 artifacts](https://southstreetseaportmuseum.org/collections/explore-the-collection/) composed of a wide variety of mediums and topics, including a printing history collection built around a working variety of printing presses, as well as a vast holding of printing equipment, printing types, photo-engravings, and hand-cut wood blocks. This collection preserves the tradition of small-batch job printing in the 19th century, while keeping an open and active dialogue with contemporary practices of printmaking and graphic design communities.

Since 1975, Bowne & Co. have taken responsibility for holding artifacts and equipment in the public trust on behalf of the Seaport Museum. The nature of most items in this collection, particularly the printing presses, requires that they be operated by trained staff in order to better preserve them, and the staff at Bowne & Co. care for the working printing equipment in collaboration with the Museum’s Collections Department. These objects are considered part of the “Working Collections” of the Museum, used and put in action on a daily basis by trained staff members for the artifacts’ own preservation, and the preservation of the related traditional skills.

![Image 4](https://southstreetseaportmuseum.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Bowne_printing-02.jpg)

![Image 5](https://southstreetseaportmuseum.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/20190619_Seaport_0423-683x1024.jpg)

As part of the first wall-to-wall inventory of the Museum’s collections in over two decades, a full catalog of accessioned printing presses and printing equipment has been ongoing since the fall of 2015. The process includes looking at the equipment in the print shops, photographing them and assessing their condition, as well matching objects with their acquisition documentation, provenance, exhibition, publication, and loan history. Through this process we uncovered many old incoming and outgoing loans that provided us with a full picture of the curatorial scope of our entire collection.

Objects come into a museum’s collections because they are determined to have value—cultural value, artistic value, or educational value that gives us special understanding of the past. For the Seaport Museum, the origins and growth of New York City as a world port is integral to our mission. However, sometimes objects that were added to the collection are found to fall outside of our mission and have little New York City significance or storytelling value. The process of reviewing and removing items from a museum’s collection is known as deaccessioning. A healthy and necessary practice, deaccessioning allows museums to better care for the collections that best reflect their mission, to reduce duplicate items, and to better maintain safe environments for the collections that remain.

### Bronstrup Philadelphia Iron Hand Press

The star of this deaccession adventure is a Bronstrup Philadelphia handpress, which represents a great technological shift in printing technology, moving away from presses made from wood, to presses made from iron. While iron presses were vastly heavier than their wooden counterparts, they were also much stronger, and allowed for bigger printable areas, and faster operation. The 1820s saw many competing patents for presses that sought to find balance between strength, simplicity, and ease of use. In the United States, the most popular style of iron hand press was the Washington, invented by Samuel Rust in 1821. The Washington Press became the favorite of many printers of the time due to the strength of the toggle mechanism, which produced a large mechanical advantage in a relatively simple and compact package.

![Image 6](https://southstreetseaportmuseum.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Bronstrup_john_Depol_1992-834x1024.jpg)

The Bronstrup Philadelphia Press is a press with two names. Initially designed by Adam Ramage as the Philadelphia Press in 1833 or 1834, the press was designed as a wrought iron construction, rather than the popular cast iron as seen in the Washington. This allowed the press to retain its strength, while drastically reducing weight. This weight reduction saw the Philadelphia press rise in popularity with printing outfits setting up in western states.

Adam Ramage was succeeded by Frederick Bronstrup upon his death in 1850. Bronstrup made small changes to the Philadelphia press, mainly in modifying the toggle mechanism to more closely resemble that of the Washington Presses. This new press was sold as the Bronstrup Press until 1875.

Bronstrup Philadelphia Hand Press engraving by Jon DePol (1913-2004), published in “American Iron Handpresses” by Stephen O. Saxe, Oak Knoll Books, 1992.

This press was on view at Bowne & Co. between 1975 and 1982, and after only 7 years on-site it started its “career” as a representative of the Museum in two other cultural institutions.

### Outgoing Loan History

The Bronstrup was on loan to the Fairleigh-Dickinson University, in Teaneck, New Jersey, from 1982-1999, and since 1999 it has been on loan to the Gomez Mill House, in Marlboro, New York.

![Image 7](https://southstreetseaportmuseum.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/1975.086_Loan_FDU-1-1024x1024.jpg)

In the past, one of the key ways that the Seaport Museum allowed the public to access the collection around the United States, and particularly the East Coast, was through long-term loans. However, in recent years, long-term loans have been paused for a variety of reasons including but not limited to the fact that a number of states have passed old loan legislation in reaction to problems that arise where loans are left in museums for indefinite or long periods of time. Such problems include the amount of administrative work needed to properly manage the relationship and the required paperwork, the increasing opportunity of being “lost in translation” between staffing changes and the lender’s personal situation, and the confusion and misunderstanding that such objects could create if stored with collections items belonging to the borrowing institution.

Since limiting the duration of the loan to a shorter term helps avoid problems that arise when lenders lose contact or relocate, we improved our long-term loans with the Gomez Mill House by specifying an annual renewal expiration date within the loan agreement. ### Gomez Mill House

The [Gomez Mill House](https://www.gomez.org/) in Marlboro, New York, in the central Hudson Valley, has a fascinating history, and it is thought to be the oldest Jewish residence still standing in the United States. Luis Moses (or Moises) Gomez bought the land that surrounded the house in 1714, but it’s unlikely that Mr. Gomez lived there, although it is likely that at least some of his four sons did, at least sporadically. He was the son of an influential Spaniard, Isaac Gomez, a wealthy man so well-positioned that he advised the King of Spain. He was educated in London, and then the family moved to the Caribbean—there is firm evidence of Gomezes in Jamaica—and he might have lived on other islands as well. Jamaica flourished as a commercial center until 1692, when a tremendous earthquake demolished its main city, Port Royal. So in 1700, Luis Moses Gomez and his wife, Esther, moved to the fast-growing financial center of New York, Lower Manhattan, and to be precise, Maiden Lane, just south of the seaport.

Gomez was a trader and an entrepreneur. He built the Mill House as an outpost, a place to stay as he and his sons oversaw the trade in timber and limestone, commodities available in profusion upstate. When the Gomez family began doing business in the central Hudson Valley, there was no Jewish community there, and wouldn’t be until more than a century later. After Gomez, the house had many owners, some of them notable.

![Image 9](https://southstreetseaportmuseum.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Gomez-House-1024x768.jpg)
From 1772 to 1799, the house was owned by Wolfert Ecker (1730-1799), descended from a prominent Dutch family that arrived in New Netherlands in 1655. Ecker was a Revolution-era patriot, and he set up a local committee for safety and inspection that, according to Gomez Mill’s director, Richie Rosencrans, was one of the tools that local leaders established—a form of ad-hoc government to keep society’s basic rules in place once the British began to lose power but before formal local, state, or federal government agencies could take over.

Next—after some gaps—came the artistic and civic-minded Armstrong family, landed gentry who lived in the Gomez Mill House from 1835 to 1904. Among the various generations of the family, David Maitland Armstrong (1836-1918) was particularly interesting. He was a diplomat, a painter, and a renowned stained glass artist, whose works are still visible in the house. Maitland was largely responsible for creating the Metropolitan Museum of Art, which opened on February 20, 1872. In his obituary, the New-York Tribune stated: “Not only did he, in company with Robert Gordon and Dr. Nevin, first start the agitation for a representative museum in this city, but he also drafted suggestions for the carrying out of the project, with the result that the Metropolitan Museum as it exists to-day is largely organized on the lines he laid out.”

![Image 10](https://southstreetseaportmuseum.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Gomez-Mill-1024x768.jpg)
Another gap, and then there was William Joseph “Dard” Hunter (1883-1966), whose tenure was short, from 1912 to 1918, but had many intriguing connections with our Museum’s mission and collection. Dard was a printer, bookbinder, and a paper craftsman. In 1913, he built a paper mill adjacent to the pond and dam across the road from the main house, fashioned after 17th-century Devonshire cottages. Until then all the world’s handmade books were made by different masters in sequence—papermakers, typographers, printers—working separately with apprentices. Dard’s creations were the world’s first handmade books designed and constructed by one person, and his success inspired other Americans to begin producing handmade paper again.

Lastly, from 1918 to 1925, the house was owned by Martha Gruening (1889-1937), an American journalist, lawyer, and Civil Rights activist. With her, there was a bit of full-circle completion to her residency; like the Gomezes, Ms. Gruening and her family were Jewish.

### Deaccessioning

In 2019, as part of the refinement of our printing history collection, we took a hard look at our collection of working printing presses, and when in 2020 the Gomez Mill House decided to end the loan, we had to make some decisions.

Over the past year or two, the debates, discussions, symposiums, and news about deaccessioning in museums flourished, but many misunderstandings about deaccessioning and museum collections remain both within and beyond the United States.

Here at the Seaport Museum we have been doing our part. We studied and analyzed some of the original and essential purposes of the deaccessioning process in museums, as well as looked at the process by which it has become—in some cases—a suspect practice. Among the many resources, webinars, and conversations we investigated is the recently published book by California museum consultant Martin Gammon, _[Deaccessioning and Its Discontents](https://mitpress.mit.edu/books/deaccessioning-and-its-discontents)_, which provided us with some wonderful guidance. One of the main findings of the publication is that deaccessioning has been an essential part of museum practice since the dawn of the museum experiment in the 17th century, and as curators manage the accumulation of multiple private collections into a growing public collection, they often come to realize the need to deaccession in order to refine the collection over time to ensure it has ongoing coherence and is improving through the evolution of each institution.

Deaccessioning has gotten a bad reputation only in the last three decades of the 20th century because of the significant pressure on leading museums to deaccession works in order to simply stay solvent and afloat—these pressures including decreased government funding, a detrimental U.S. tax reform act, and a booming art market. This burden has resulted in a situation where museums are more financially pressured than ever to sell off works for the wrong reasons—even though both the American Alliance of Museums and the Association of Art Museum Directors say that selling off artworks is only acceptable when the proceeds are used toward new acquisitions, not operating expenses, salaries, or capital projects.

The Seaport Museum chooses to deaccession objects for a few reasons. An item might not fit our mission or collections plan. Items with unknown provenance or otherwise lacking in historical value or usefulness are also candidates for deaccession. Poor condition or duplication are other reasons.

Since 2015, when we were both hired, we have approached both acquisitions and accessioning, as well as disposal and deaccessioning, in practical terms. We both believe deaccessioning is a fundamental business practice necessary for the responsible preservation and health of our collections.

Assessing candidates for deaccession is a slow and deliberate process. We have set guidelines for careful selection, which involves gathering all the information known about the item and then making a recommendation. The information and recommendations are reviewed and approved by a Staff Collections Committee, then by the Museum’s Board of Trustees, and, overall, guided by state statute. Depending on the condition of the deaccessioned piece, it may be transferred to another educational institution, exchanged, destroyed, or sold at public auction. The proceeds are restricted and can only be used to obtain new collections items or for direct care of collections. Going through a deaccessioning process allows us to complete targeted research on the collection, often increasing our knowledge about the objects we hold.

The Bronstrup was the third similar type of press after the R. Hoe Washington Hand Press, on view and used for demonstrations at Bowne & Co. at 207-209 Water Street, and the Cincinnati Washington Hand Press that we were also considering deaccessioning for redundancy reasons. As part of the refinement of the Museum’s printing history collection, the Bronstrup was then deemed not to be essential to tell the history of Bowne & Co. and printing in New York, due to her manufacturer and limited history at the Museum. So, after having her deaccession approved by the Collection Committee, we started to look for a new home for it.

### International Printing Museum

Much of this story was made possible by a visit to Bowne & Co. from Mark Barbour of the [International Printing Museum](https://www.printmuseum.org/) in Carson, California. The letterpress community is mighty but small, and smaller yet is the printing museum community. In early April of 2021, Mark happened to be on a trip to New York to install a press for a film shoot. The South Street Seaport Museum and the International Printing Museum have had an open dialogue for many years, but being on opposite coasts, it’s a rare treat to be able to physically visit each other’s collections. Mark had not visited Bowne & Co. for at least a decade, and a lot had moved around the Museum in that time. It was a great opportunity to reorient both the collections and mission of the Seaport Museum with a similar institution.

Part of what came out of his visit was a deeper understanding of where the missions of both museums cross over, and where they differ. The South Street Seaport Museum’s mission is fundamentally rooted in telling the story of the rise of New York as a port city. Printing plays a huge role in that story, but its role is in the service that printing offices offered to the financial growth of the city, and the technology that supported that rapid growth. The mission of the Seaport Museum is not to encapsulate the minutiae of technological development amongst similar printing equipment.

The Bronstrup is much better suited in the collection of the International Printing Museum—a collection which covers the incremental advancements in printing technology made throughout history. Transferring the Bronstrup from the Gomez Mill House to the International Printing Museum both helped the Seaport Museum refine its collection to best express its mission and increased the breadth of the collection at the International Printing Museum. We are thrilled that this press found such a good home, and we look forward to working together in the future.

### Conclusion

Inventorying, reexamining old loans, and refining the collection can be a long, but rewarding process. Not only do staff rediscover lost collection items, they can also uncover lost stories that help us better understand the people who’ve lived and worked in the port of New York over the centuries. Removing an item that no longer supports the Museum’s mission leaves more collection care resources, storage space, and conservation budget for those pieces that still have research and education potential. When a collections item can better tell its story at another institution, like the Bronstrup Philadelphia Hand Press with our friends at the International Printing Museum, deaccessioning is especially rewarding.
