One of 11 children, Lackington was apprenticed to a cobbler as a boy. He had no formal education, but at an early age he recognized the value of books, and he and his friends scoured the markets for cheap editions of poetry, plays, and classical literature in translation in order to teach themselves to read and expand their understanding of the world. Later, as a shoemaker, he moved to London with his wife, Nancy, and years later in his memoirs he describes how, upon arriving in the city, he spent their last half-crown on a book of poems, Edward Young’s _Night Thoughts_: “For had I bought a dinner, we should have eaten it tomorrow, and the pleasure would have been soon over, but should we live fifty years longer, we shall have the _Night Thoughts_ to feast upon.” Shortly thereafter, in 1774, Lackington was able to rent his own shop, and he began selling both shoes and books together.

Late 18th-century London was a time of great social change. More people were learning to read, and the increase in leisure time among the working and middle classes meant an increased demand for books. But books were still an expensive luxury, and bookstores could be intimidating places. At the time, the typical bookstore did not encourage idle browsing or lounging. Lackington wanted to find a way to make books more affordable and accessible while still turning a profit, and with this in mind, he set about revolutionizing the book trade in at least four ways. His first innovation was to eliminate a staple of 18th-century commercial life: _credit_. He ran a cash-only business, which initially shocked his competitors and insulted some of his customers, but he reasoned that if he sold for cash, he could buy for cash instead of taking out costly loans; in this way he avoided interest charges as well as the losses incurred by customers unable to pay their debts. His second innovation had to do with his handling of remainder sales. The standard practice was for booksellers to buy large quantities of remaindered titles and then destroy as many as three-quarters of the books in order to drive up prices. But Lackington bought huge lots—sometimes entire libraries—and then drastically reduced the prices of all the books in order to sell them at high volume. In this way he kept books in circulation, made them affordable to a wider range of buyers, and turned a substantial profit all at the same time. Lackington’s third innovation will be familiar to anyone today who loves a bargain: he convinced his customers that they were getting a deal by refusing to haggle over prices. He posted this sign in his shop: _The lowest priced is marked on every book, and no abatement made on any article._

By 1794, he had amassed a large enough inventory to move into a massive shop on Finsbury Square with his partner Robert Allen. He named the shop The Temple of the Muses, and above the entrance a plaque boldly announced: _Cheapest Bookstore in the World_. The Temple of the Muses became a tourist attraction, and this was Lackington’s fourth innovation: the sheer size of his bookstore—a spectacle that dwarfed all other bookshops of the time—made it a destination in itself. With a shop front 140 feet long, the cavernous lobby featured a circular counter with space for a mail coach and six horses to pass through. Above this counter, a staircase led up to “lounging rooms” where patrons could read beneath galleries lined with book-filled shelves, four floors in all. The higher patrons climbed, the cheaper and more tattered the books became. The poet John Keats spent many hours reading for free in the lounging rooms, and it was here that he met his first publishers, Taylor and Hessy, who worked in the shop.

As was common in the period, many booksellers were also publishers, and Lackington occasionally joined others in publishing ventures. Most notably, in 1818, Lackington partnered with Hughes, Harding, Mavor & Jones to publish a very small number (a scant 500 copies!) of an unusual novel by an unknown writer, Mary Shelley. The novel, of course, was _Frankenstein_. As a bookseller turned publisher, Lackington also published multiple editions of his own autobiography, in part because he was acutely aware that his reputation was at stake, since his success drew criticism from other booksellers. Some detractors argued that his catalogues exaggerated the quality of his stock, and others insisted that his wealth must have actually come from lottery winnings because it seemed impossible that he earned it from book sales alone. And still others accused Lackington of unfair competition; they argued that he controlled too great a share of the market and should “decline” his business, since he had already made his fortune. A similar argument can still be heard today; now that Amazon has begun opening brick and mortar stores (the first in Seattle in November 2015, with another to come in San Diego) some have asked if this is necessary or desirable, since the online retailer already controls as much as 60 percent of the book market.

And like Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Lackington himself became something of a celebrity. A flag flew above The Temple of the Muses to let customers know when he was present in the shop, and he rode through the streets of London in a carriage inscribed with his motto: “_Small profits do great things._” He even minted tokens bearing his image, which could be redeemed in the shop. A catalogue of his available stock was printed on a regular basis, and orders were filled for customers as far away as America. Lackington eventually sold the shop to his third cousin in 1798 and retired to the countryside to become a part-time Methodist preacher. Sadly, The Temple of the Muses was destroyed by fire in 1841 and was never rebuilt. Although the mammoth bookshop was not part of a chain of stores—the modern chain store would not be established until a decade later when A&P Supermarket opened its doors in America—Lackington’s innovations and his controversial practice of undercutting competitors through deep-discounts and high-volume sales continue to be part of the business model for large book chains and online retailers like Barnes & Noble and Amazon to this day.

# The Man Who Invented Bookselling As We Know It

## On James Lackington's Temple of the Muses, "The Cheapest Bookstore in the World"

[VIA Bloomsbury](http://www.bloomsbury.com/us/the-blind-astronomers-daughter-9781632861870/)

[John Pipkin](https://lithub.com/author/john-pipkin/ "John Pipkin")October 11, 2016

Today, few people are likely to remember James Lackington (1746-1815) and his once-famous London bookshop, The Temple of the Muses, but if, as a customer, you’ve ever bought a remaindered book at deep discount, or wandered thoughtfully through the over-stocked shelves of a cavernous bookstore, or spent an afternoon lounging in the reading area of a bookshop (without buying anything!) then you’ve already experienced some of the ways that Lackington revolutionized bookselling in the late 18th century. And if you’re a bookseller, then the chances are that you’ve encountered marketing strategies and competitive pressures that trace their origins to Lackington’s shop. In the 21st-century marketplace, there is sometimes a longing for an earlier, simpler age, but the uneasy tension between giant and small retailers seems to have been a constant since the beginning. The Temple of the Muses, which was one of the first modern bookstores, was a mammoth enterprise, by far the largest bookstore in England, boasting an inventory of over 500,000 volumes, annual sales of 100,000 books, and yearly revenues of £5,000 (_roughly $700,000 today_). All of this made Lackington a very wealthy man—admired by some and despised by others—but London’s greatest bookseller began his career inauspiciously as an illiterate shoemaker.

One of 11 children, Lackington was apprenticed to a cobbler as a boy. He had no formal education, but at an early age he recognized the value of books, and he and his friends scoured the markets for cheap editions of poetry, plays, and classical literature in translation in order to teach themselves to read and expand their understanding of the world. Later, as a shoemaker, he moved to London with his wife, Nancy, and years later in his memoirs he describes how, upon arriving in the city, he spent their last half-crown on a book of poems, Edward Young’s _Night Thoughts_: “For had I bought a dinner, we should have eaten it tomorrow, and the pleasure would have been soon over, but should we live fifty years longer, we shall have the _Night Thoughts_ to feast upon.” Shortly thereafter, in 1774, Lackington was able to rent his own shop, and he began selling both shoes and books together.

Late 18th-century London was a time of great social change. More people were learning to read, and the increase in leisure time among the working and middle classes meant an increased demand for books. But books were still an expensive luxury, and bookstores could be intimidating places. At the time, the typical bookstore did not encourage idle browsing or lounging. Lackington wanted to find a way to make books more affordable and accessible while still turning a profit, and with this in mind, he set about revolutionizing the book trade in at least four ways. His first innovation was to eliminate a staple of 18th-century commercial life: _credit_. He ran a cash-only business, which initially shocked his competitors and insulted some of his customers, but he reasoned that if he sold for cash, he could buy for cash instead of taking out costly loans; in this way he avoided interest charges as well as the losses incurred by customers unable to pay their debts. His second innovation had to do with his handling of remainder sales. The standard practice was for booksellers to buy large quantities of remaindered titles and then destroy as many as three-quarters of the books in order to drive up prices. But Lackington bought huge lots—sometimes entire libraries—and then drastically reduced the prices of all the books in order to sell them at high volume. In this way he kept books in circulation, made them affordable to a wider range of buyers, and turned a substantial profit all at the same time. Lackington’s third innovation will be familiar to anyone today who loves a bargain: he convinced his customers that they were getting a deal by refusing to haggle over prices. He posted this sign in his shop: _The lowest priced is marked on every book, and no abatement made on any article._

By 1794, he had amassed a large enough inventory to move into a massive shop on Finsbury Square with his partner Robert Allen. He named the shop The Temple of the Muses, and above the entrance a plaque boldly announced: _Cheapest Bookstore in the World_. The Temple of the Muses became a tourist attraction, and this was Lackington’s fourth innovation: the sheer size of his bookstore—a spectacle that dwarfed all other bookshops of the time—made it a destination in itself. With a shop front 140 feet long, the cavernous lobby featured a circular counter with space for a mail coach and six horses to pass through. Above this counter, a staircase led up to “lounging rooms” where patrons could read beneath galleries lined with book-filled shelves, four floors in all. The higher patrons climbed, the cheaper and more tattered the books became. The poet John Keats spent many hours reading for free in the lounging rooms, and it was here that he met his first publishers, Taylor and Hessy, who worked in the shop.

As was common in the period, many booksellers were also publishers, and Lackington occasionally joined others in publishing ventures. Most notably, in 1818, Lackington partnered with Hughes, Harding, Mavor & Jones to publish a very small number (a scant 500 copies!) of an unusual novel by an unknown writer, Mary Shelley. The novel, of course, was _Frankenstein_. As a bookseller turned publisher, Lackington also published multiple editions of his own autobiography, in part because he was acutely aware that his reputation was at stake, since his success drew criticism from other booksellers. Some detractors argued that his catalogues exaggerated the quality of his stock, and others insisted that his wealth must have actually come from lottery winnings because it seemed impossible that he earned it from book sales alone. And still others accused Lackington of unfair competition; they argued that he controlled too great a share of the market and should “decline” his business, since he had already made his fortune. A similar argument can still be heard today; now that Amazon has begun opening brick and mortar stores (the first in Seattle in November 2015, with another to come in San Diego) some have asked if this is necessary or desirable, since the online retailer already controls as much as 60 percent of the book market.

And like Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Lackington himself became something of a celebrity. A flag flew above The Temple of the Muses to let customers know when he was present in the shop, and he rode through the streets of London in a carriage inscribed with his motto: “_Small profits do great things._” He even minted tokens bearing his image, which could be redeemed in the shop. A catalogue of his available stock was printed on a regular basis, and orders were filled for customers as far away as America. Lackington eventually sold the shop to his third cousin in 1798 and retired to the countryside to become a part-time Methodist preacher. Sadly, The Temple of the Muses was destroyed by fire in 1841 and was never rebuilt. Although the mammoth bookshop was not part of a chain of stores—the modern chain store would not be established until a decade later when A&P Supermarket opened its doors in America—Lackington’s innovations and his controversial practice of undercutting competitors through deep-discounts and high-volume sales continue to be part of the business model for large book chains and online retailers like Barnes & Noble and Amazon to this day.

### Paris reading #bookreviews: The Paris Bookseller by Kerri Maher and The Girl Who Reads on the Metro by Christine Feret-Fleury

Posted on 15/09/2025 12/09/2025 by [Joanne](https://portobellobookblog.com/author/portybelle/)

[![Image 1](https://portobellobookblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/wp-17574939658396913811237842994047.jpg?w=771)](https://portobellobookblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/wp-17574939658396913811237842994047.jpg)[![Image 2](https://portobellobookblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/wp-17576924820572332512045679859288.jpg?w=771)](https://portobellobookblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/wp-17576924820572332512045679859288.jpg)[![Image 3](https://portobellobookblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/wp-17576924822119147879327405697542.jpg?w=771)](https://portobellobookblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/wp-17576924822119147879327405697542.jpg)
I was recently in Paris (I may have mentioned this once or twice!) and wanted to read a book set in the city while I was there. I borrowed **_The Paris Bookseller_** by Kerri Maher from my library and what a fabulous choice that was. It’s inspired by the true story of Sylvia Beach who founded Shakespeare And Company, an English language bookshop in Paris.

The book is full of real life characters such as Ernest Hemingway, Ezra Pound, Gertrude Stein and James Joyce, as well as lesser known people such as Adrienne Monnier. Adrienne owned a bookshop and library in Paris and encouraged Sylvia to open her own bookshop. The two were close friends who became lovers and were in a relationship for over thirty years.

Sylvia is also renowned as a publisher. As a close friend of James Joyce, she resolved to ensure that his controversial novel **_Ulysses_**would be published in English at a time when court cases banned its publication. This took a considerable amount of money and determination. It was quite sobering to read about the censorship, homophobia and xenophobia which seemed to be taking hold in America at the time of publication in the 1920s, something which it seems is happening all over again.

I visited Shakespeare and Company while in Paris and while it’s not the actual shop founded by Sylvia, there are many photos inside of Sylvia herself, her shop and many authors who frequented the original shop. Much in keeping with her ideology, the top floor is a reading room where you can just sit and read. You aren’t allowed to take photos inside which is a shame but I understand – it’s all about the books!

I loved **_The Paris Bookseller_** which I found so informative as well as a gripping read. Sylvia was such an admirable character. Reading it while in Paris really added an extra dimension of pleasure for me as I read about places I was becoming familiar with – a really immersive read. If you read this one, do be sure to read the author’s notes at the end. They add more context to the story as well as explaining where the author took liberties with the facts and what was true.

**Full book details**

_**PARIS, 1920.**On the bohemian Left Bank, Sylvia runs a little bookshop called Shakespeare and Company. Here she welcomes the greatest writers of the day – and from the moment James Joyce finally walks through her door, the two become friends.  
  
When Joyce’s controversial novel Ulysses is banned, Sylvia is determined to publish it herself.  
  
But championing the most scandalous book of the century will come at a cost – and Sylvia finds herself risking ruin, her reputation and her heart, all in the name of the life-changing power of books.  
  
**Set in post-war Paris,The Paris Bookseller is a sweeping story of love, courage and betrayal – and a breathtakingly beautiful love letter to books.**_

[![Image 4](https://portobellobookblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/wp-17574937439443700599137418877371.jpg?w=748)](https://portobellobookblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/wp-17574937439443700599137418877371.jpg)

While I was visiting Shakespeare and Company I really wanted to buy another book which was set in Paris. When I saw **_The Girl Who Reads on the Metro_**, I knew that I had to buy that one. Another book about books set in Paris – count me in!

This is a quirky little novel which I read in a couple of sittings, neither of which were on the metro! Juliette is the eponymous girl on the metro and while travelling to her boring office job, she sees the same people every day and makes up stories about them. I really enjoyed following Juliette as she travelled along Metro Line 6, a line we used a lot when we were in Paris. One day, she decides to get off the metro early and as a result meets young Zaide and her father Soliman, who owns a bookshop.

I liked the idea of matching books to people and the right book coming along at the right time. I think most booklovers will agree this sometimes seems to be the case. It’s a book which has a feel of magical realism without actually having any magic in it! The magic is in the written word and the power of books to transform lives. One thing I thought was quite amusing or ironic, take your pick, is that page 247 is a significant page number for one of the characters, something that’s mentioned a lot. Yet, this book is less that 200 pages. The publisher missed a trick there I’d say!

I have to admit that I didn’t really understand the end of this book. It took quite a sorrowful turn, felt a little vague and I was a bit disappointed in the ending. Nonetheless, for the most part I’d say that I liked the book. I guess overall, it’s a kind of coming of age story although Juliette seems older than your average character in that kind of story. Books change her life and enable her to step outside her humdrum life.

**Full Book Details**

**For fans of _The Little Paris Bookshop_ and _The Ele_**_**gance of the Hedgehog,The Girl Who Reads on the Métro is the French phenomenon by Christine Féret-Fleury, ready to charm book-lovers everywhere . . .**  
  
When Juliette takes the métro to her loathed office job each morning, her only escape is in books – she avidly reads on her journey and imagines what her fellow commuters’ choices might say about them.  
  
Then she meets Soliman – the mysterious owner of the most enchanting bookshop Juliette has ever seen – and things will never be the same again. For Soliman believes in the power of books to change the course of a life, and he’s about to change Juliette’s forever . . ._

### Paris reading #bookreviews: The Paris Bookseller by Kerri Maher and The Girl Who Reads on the Metro by Christine Feret-Fleury

Posted on 15/09/2025 12/09/2025 by [Joanne](https://portobellobookblog.com/author/portybelle/)

[![Image 1](https://portobellobookblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/wp-17574939658396913811237842994047.jpg?w=771)](https://portobellobookblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/wp-17574939658396913811237842994047.jpg)[![Image 2](https://portobellobookblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/wp-17576924820572332512045679859288.jpg?w=771)](https://portobellobookblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/wp-17576924820572332512045679859288.jpg)[![Image 3](https://portobellobookblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/wp-17576924822119147879327405697542.jpg?w=771)](https://portobellobookblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/wp-17576924822119147879327405697542.jpg)
I was recently in Paris (I may have mentioned this once or twice!) and wanted to read a book set in the city while I was there. I borrowed **_The Paris Bookseller_** by Kerri Maher from my library and what a fabulous choice that was. It’s inspired by the true story of Sylvia Beach who founded Shakespeare And Company, an English language bookshop in Paris.

The book is full of real life characters such as Ernest Hemingway, Ezra Pound, Gertrude Stein and James Joyce, as well as lesser known people such as Adrienne Monnier. Adrienne owned a bookshop and library in Paris and encouraged Sylvia to open her own bookshop. The two were close friends who became lovers and were in a relationship for over thirty years.

Sylvia is also renowned as a publisher. As a close friend of James Joyce, she resolved to ensure that his controversial novel **_Ulysses_**would be published in English at a time when court cases banned its publication. This took a considerable amount of money and determination. It was quite sobering to read about the censorship, homophobia and xenophobia which seemed to be taking hold in America at the time of publication in the 1920s, something which it seems is happening all over again.

I visited Shakespeare and Company while in Paris and while it’s not the actual shop founded by Sylvia, there are many photos inside of Sylvia herself, her shop and many authors who frequented the original shop. Much in keeping with her ideology, the top floor is a reading room where you can just sit and read. You aren’t allowed to take photos inside which is a shame but I understand – it’s all about the books!

I loved **_The Paris Bookseller_** which I found so informative as well as a gripping read. Sylvia was such an admirable character. Reading it while in Paris really added an extra dimension of pleasure for me as I read about places I was becoming familiar with – a really immersive read. If you read this one, do be sure to read the author’s notes at the end. They add more context to the story as well as explaining where the author took liberties with the facts and what was true.

**Full book details**

_**PARIS, 1920.**On the bohemian Left Bank, Sylvia runs a little bookshop called Shakespeare and Company. Here she welcomes the greatest writers of the day – and from the moment James Joyce finally walks through her door, the two become friends.  
  
When Joyce’s controversial novel Ulysses is banned, Sylvia is determined to publish it herself.  
  
But championing the most scandalous book of the century will come at a cost – and Sylvia finds herself risking ruin, her reputation and her heart, all in the name of the life-changing power of books.  
  
**Set in post-war Paris,The Paris Bookseller is a sweeping story of love, courage and betrayal – and a breathtakingly beautiful love letter to books.**_

[![Image 4](https://portobellobookblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/wp-17574937439443700599137418877371.jpg?w=748)](https://portobellobookblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/wp-17574937439443700599137418877371.jpg)

While I was visiting Shakespeare and Company I really wanted to buy another book which was set in Paris. When I saw **_The Girl Who Reads on the Metro_**, I knew that I had to buy that one. Another book about books set in Paris – count me in!

This is a quirky little novel which I read in a couple of sittings, neither of which were on the metro! Juliette is the eponymous girl on the metro and while travelling to her boring office job, she sees the same people every day and makes up stories about them. I really enjoyed following Juliette as she travelled along Metro Line 6, a line we used a lot when we were in Paris. One day, she decides to get off the metro early and as a result meets young Zaide and her father Soliman, who owns a bookshop.

I liked the idea of matching books to people and the right book coming along at the right time. I think most booklovers will agree this sometimes seems to be the case. It’s a book which has a feel of magical realism without actually having any magic in it! The magic is in the written word and the power of books to transform lives. One thing I thought was quite amusing or ironic, take your pick, is that page 247 is a significant page number for one of the characters, something that’s mentioned a lot. Yet, this book is less that 200 pages. The publisher missed a trick there I’d say!

I have to admit that I didn’t really understand the end of this book. It took quite a sorrowful turn, felt a little vague and I was a bit disappointed in the ending. Nonetheless, for the most part I’d say that I liked the book. I guess overall, it’s a kind of coming of age story although Juliette seems older than your average character in that kind of story. Books change her life and enable her to step outside her humdrum life.

**Full Book Details**

**For fans of _The Little Paris Bookshop_ and _The Ele_**_**gance of the Hedgehog,The Girl Who Reads on the Métro is the French phenomenon by Christine Féret-Fleury, ready to charm book-lovers everywhere . . .**  
  
When Juliette takes the métro to her loathed office job each morning, her only escape is in books – she avidly reads on her journey and imagines what her fellow commuters’ choices might say about them.  
  
Then she meets Soliman – the mysterious owner of the most enchanting bookshop Juliette has ever seen – and things will never be the same again. For Soliman believes in the power of books to change the course of a life, and he’s about to change Juliette’s forever . . ._

Title: Giorgio P. Lodetti on Instagram: "Still together, with Centuries-Old Historical Roots!

May, Anno Domini 2025
250th Anniversary of the Bocca Bookstore, the oldest bookstore in Italy, located at Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II 12 since September 29, 1936.

Significant numbers, dates, years, months, and days for a historic institution that has spanned over two and a half centuries of Italian history, with branches in Turin, Milan, Florence, Rome, and Paris — in a not yet united Europe.

Letters, texts, images, books, series, edicts, posters, and proclamations fade into the mists of time — published, printed, sold, and curated by the Bocca Family, booksellers and printers in Piedmont since the early decades of the 18th century — are today being brought back to light by the Lodetti Family, who persist in carrying forward a meaningful tradition that continues to amaze and inspire us.
We are following the traces of a past we believed already written, but which still offers us new discoveries and astonishing new realities, such as the founding date being much earlier than 1775 — the year commonly known and passed down.
As I write, I can confidently state that on August 9, 1741, Bocca was granted the honour of displaying the coat of arms of the city of Cuneo on its bookseller and printer's sign — source that leads us from Asti to Cuneo and moves the founding date from 1775 back to 1741. It also tells us that Bocca was the successor to Benentino, who died in 1730, the last heir of a family of printers and booksellers active since the second half of the 17th century.
So, what can one say? Seek and you shall find! Today, Bocca finds its place in the marvellous setting of the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele, thanks to the foresight of a City Council dedicated to preserving, maintaining, and safeguarding this small yet significant Milanese institution, recognizing its merit in maintaining continuity!
Giorgio Lodetti

The history of the Family and the Bookstore is collected in the book, with texts in Italian and English: Historical Archives of a Family of Milanese Booksellers, Libreria Bocca from the 18th Century!

Title: Giorgio P. Lodetti on Instagram: "Still together, with Centuries-Old Historical Roots!
.
May, Anno Domini 2025
250th Anniversary of the Bocca Bookstore, the oldest bookstore in Italy, located at Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II 12 since September 29, 1936.

Significant numbers, dates, years, months, and days for a historic institution that has spanned over two and a half centuries of Italian history, with branches in Turin, Milan, Florence, Rome, and Paris — in a not yet united Europe.

Letters, texts, images, books, series, edicts, posters, and proclamations fade into the mists of time — published, printed, sold, and curated by the Bocca Family, booksellers and printers in Piedmont since the early decades of the 18th century — are today being brought back to light by the Lodetti Family, who persist in carrying forward a meaningful tradition that continues to amaze and inspire us.
We are following the traces of a past we believed already written, but which still offers us new discoveries and astonishing new realities, such as the founding date being much earlier than 1775 — the year commonly known and passed down.
As I write, I can confidently state that on August 9, 1741, Bocca was granted the honour of displaying the coat of arms of the city of Cuneo on its bookseller and printer's sign — source that leads us from Asti to Cuneo and moves the founding date from 1775 back to 1741. It also tells us that Bocca was the successor to Benentino, who died in 1730, the last heir of a family of printers and booksellers active since the second half of the 17th century.
So, what can one say? Seek and you shall find! Today, Bocca finds its place in the marvellous setting of the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele, thanks to the foresight of a City Council dedicated to preserving, maintaining, and safeguarding this small yet significant Milanese institution, recognizing its merit in maintaining continuity!
Giorgio Lodetti

The history of the Family and the Bookstore is collected in the book, with texts in Italian and English: Historical Archives of a Family of Milanese Booksellers, Libreria Bocca from the 18th Century!

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Bookshop_in_Much_Wenlock.jpg/250px-Bookshop_in_Much_Wenlock.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bookshop_in_Much_Wenlock.jpg)

The selling of [books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book "Book") dates back to ancient times. The founding of [libraries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libraries "Libraries") in c.300 BC stimulated the energies of the [Athenian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athenian "Athenian")[booksellers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booksellers "Booksellers"). In [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome"), toward the end of the [republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic"), it became the fashion to have a library, and Roman booksellers carried on a flourishing trade.

## Greek and Roman booksellers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_bookselling&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Greek and Roman booksellers")]

In the book of [Jeremiah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremiah "Jeremiah") the prophet is represented as dictating to Baruch the scribe, who described the mode in which his book was written. These scribes were the earliest booksellers, and supplied copies as they were demanded. [Aristotle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle") possessed a somewhat extensive library, and [Plato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plato "Plato") is recorded to have paid the large sum of one hundred [minae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mina_(unit) "Mina (unit)") for three small treatises of [Philolaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philolaus "Philolaus") the [Pythagorean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagoreanism "Pythagoreanism"). When the [Alexandrian library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandrian_library "Alexandrian library") was founded about 300 BC, various expedients were used for the purpose of procuring books, and this appears to have stimulated the energies of the [Athenian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens") booksellers. In [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"), toward the end of the republic, it became the fashion to have a library as part of the household furniture. Roman booksellers carried on a flourishing trade. Their shops (_taberna librarii_) were chiefly in the [Argiletum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argiletum "Argiletum"), and in the Vicus Sandalarius. On the door, or on the side posts, was a list of the books on sale; and [Martial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial "Martial"), who mentions this also, says that a copy of his First Book of Epigrams might be purchased for five [denarii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denarii "Denarii"). In the time of [Augustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus "Augustus") the great booksellers were the Sosii. According to [Justinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justinian "Justinian"), a law was passed granting to the scribes the ownership of the material written; this may be the beginnings of the modern law of [copyright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright "Copyright").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

## Islamic bookshops

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_bookselling&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Islamic bookshops")]

[Abbasid Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Caliphate "Abbasid Caliphate") in the east and [Caliphate of Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphate_of_C%C3%B3rdoba "Caliphate of Córdoba") in the west, encouraged the development of bookshops, copyists, and book dealers across the entire [Muslim world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_world "Muslim world"), in Islāmic cities such as [Damascus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damascus "Damascus"), [Baghdad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baghdad "Baghdad"), and [Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B3rdoba,_Spain "Córdoba, Spain"). According to _[Encyclopædia Britannica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encyclop%C3%A6dia\_Britannica "Encyclopædia Britannica")_:

> Scholars and students spent many hours in these bookshop schools reading, examining, and studying available books or purchasing favourite selections for their private libraries. Book dealers traveled to famous bookstores in search of rare manuscripts for purchase and resale to collectors and scholars and thus contributed to the spread of learning. Many such manuscripts found their way to private libraries of famous Muslim scholars such as [Avicenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avicenna "Avicenna"), [al-Ghazālī](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Ghazali "Al-Ghazali"), and [al-Fārābī](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Farabi "Al-Farabi"), who in turn made their homes centres of scholarly pursuits for their favourite students.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-2)

There is a popular turn of phrase from the 1960s, "Books are written in [Cairo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo "Cairo"), published in [Beirut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beirut "Beirut"), and read in [Baghdad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baghdad "Baghdad")".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-4) One of the most famous and prestigious Arab publishers is Dar al-Asab.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-5)

## French booksellers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_bookselling&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: French booksellers")]

The first wave of French booksellers came soon after [Johannes Gutenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Gutenberg "Johannes Gutenberg") introduced his new printing technologies in Europe. The oldest known bookstore still opened in France (and Europe) is the Librairie Nouvelle d'Orléans. Its owner in 1545 was Étienne Rouzeau,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-6) it now belongs to publisher [Albin Michel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albin_Michel "Albin Michel").

_The Book-Hunter in Paris_ by [Octave Uzanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octave_Uzanne "Octave Uzanne") explores second hand and used booksellers and stalls in Paris during the late 19th century.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-7)

The [Société typographique de Neuchâtel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soci%C3%A9t%C3%A9_typographique_de_Neuch%C3%A2tel "Société typographique de Neuchâtel") sales representative, Jean-François Favarger, made several tours of France and Switzerland, selling books and negotiating deals with booksellers in 1775–1776.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-8)

In 1810 Napoleon created a system by which, a would-be bookseller had to apply for a license (brevet), and supply four references testifying to his morality, and four confirmations of his professional ability to perform the job. All references had to be certified by the local mayor. If the application was accepted, the bookseller would have to swear an oath of loyalty to the régime. The application process was conducted to ensure that the new bookstore was not a place that distributed rebellious publications. The brevet process continued until 1870.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-9)

## Christianity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_bookselling&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Christianity")]

The spread of [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") naturally created a great demand for copies of the [Gospels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel "Gospel"), other sacred books, and later on for missals and other devotional volumes for both church and private use. Before the [Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Reformation "Protestant Reformation") and the introduction of printing, scribes and stationers who sold books formed guilds. Some of these stationers had stations built against the walls of cathedrals.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1) Besides the sworn stationers there were many booksellers in [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford "Oxford") who were not sworn; for one of the statutes, passed in 1373, expressly states that, in consequence of their presence,

> [B]ooks of great value are sold and carried away from Oxford, the owners of them are cheated, and the sworn stationers are deprived of their lawful business. It was, therefore, enacted that no bookseller except two sworn stationers or their deputies, should sell any book being either his own property or that of another, exceeding half a mark in value, under a pain of imprisonment, or, if the offence was repeated, of forfeiting his trade within the university.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-10)

## Modern bookselling

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_bookselling&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Modern bookselling")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/02/Caen_maisonchibourg_flickr.jpg/250px-Caen_maisonchibourg_flickr.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Caen_maisonchibourg_flickr.jpg)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/El_Ateneo_Bookstore.jpg/250px-El_Ateneo_Bookstore.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:El_Ateneo_Bookstore.jpg)

[El Ateneo Grand Splendid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Ateneo_Grand_Splendid "El Ateneo Grand Splendid") bookstore in [Buenos Aires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buenos_Aires "Buenos Aires"), [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina")

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/Eglise_des_Dominicains_20190111_08.jpg/250px-Eglise_des_Dominicains_20190111_08.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eglise_des_Dominicains_20190111_08.jpg)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/de/Gare_Metz_d%C3%A9cor_20.png/250px-Gare_Metz_d%C3%A9cor_20.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gare_Metz_d%C3%A9cor_20.png)

In many parts of the world, bookstores—like this one in the [train station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Train_station "Train station") in [Metz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metz "Metz"), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France")—are often found in transport facilities.

The modern system of bookselling dates from soon after the introduction of [printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing "Printing"). Through the new mechanized process for printing, books became more affordable.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-11) By the nineteenth century, the model of bookselling as we know it began to emerge. A professional group of booksellers in [Leipzig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leipzig "Leipzig") decided to form their own association in 1824, and in 1825 the [Börsenverein der Deutschen Buchhändler zu Leipzig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%B6rsenverein_der_Deutschen_Buchh%C3%A4ndler_zu_Leipzig?action=edit&redlink=1 "Börsenverein der Deutschen Buchhändler zu Leipzig (page does not exist)")[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%B6rsenverein%20der%20Deutschen%20Buchh%C3%A4ndler%20zu%20Leipzig "de:Börsenverein der Deutschen Buchhändler zu Leipzig")] became the first group to publish outside of the printer's guilds, leading to more people joining the profession without needing to be attached to a guild.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-12)[_[need quotation to verify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] The earliest printers were also [editors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Editing "Editing") and booksellers; but being unable to sell every copy of the works they printed, they had agents at most of the seats of learning, such as [Anton Koberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_Koberger "Anton Koberger"), who introduced the art of printing into [Nuremberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuremberg "Nuremberg") in 1470. The most common types of books printed in large quantities were able to be cheaply produced like [catechisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catechisms "Catechisms") and [almanacs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almanacs "Almanacs") and often not bound at all.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-13)

The religious dissensions of the [Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation "Reformation") in 16th-century continental Europe and the [English Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Reformation "English Reformation") in [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") under [Henry VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII "Henry VIII") and [Edward VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_VI "Edward VI") fostered a great demand for books; but in England governments of both the [Tudor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Tudor "House of Tudor") and [Stuart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Stuart "House of Stuart") dynasties feared a [free press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_press "Freedom of the press") and made various efforts to control the distribution of printed materials.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

The first patent for the office of king's printer was granted to [Thomas Berthelet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Berthelet "Thomas Berthelet") by [Henry VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII "Henry VIII") in 1529, but only such books as were first licensed were to be printed. At that time even the purchase or possession of an unlicensed book was a punishable offense. In 1556 the [Company of Stationers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Company_of_Stationers "Company of Stationers") was [incorporated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incorporation_(business) "Incorporation (business)"), and very extensive powers were granted in order that obnoxious books might be repressed. In the following reigns the [Star Chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Chamber "Star Chamber") exercised a rather effectual censorship; but, in spite of all precautions, such was the demand for books of a [polemical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polemic "Polemic") nature, that entrepreneurs and subversives printed many abroad and surreptitiously introduced them into England.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

In the course of the 16th and 17th centuries the Low Countries for a time became the chief centre of the bookselling world, and many of the folios and quartos in their libraries bear the names of Jansen, Blauw or [Plantin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plantin_Press "Plantin Press"), with the imprint of [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam"), [Utrecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utrecht "Utrecht"), [Leiden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leiden "Leiden") or [Antwerp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antwerp "Antwerp"), while the [Elzevirs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Elzevir "House of Elzevir") produced - besides other works - pocket classics. The southern towns of [Douai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douai "Douai") and [Saint-Omer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Omer "Saint-Omer") (both in present-day France) at the same time furnished polemical works in English.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

Queen [Elizabeth I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_I "Elizabeth I") (r.1558–1603) interfered little with books except when they emanated from [Roman Catholics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholics "Roman Catholics"), or touched upon her royal prerogatives; and towards the end of her reign, and during that of her successor, [James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_VI_and_I "James VI and I") (r.1603–1625), bookselling flourished. So much had bookselling increased during [the Protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Protectorate "The Protectorate") of 1653–1659 that in 1658 [William London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_London "William London") published _A Catalogue of the most Vendible Books in England_. A bad time immediately followed. Although there were provincial booksellers, the centre of the trade was [St. Paul's Churchyard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul's_Churchyard "St. Paul's Churchyard"). When the [Great Fire of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London "Great Fire of London") began in 1666 the booksellers put most of their stock in the vaults of the church, where it was destroyed. The [Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Restoration "English Restoration") of 1660 restored the office of Licenser of the Press, which continued until 1694.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

The first British copyright statute, the [Statute of Anne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_Anne "Statute of Anne") (1709), which specially relates to booksellers, enacted that, if any person shall think the published price of a book unreasonably high, he may make a complaint to the [Archbishop of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_Canterbury "Archbishop of Canterbury"), and to certain other persons named, who shall examine his complaint, and if well founded reduce the price; and any bookseller charging more than the price so fixed shall be fined [£](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_pound "English pound")5 for every copy sold. The complaint procedure prescribed in this statute was apparently never used.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

Modern book-selling has changed dramatically with the advent of the computer. With major websites such as [Amazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon.com "Amazon.com"), [eBay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EBay "EBay"), and other [book distributors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_book_distributors "List of book distributors") offering [affiliate programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affiliate_programs "Affiliate programs"), book sales can be facilitated through an [affiliate program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affiliate_program "Affiliate program").

## Selling and publishing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_bookselling&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Selling and publishing")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/Borders_bookshelf.jpg/250px-Borders_bookshelf.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Borders_bookshelf.jpg)

Books on a table in a [Borders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borders_(retailer) "Borders (retailer)") store in [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"), USA. Borders stores started closing in 2010.

For later times it is necessary to make a gradual distinction between _booksellers_, whose trade consists in selling books, either by retail or wholesale, and _[publishers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publisher "Publisher")_, whose business involves the production of the books from the author's [manuscripts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuscript "Manuscript"), and who are the intermediaries between author and bookseller, just as the booksellers (in the restricted sense) are intermediaries between the author and publisher and the public. The convenience of this distinction is not impaired by the fact either that a publisher is also a wholesale bookseller, or that a still more recent development in publishing started a reaction to some extent in the way of amalgamating the two functions. The scheme of _The Times_ Book Club (started in 1905) was, again, a combination of a subscription library with the business of bookselling and it brought the organization of a [newspaper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newspaper "Newspaper"), with all its means of achieving publicity, into the work of promoting the sale of books, in a way which practically introduced a new factor into the bookselling business.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

[James Lackington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lackington "James Lackington") is credited as the person responsible for changing this profession. His bookshop, known as The Temple of the Muses, was in Finsbury Square in north London.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-14)

### Specialty developments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_bookselling&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section:  Specialty developments")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Modern_paperback_spines_of_NHK_Books_in_Tokyo_20040116.jpg/330px-Modern_paperback_spines_of_NHK_Books_in_Tokyo_20040116.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Modern_paperback_spines_of_NHK_Books_in_Tokyo_20040116.jpg)

Books in a Tokyo bookstore

See also: [Antiquarian Booksellers Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiquarian_Booksellers_Association "Antiquarian Booksellers Association")

During the 19th century it remains the fact that the distinction between publisher and bookseller—literary promoter and shopkeeper—became fundamental. The booksellers, as such, were engaged either in wholesale bookselling, or in the retail, the old or [second-hand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second-hand "Second-hand") (now includes rare and very old books trade, called **antiquarian books**), and the [periodicals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodical "Periodical") publishing or retailing trades.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

Coming between the publisher and the retail bookseller is the important distributing agency of the _wholesale bookseller_. It is to him that the retailer and libraries look for supplies, as it is impossible to stock all of the books published. [Paternoster Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paternoster_Row "Paternoster Row"), [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), was for over a hundred years the centre of this industry, where retail booksellers, busily engaged in obtaining the books ordered by the book-buying public. It is where the publisher calls first on showing or "subscribing" a new book, a critical process, for by the number thus ordered the fate of a book is sometimes determined.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1) In the United States, [Baker & Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker_&_Taylor "Baker & Taylor") is a major distributor.

What may be termed the third partner in publishing is the _retail bookseller_; and to protect their interests there was established in 1890 a London booksellers' society, which had for its object the restriction of discounts to 25%, and also to arrange prices generally and control all details connected with the trade. The society a few years afterwards widened its field of operations so as to include the whole of the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), and it became "The Associated Booksellers of Great Britain and Ireland."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

## Bookselling in the United States

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_bookselling&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Bookselling in the United States")]

See also: [Antiquarian book trade in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiquarian_book_trade_in_the_United_States "Antiquarian book trade in the United States") and [Books in the United States §Bookselling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Books_in_the_United_States#Bookselling "Books in the United States")

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Tattered-cover-16th-st.jpg/250px-Tattered-cover-16th-st.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tattered-cover-16th-st.jpg)

The [Tattered Cover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tattered_Cover "Tattered Cover") is a bookstore in Denver, Colorado, and one of the largest [independent bookstores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_bookstore "Independent bookstore") in the United States.

The history of bookselling in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") is of special interest. The [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain") settlements drew away from the old country much of its enterprise and best talent, and the presses of [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico") and other cities teemed with publications mostly of a religious character, but many others, especially linguistic and historical, were also published. Bookselling in the United States was of a somewhat later growth, although printing and bookselling was introduced into [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts"), as early as 1640 by [Hezekiah Usher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hezekiah_Usher "Hezekiah Usher") and by Usher in 1652 in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"). Bookselling was happening in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") in 1685, and [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") in 1693. [Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Franklin "Ben Franklin") had served to make the trade illustrious, yet few persons were engaged in it at the commencement of the 19th century. Books chiefly for scholars and libraries were imported from [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe"); but after the [War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_1812 "War of 1812") printing-presses multiplied rapidly, and with the spread of newspapers and education there also arose a demand for books, and publishers set to work to secure the advantages offered by the wide field of English literature, the whole of which they had the liberty of reaping free of all cost beyond that of production. The works of [Walter Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Scott "Walter Scott"), [Lord Byron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Byron "Lord Byron"), [Thomas Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Moore "Thomas Moore"), [Robert Southey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Southey "Robert Southey"), [William Wordsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wordsworth "William Wordsworth"), and indeed of every author of note, were reprinted without the smallest payment to author or proprietor. Half the names of the authors in the so-called "American" catalogue of books printed between 1820 and 1852 are British. These titles were made available and affordable to the public. In consequence of the [Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), the high price of labour, and the restrictive duties laid on in order to protect native industry, coupled with the frequent dealings with England, a great change took place, and American publishers and booksellers, while there was still no international copyright, made liberal offers for early sheets of new publications. Boston, New York and Philadelphia still retained their old supremacy as bookselling centres. Meanwhile, the distinct publishing business also grew, until gradually the conditions of business became assimilated to those of Europe.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

### African-American booksellers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_bookselling&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: African-American booksellers")]

Bookselling is a profession historically dominated by white Americans, but African Americans developed their own tradition of book selling, particularly in conjunction with radical political movements such as abolitionism, black nationalism, Black Power, and Marxism. The first documented [African American bookstore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American_Bookstores "African-American Bookstores") was owned and operated by the abolitionist [David Ruggles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Ruggles "David Ruggles") in the 1830s in New York City. In the years of the civil rights and Black Power era of the 1950s and 1960s, [Lewis Michaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Michaux "Lewis Michaux")'s National Memorial African Bookstore became arguably the most prominent Black-owned bookstore in the United States. In the 1980s and '90s, Clara Villarosa's Hue Man Books became the most prominent Black-owned bookstore in the nation, first in Denver and later in Harlem.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-15)

The selling of [books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book "Book") dates back to ancient times. The founding of [libraries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libraries "Libraries") in c.300 BC stimulated the energies of the [Athenian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athenian "Athenian")[booksellers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booksellers "Booksellers"). In [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome"), toward the end of the [republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic"), it became the fashion to have a library, and Roman booksellers carried on a flourishing trade.

## Greek and Roman booksellers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_bookselling&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Greek and Roman booksellers")]

In the book of [Jeremiah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremiah "Jeremiah") the prophet is represented as dictating to Baruch the scribe, who described the mode in which his book was written. These scribes were the earliest booksellers, and supplied copies as they were demanded. [Aristotle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle") possessed a somewhat extensive library, and [Plato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plato "Plato") is recorded to have paid the large sum of one hundred [minae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mina_(unit) "Mina (unit)") for three small treatises of [Philolaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philolaus "Philolaus") the [Pythagorean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagoreanism "Pythagoreanism"). When the [Alexandrian library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandrian_library "Alexandrian library") was founded about 300 BC, various expedients were used for the purpose of procuring books, and this appears to have stimulated the energies of the [Athenian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens") booksellers. In [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"), toward the end of the republic, it became the fashion to have a library as part of the household furniture. Roman booksellers carried on a flourishing trade. Their shops (_taberna librarii_) were chiefly in the [Argiletum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argiletum "Argiletum"), and in the Vicus Sandalarius. On the door, or on the side posts, was a list of the books on sale; and [Martial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial "Martial"), who mentions this also, says that a copy of his First Book of Epigrams might be purchased for five [denarii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denarii "Denarii"). In the time of [Augustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus "Augustus") the great booksellers were the Sosii. According to [Justinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justinian "Justinian"), a law was passed granting to the scribes the ownership of the material written; this may be the beginnings of the modern law of [copyright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright "Copyright").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

## Islamic bookshops

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_bookselling&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Islamic bookshops")]

[Abbasid Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Caliphate "Abbasid Caliphate") in the east and [Caliphate of Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphate_of_C%C3%B3rdoba "Caliphate of Córdoba") in the west, encouraged the development of bookshops, copyists, and book dealers across the entire [Muslim world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_world "Muslim world"), in Islāmic cities such as [Damascus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damascus "Damascus"), [Baghdad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baghdad "Baghdad"), and [Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B3rdoba,_Spain "Córdoba, Spain"). According to _[Encyclopædia Britannica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encyclop%C3%A6dia\_Britannica "Encyclopædia Britannica")_:

> Scholars and students spent many hours in these bookshop schools reading, examining, and studying available books or purchasing favourite selections for their private libraries. Book dealers traveled to famous bookstores in search of rare manuscripts for purchase and resale to collectors and scholars and thus contributed to the spread of learning. Many such manuscripts found their way to private libraries of famous Muslim scholars such as [Avicenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avicenna "Avicenna"), [al-Ghazālī](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Ghazali "Al-Ghazali"), and [al-Fārābī](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Farabi "Al-Farabi"), who in turn made their homes centres of scholarly pursuits for their favourite students.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-2)

There is a popular turn of phrase from the 1960s, "Books are written in [Cairo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo "Cairo"), published in [Beirut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beirut "Beirut"), and read in [Baghdad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baghdad "Baghdad")".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-4) One of the most famous and prestigious Arab publishers is Dar al-Asab.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-5)

## French booksellers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_bookselling&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: French booksellers")]

The first wave of French booksellers came soon after [Johannes Gutenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Gutenberg "Johannes Gutenberg") introduced his new printing technologies in Europe. The oldest known bookstore still opened in France (and Europe) is the Librairie Nouvelle d'Orléans. Its owner in 1545 was Étienne Rouzeau,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-6) it now belongs to publisher [Albin Michel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albin_Michel "Albin Michel").

_The Book-Hunter in Paris_ by [Octave Uzanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octave_Uzanne "Octave Uzanne") explores second hand and used booksellers and stalls in Paris during the late 19th century.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-7)

The [Société typographique de Neuchâtel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soci%C3%A9t%C3%A9_typographique_de_Neuch%C3%A2tel "Société typographique de Neuchâtel") sales representative, Jean-François Favarger, made several tours of France and Switzerland, selling books and negotiating deals with booksellers in 1775–1776.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-8)

In 1810 Napoleon created a system by which, a would-be bookseller had to apply for a license (brevet), and supply four references testifying to his morality, and four confirmations of his professional ability to perform the job. All references had to be certified by the local mayor. If the application was accepted, the bookseller would have to swear an oath of loyalty to the régime. The application process was conducted to ensure that the new bookstore was not a place that distributed rebellious publications. The brevet process continued until 1870.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-9)

## Christianity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_bookselling&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Christianity")]

The spread of [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") naturally created a great demand for copies of the [Gospels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel "Gospel"), other sacred books, and later on for missals and other devotional volumes for both church and private use. Before the [Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Reformation "Protestant Reformation") and the introduction of printing, scribes and stationers who sold books formed guilds. Some of these stationers had stations built against the walls of cathedrals.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1) Besides the sworn stationers there were many booksellers in [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford "Oxford") who were not sworn; for one of the statutes, passed in 1373, expressly states that, in consequence of their presence,

> [B]ooks of great value are sold and carried away from Oxford, the owners of them are cheated, and the sworn stationers are deprived of their lawful business. It was, therefore, enacted that no bookseller except two sworn stationers or their deputies, should sell any book being either his own property or that of another, exceeding half a mark in value, under a pain of imprisonment, or, if the offence was repeated, of forfeiting his trade within the university.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-10)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_bookselling&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Modern bookselling")]
