In many parts of the world, bookstores—like this one in the [train station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Train_station "Train station") in [Metz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metz "Metz"), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France")—are often found in transport facilities.

The modern system of bookselling dates from soon after the introduction of [printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing "Printing"). Through the new mechanized process for printing, books became more affordable.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-11) By the nineteenth century, the model of bookselling as we know it began to emerge. A professional group of booksellers in [Leipzig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leipzig "Leipzig") decided to form their own association in 1824, and in 1825 the [Börsenverein der Deutschen Buchhändler zu Leipzig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%B6rsenverein_der_Deutschen_Buchh%C3%A4ndler_zu_Leipzig?action=edit&redlink=1 "Börsenverein der Deutschen Buchhändler zu Leipzig (page does not exist)")[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%B6rsenverein%20der%20Deutschen%20Buchh%C3%A4ndler%20zu%20Leipzig "de:Börsenverein der Deutschen Buchhändler zu Leipzig")] became the first group to publish outside of the printer's guilds, leading to more people joining the profession without needing to be attached to a guild.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-12)[_[need quotation to verify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] The earliest printers were also [editors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Editing "Editing") and booksellers; but being unable to sell every copy of the works they printed, they had agents at most of the seats of learning, such as [Anton Koberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_Koberger "Anton Koberger"), who introduced the art of printing into [Nuremberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuremberg "Nuremberg") in 1470. The most common types of books printed in large quantities were able to be cheaply produced like [catechisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catechisms "Catechisms") and [almanacs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almanacs "Almanacs") and often not bound at all.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-13)

The religious dissensions of the [Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation "Reformation") in 16th-century continental Europe and the [English Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Reformation "English Reformation") in [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") under [Henry VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII "Henry VIII") and [Edward VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_VI "Edward VI") fostered a great demand for books; but in England governments of both the [Tudor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Tudor "House of Tudor") and [Stuart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Stuart "House of Stuart") dynasties feared a [free press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_press "Freedom of the press") and made various efforts to control the distribution of printed materials.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

The first patent for the office of king's printer was granted to [Thomas Berthelet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Berthelet "Thomas Berthelet") by [Henry VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII "Henry VIII") in 1529, but only such books as were first licensed were to be printed. At that time even the purchase or possession of an unlicensed book was a punishable offense. In 1556 the [Company of Stationers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Company_of_Stationers "Company of Stationers") was [incorporated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incorporation_(business) "Incorporation (business)"), and very extensive powers were granted in order that obnoxious books might be repressed. In the following reigns the [Star Chamber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Chamber "Star Chamber") exercised a rather effectual censorship; but, in spite of all precautions, such was the demand for books of a [polemical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polemic "Polemic") nature, that entrepreneurs and subversives printed many abroad and surreptitiously introduced them into England.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

In the course of the 16th and 17th centuries the Low Countries for a time became the chief centre of the bookselling world, and many of the folios and quartos in their libraries bear the names of Jansen, Blauw or [Plantin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plantin_Press "Plantin Press"), with the imprint of [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam"), [Utrecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utrecht "Utrecht"), [Leiden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leiden "Leiden") or [Antwerp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antwerp "Antwerp"), while the [Elzevirs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Elzevir "House of Elzevir") produced - besides other works - pocket classics. The southern towns of [Douai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douai "Douai") and [Saint-Omer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Omer "Saint-Omer") (both in present-day France) at the same time furnished polemical works in English.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

Queen [Elizabeth I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_I "Elizabeth I") (r.1558–1603) interfered little with books except when they emanated from [Roman Catholics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholics "Roman Catholics"), or touched upon her royal prerogatives; and towards the end of her reign, and during that of her successor, [James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_VI_and_I "James VI and I") (r.1603–1625), bookselling flourished. So much had bookselling increased during [the Protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Protectorate "The Protectorate") of 1653–1659 that in 1658 [William London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_London "William London") published _A Catalogue of the most Vendible Books in England_. A bad time immediately followed. Although there were provincial booksellers, the centre of the trade was [St. Paul's Churchyard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul's_Churchyard "St. Paul's Churchyard"). When the [Great Fire of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London "Great Fire of London") began in 1666 the booksellers put most of their stock in the vaults of the church, where it was destroyed. The [Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Restoration "English Restoration") of 1660 restored the office of Licenser of the Press, which continued until 1694.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

The first British copyright statute, the [Statute of Anne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_Anne "Statute of Anne") (1709), which specially relates to booksellers, enacted that, if any person shall think the published price of a book unreasonably high, he may make a complaint to the [Archbishop of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_Canterbury "Archbishop of Canterbury"), and to certain other persons named, who shall examine his complaint, and if well founded reduce the price; and any bookseller charging more than the price so fixed shall be fined [£](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_pound "English pound")5 for every copy sold. The complaint procedure prescribed in this statute was apparently never used.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

Modern book-selling has changed dramatically with the advent of the computer. With major websites such as [Amazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon.com "Amazon.com"), [eBay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EBay "EBay"), and other [book distributors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_book_distributors "List of book distributors") offering [affiliate programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affiliate_programs "Affiliate programs"), book sales can be facilitated through an [affiliate program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affiliate_program "Affiliate program").

## Selling and publishing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_bookselling&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Selling and publishing")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/Borders_bookshelf.jpg/250px-Borders_bookshelf.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Borders_bookshelf.jpg)

Books on a table in a [Borders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borders_(retailer) "Borders (retailer)") store in [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"), USA. Borders stores started closing in 2010.

For later times it is necessary to make a gradual distinction between _booksellers_, whose trade consists in selling books, either by retail or wholesale, and _[publishers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publisher "Publisher")_, whose business involves the production of the books from the author's [manuscripts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuscript "Manuscript"), and who are the intermediaries between author and bookseller, just as the booksellers (in the restricted sense) are intermediaries between the author and publisher and the public. The convenience of this distinction is not impaired by the fact either that a publisher is also a wholesale bookseller, or that a still more recent development in publishing started a reaction to some extent in the way of amalgamating the two functions. The scheme of _The Times_ Book Club (started in 1905) was, again, a combination of a subscription library with the business of bookselling and it brought the organization of a [newspaper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newspaper "Newspaper"), with all its means of achieving publicity, into the work of promoting the sale of books, in a way which practically introduced a new factor into the bookselling business.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

[James Lackington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lackington "James Lackington") is credited as the person responsible for changing this profession. His bookshop, known as The Temple of the Muses, was in Finsbury Square in north London.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-14)

### Specialty developments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_bookselling&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section:  Specialty developments")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Modern_paperback_spines_of_NHK_Books_in_Tokyo_20040116.jpg/330px-Modern_paperback_spines_of_NHK_Books_in_Tokyo_20040116.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Modern_paperback_spines_of_NHK_Books_in_Tokyo_20040116.jpg)

Books in a Tokyo bookstore

See also: [Antiquarian Booksellers Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiquarian_Booksellers_Association "Antiquarian Booksellers Association")

During the 19th century it remains the fact that the distinction between publisher and bookseller—literary promoter and shopkeeper—became fundamental. The booksellers, as such, were engaged either in wholesale bookselling, or in the retail, the old or [second-hand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second-hand "Second-hand") (now includes rare and very old books trade, called **antiquarian books**), and the [periodicals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodical "Periodical") publishing or retailing trades.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

Coming between the publisher and the retail bookseller is the important distributing agency of the _wholesale bookseller_. It is to him that the retailer and libraries look for supplies, as it is impossible to stock all of the books published. [Paternoster Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paternoster_Row "Paternoster Row"), [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), was for over a hundred years the centre of this industry, where retail booksellers, busily engaged in obtaining the books ordered by the book-buying public. It is where the publisher calls first on showing or "subscribing" a new book, a critical process, for by the number thus ordered the fate of a book is sometimes determined.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1) In the United States, [Baker & Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker_&_Taylor "Baker & Taylor") is a major distributor.

What may be termed the third partner in publishing is the _retail bookseller_; and to protect their interests there was established in 1890 a London booksellers' society, which had for its object the restriction of discounts to 25%, and also to arrange prices generally and control all details connected with the trade. The society a few years afterwards widened its field of operations so as to include the whole of the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), and it became "The Associated Booksellers of Great Britain and Ireland."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

## Bookselling in the United States

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_bookselling&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Bookselling in the United States")]

See also: [Antiquarian book trade in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiquarian_book_trade_in_the_United_States "Antiquarian book trade in the United States") and [Books in the United States §Bookselling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Books_in_the_United_States#Bookselling "Books in the United States")

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Tattered-cover-16th-st.jpg/250px-Tattered-cover-16th-st.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tattered-cover-16th-st.jpg)

The [Tattered Cover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tattered_Cover "Tattered Cover") is a bookstore in Denver, Colorado, and one of the largest [independent bookstores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_bookstore "Independent bookstore") in the United States.

The history of bookselling in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") is of special interest. The [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain") settlements drew away from the old country much of its enterprise and best talent, and the presses of [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico") and other cities teemed with publications mostly of a religious character, but many others, especially linguistic and historical, were also published. Bookselling in the United States was of a somewhat later growth, although printing and bookselling was introduced into [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts"), as early as 1640 by [Hezekiah Usher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hezekiah_Usher "Hezekiah Usher") and by Usher in 1652 in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"). Bookselling was happening in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") in 1685, and [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") in 1693. [Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Franklin "Ben Franklin") had served to make the trade illustrious, yet few persons were engaged in it at the commencement of the 19th century. Books chiefly for scholars and libraries were imported from [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe"); but after the [War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_1812 "War of 1812") printing-presses multiplied rapidly, and with the spread of newspapers and education there also arose a demand for books, and publishers set to work to secure the advantages offered by the wide field of English literature, the whole of which they had the liberty of reaping free of all cost beyond that of production. The works of [Walter Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Scott "Walter Scott"), [Lord Byron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Byron "Lord Byron"), [Thomas Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Moore "Thomas Moore"), [Robert Southey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Southey "Robert Southey"), [William Wordsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wordsworth "William Wordsworth"), and indeed of every author of note, were reprinted without the smallest payment to author or proprietor. Half the names of the authors in the so-called "American" catalogue of books printed between 1820 and 1852 are British. These titles were made available and affordable to the public. In consequence of the [Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), the high price of labour, and the restrictive duties laid on in order to protect native industry, coupled with the frequent dealings with England, a great change took place, and American publishers and booksellers, while there was still no international copyright, made liberal offers for early sheets of new publications. Boston, New York and Philadelphia still retained their old supremacy as bookselling centres. Meanwhile, the distinct publishing business also grew, until gradually the conditions of business became assimilated to those of Europe.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-EB1911-1)

### African-American booksellers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_bookselling&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: African-American booksellers")]

Bookselling is a profession historically dominated by white Americans, but African Americans developed their own tradition of book selling, particularly in conjunction with radical political movements such as abolitionism, black nationalism, Black Power, and Marxism. The first documented [African American bookstore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American_Bookstores "African-American Bookstores") was owned and operated by the abolitionist [David Ruggles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Ruggles "David Ruggles") in the 1830s in New York City. In the years of the civil rights and Black Power era of the 1950s and 1960s, [Lewis Michaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Michaux "Lewis Michaux")'s National Memorial African Bookstore became arguably the most prominent Black-owned bookstore in the United States. In the 1980s and '90s, Clara Villarosa's Hue Man Books became the most prominent Black-owned bookstore in the nation, first in Denver and later in Harlem.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_bookselling#cite_note-15)

W ith almost 20 years of bookselling experience behind me and (hopefully) a good many more to come, compiling a list of fictional booksellers appeared at first to be an effortless task, but after a little research I was astonished to find out quite how many books have been set in bookshops.

[![Image 14](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/271/0*RtUOxyISDyj-erc3)](https://amzn.to/2xzqG1r)

Purchase the book

I suppose there’s a kind of romance associated with the place where old books await a new life in fresh hands, and a sense that a place that contains thousands of stories bound within the books on its shelves should be a natural home to the setting of a story.

My book, [_The Diary of a Bookseller_](https://amzn.to/2xzqG1r), recounts a year of buying and selling books in my shop in rural Scotland, but there is a world of other tales set in and around bookshops. Below are some of my favorites booksellers in fiction:

![Image 15](https://electricliterature.com/electric-lit/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/1*OSmKo9FBbPdpvOYrG7muIg.png)
#### **Comic Book Guy from The Simpsons**

Stereotype one— the ‘know-it-all’ sneering bookseller who appears to care less about making sales than he does about making his customers feel stupid. The creators of The Simpsons creators have distilled the most obvious characteristics of the obsessive into a character who is both odious and pitiable in equal measure. Comic Book Guy’s passion for his subject it matched only by his contempt for his customers, and in many respects this reflects the reason why people who are passionate about their subject find it frustrating dealing with others who are less well informed than they are.

[![Image 16](https://electricliterature.com/electric-lit/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/1*P1TRi1vKBbNrLBvfQe8R4w.jpeg)](https://amzn.to/2QRKV3k)
#### **_John Baxter from_**[**_The Intimate Thoughts of John Baxter_**](https://amzn.to/2QRKV3k)**_, Bookseller by Augustus Muir_**

Although Muir attempted to pass this off as a genuine diary, it quickly becomes obvious from reading it that this is a work of fiction, and Baxter — charming, knowledgeable, frustrated, and vaguely incompetent — is Muir’s parody of the booksellers he encountered in Edinburgh at the time in which he wrote it. Booksellers in fiction appear to conform to one of several stereotypes, and Muir’s protagonist certainly conforms to the most obvious; the autodidact who believes that his hard-learned knowledge entitles him to a better life than the lot he has been cast. Despite the inevitable bitterness that accompanies such a character, Baxter is someone to whom it is impossible not to warm as the book unfolds, and his final realization that he is content with his quiet life in a small Scottish bookshop comes as no surprise at the conclusion of the book.

#### **Dean Corso from The Ninth Gate based on**[The Club Dumas](https://amzn.to/2MNhSdZ) by **Arturo Perez-Reverte, translated by Sonia Soto**

Another stereotype manifests itself — this time it is of the unscrupulous book dealer Dean Corso (played by Johnny Depp). No depths of dishonesty and manipulation are too low for Corso to sink in his avarice, and the premise of the story is that Depp’s bookseller is charged with acquiring the three remaining copies of a 17th century book which — when put together — contain the requisite information to summon the devil. Corso’s character in the film throws into relief the moral dilemma faced by booksellers on a daily basis; what are you prepared to sell in order to make a living, even if it conflicts with your own beliefs. Corso, though, appears to be so devoid of a magnetic field in his moral compass that this doesn’t seem to cause him any problems.

[![Image 19](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/293/0*LUfc-KDDBGx-Fuyc)](https://amzn.to/2pl7Jvx)
#### [**The Shadow of the Wind**](https://amzn.to/2pl7Jvx)**by Carlos Ruis**Zafón**, translated by Lucia Graves**

This is less about a fictional bookseller, and more about a fictional book. And another one about the devil, but this time the protagonist is a young boy whose father (an antiquarian bookseller) takes him to a secret library in post-Civil War Barcelona to pick a book which he has to protect for the rest of his life. The story is utterly spellbinding, and the message about the power of books — although far from subtle — is something which both booksellers and readers have found hard to resist.

#### **Florence from**[**The Bookshop**](https://amzn.to/2xyeY78)**by Penelope Fitzgerald**

This is a book which — I have to confess — I haven’t read. The film, though, I have watched, and as a bookseller found a little two-dimensional. Florence (the widow around whom the story is based) moves to rural Suffolk to open a bookshop in a building which the upstanding elders of the town have earmarked for use as a centre for the arts. She finds herself embroiled in a conflict with them, employing the daughter of a poor family (who she turns into a bibliophile) and being almost rescued from financial ruin by a reclusive aristocrat but ultimately losing her fight to keep her shop open.

[![Image 21](https://electricliterature.com/electric-lit/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/1*3h2_rFe4MjN88Tw3N9y4pA.jpeg)](https://amzn.to/2NXbqW9)
#### [**The Private Papers of a Bankrupt Bookseller**](https://amzn.to/2NXbqW9)**by Will Y Darling**

Darling’s bookseller is — like John Baxter — a fictional creation. The melancholy essays which make up the book were purportedly written by a man who — after suffering the trauma of the First World War — decided to open a bookshop. In the foreword, the author (under the guise of a character known only as X. Z. E) describes the bookseller as having been ‘hit on the head in the War’ as a possible explanation for why he decided to become a bookseller. The essays are at times poignant, at others unspeakably funny. Even Darling’s foreword (to the foreword — there are two) is brilliantly understated. In describing how the bankrupt bookseller committed suicide, Darling explains how, on being notified of his impending financial catastrophe, he ended his life by putting his head in a gas stove; ‘The gas was full on and not lighted. The stove was one of the new kind — more like an ordinary grate than the upright sort’, paying more attention to the detail of the stove than the tragedy with which it was associated.

![Image 22](https://electricliterature.com/electric-lit/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/1*cJXovgeKExMYoZu9X0IgJg.jpeg)
#### **Bernard Black from Black Books**

No list of fictional booksellers would be complete without the inclusion of Bernard Black, Dylan Moran’s superbly drawn character from the 18 episodes of this fine comedy series. Cranky, irascible, frequently drunk and with little or no patience for his customers, Bernard is the fictional bookseller with whom I most readily identify. The observations and detail made by the writers (Moran and Graham Lenahan) are precise and accurate, and the other members of the cast — Manny and Fran provide the eccentric characters who are the perfect foil to Bernard’s incessant fury at the world and his customers in particular.

# A Real-Life Bookseller Weighs In on 7 Fictional Ones

#### Shaun Bythell examines the stereotypes of booksellers in pop culture

![Image 11](https://electricliterature.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/1*kSAhkLKjDN9BOpVw17J6KA.jpeg)

###### Oct 5, 2018

##### [Shaun Bythell](https://electricliterature.com/el-author/shaun-bythell/)

W ith almost 20 years of bookselling experience behind me and (hopefully) a good many more to come, compiling a list of fictional booksellers appeared at first to be an effortless task, but after a little research I was astonished to find out quite how many books have been set in bookshops.

[![Image 14](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/271/0*RtUOxyISDyj-erc3)](https://amzn.to/2xzqG1r)

Purchase the book

I suppose there’s a kind of romance associated with the place where old books await a new life in fresh hands, and a sense that a place that contains thousands of stories bound within the books on its shelves should be a natural home to the setting of a story.

My book, [_The Diary of a Bookseller_](https://amzn.to/2xzqG1r), recounts a year of buying and selling books in my shop in rural Scotland, but there is a world of other tales set in and around bookshops. Below are some of my favorites booksellers in fiction:

![Image 15](https://electricliterature.com/electric-lit/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/1*OSmKo9FBbPdpvOYrG7muIg.png)
#### **Comic Book Guy from The Simpsons**

Stereotype one— the ‘know-it-all’ sneering bookseller who appears to care less about making sales than he does about making his customers feel stupid. The creators of The Simpsons creators have distilled the most obvious characteristics of the obsessive into a character who is both odious and pitiable in equal measure. Comic Book Guy’s passion for his subject it matched only by his contempt for his customers, and in many respects this reflects the reason why people who are passionate about their subject find it frustrating dealing with others who are less well informed than they are.

[![Image 16](https://electricliterature.com/electric-lit/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/1*P1TRi1vKBbNrLBvfQe8R4w.jpeg)](https://amzn.to/2QRKV3k)
#### **_John Baxter from_**[**_The Intimate Thoughts of John Baxter_**](https://amzn.to/2QRKV3k)**_, Bookseller by Augustus Muir_**

Although Muir attempted to pass this off as a genuine diary, it quickly becomes obvious from reading it that this is a work of fiction, and Baxter — charming, knowledgeable, frustrated, and vaguely incompetent — is Muir’s parody of the booksellers he encountered in Edinburgh at the time in which he wrote it. Booksellers in fiction appear to conform to one of several stereotypes, and Muir’s protagonist certainly conforms to the most obvious; the autodidact who believes that his hard-learned knowledge entitles him to a better life than the lot he has been cast. Despite the inevitable bitterness that accompanies such a character, Baxter is someone to whom it is impossible not to warm as the book unfolds, and his final realization that he is content with his quiet life in a small Scottish bookshop comes as no surprise at the conclusion of the book.

![Image 18](https://electricliterature.com/electric-lit/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/1*KNeWbGp0q_kDvQ3KTmky4w.png)
#### **Dean Corso from The Ninth Gate based on**[The Club Dumas](https://amzn.to/2MNhSdZ) by **Arturo Perez-Reverte, translated by Sonia Soto**

Another stereotype manifests itself — this time it is of the unscrupulous book dealer Dean Corso (played by Johnny Depp). No depths of dishonesty and manipulation are too low for Corso to sink in his avarice, and the premise of the story is that Depp’s bookseller is charged with acquiring the three remaining copies of a 17th century book which — when put together — contain the requisite information to summon the devil. Corso’s character in the film throws into relief the moral dilemma faced by booksellers on a daily basis; what are you prepared to sell in order to make a living, even if it conflicts with your own beliefs. Corso, though, appears to be so devoid of a magnetic field in his moral compass that this doesn’t seem to cause him any problems.

[![Image 19](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/293/0*LUfc-KDDBGx-Fuyc)](https://amzn.to/2pl7Jvx)
#### [**The Shadow of the Wind**](https://amzn.to/2pl7Jvx)**by Carlos Ruis**Zafón**, translated by Lucia Graves**

This is less about a fictional bookseller, and more about a fictional book. And another one about the devil, but this time the protagonist is a young boy whose father (an antiquarian bookseller) takes him to a secret library in post-Civil War Barcelona to pick a book which he has to protect for the rest of his life. The story is utterly spellbinding, and the message about the power of books — although far from subtle — is something which both booksellers and readers have found hard to resist.

[12 Fictional Bookstores We Wish Were Real](https://electricliterature.com/12-fictional-bookstores-we-wish-were-real-5f4314c9ff5d)

![Image 20](https://electricliterature.com/electric-lit/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/1*RZJCZ0M1AWmEXvA5lli4JA.jpeg)
#### **Florence from**[**The Bookshop**](https://amzn.to/2xyeY78)**by Penelope Fitzgerald**

This is a book which — I have to confess — I haven’t read. The film, though, I have watched, and as a bookseller found a little two-dimensional. Florence (the widow around whom the story is based) moves to rural Suffolk to open a bookshop in a building which the upstanding elders of the town have earmarked for use as a centre for the arts. She finds herself embroiled in a conflict with them, employing the daughter of a poor family (who she turns into a bibliophile) and being almost rescued from financial ruin by a reclusive aristocrat but ultimately losing her fight to keep her shop open.

[![Image 21](https://electricliterature.com/electric-lit/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/1*3h2_rFe4MjN88Tw3N9y4pA.jpeg)](https://amzn.to/2NXbqW9)
#### [**The Private Papers of a Bankrupt Bookseller**](https://amzn.to/2NXbqW9)**by Will Y Darling**

Darling’s bookseller is — like John Baxter — a fictional creation. The melancholy essays which make up the book were purportedly written by a man who — after suffering the trauma of the First World War — decided to open a bookshop. In the foreword, the author (under the guise of a character known only as X. Z. E) describes the bookseller as having been ‘hit on the head in the War’ as a possible explanation for why he decided to become a bookseller. The essays are at times poignant, at others unspeakably funny. Even Darling’s foreword (to the foreword — there are two) is brilliantly understated. In describing how the bankrupt bookseller committed suicide, Darling explains how, on being notified of his impending financial catastrophe, he ended his life by putting his head in a gas stove; ‘The gas was full on and not lighted. The stove was one of the new kind — more like an ordinary grate than the upright sort’, paying more attention to the detail of the stove than the tragedy with which it was associated.

![Image 22](https://electricliterature.com/electric-lit/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/1*cJXovgeKExMYoZu9X0IgJg.jpeg)
#### **Bernard Black from Black Books**

No list of fictional booksellers would be complete without the inclusion of Bernard Black, Dylan Moran’s superbly drawn character from the 18 episodes of this fine comedy series. Cranky, irascible, frequently drunk and with little or no patience for his customers, Bernard is the fictional bookseller with whom I most readily identify. The observations and detail made by the writers (Moran and Graham Lenahan) are precise and accurate, and the other members of the cast — Manny and Fran provide the eccentric characters who are the perfect foil to Bernard’s incessant fury at the world and his customers in particular.

![Image 23](https://electricliterature.com/electric-lit/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/1*1yg7_kHrD3Qs0qayytptEw.png)
#### About the Author

Shaun Bythell is the owner of The Bookshop in Wigtown, Scotland — Scotland’s largest second-hand bookshop — and is the author of _The Diary of a Bookseller._

### **_The Pilgrim’s Progress_ by John Bunyan, illustrated by Clarke Hutton**

_The Pilgrim’s Progress: from this world to that which is to come delivered under the similitude of a dream_ by John Bunyan has never been out-of-print since its first publication in 1678 and is one of the most reprinted books ever. It has also been produced in a dizzying number of different editions. These multifarious reprints and different editions started multiplying almost immediately after the first publication.Wikipedia tells us:

_“There were**eleven editions**of the first part in John Bunyan's lifetime, published in successive years from 1678 to 1685 and in 1688, and there were two editions of the second part, published in 1684 and 1686.”_

Modern day rare book dealers, Adrian Harrington can update this to some extent:

_“The Pilgrim's Progress became one of the most published books in the English language; 1,300 editions having been printed by 1938, 250 years after the author's death.”_

It probably wouldn’t be an outlandish guess to think that by the time I sat down to start writing this short piece, the number of editions probably exceed 5,000.

It is, of course, a famous Christian allegory and its accessibility in dramatizing Biblical sermonizing probably accounts not just for the number of editions (it’s always been a favourite of prize giving, especially in Sunday Schools, for children) but also for the number that are illustrated editions. Illustrating the text expands the reading audience for those who rely on the illustrations to supplement some of the difficulties they may face with literacy skills.

But it’s not Bunyan’s text I’m interested in here but a very specific edition I have picked up, published by SCM Press Limited in 1947 and which is superbly illustrated by Clarke Hutton.

SCM Press is, of course, a specialist Christian publisher that appears to be still flourishing today. I love it when the publisher respects the reader and gives full details of the production values:

_“The lithographed illustrations were drawn direct on the plate by the artist. The type is Perpetua, designed by Eric Gill, printed on paper supplied by A. Archibald & Co., and bound by James Burn & Co. The book as a whole was designed by John R. Biggs. Printed in Great Britain by W.S. Cowell Limited at Butter Market, Ipswich in 1947.”_

Reference to the lithographed illustrations brings us on to the work of Clarke Hutton. The University of [Warwick Art Collection website](https://warwick.ac.uk/services/art/artist/clarkehutton/)gives us a useful potted biography:

_“Born: 1898. Died: 1966. Nationality: British._

_Hutton became one of the most eminent and influential book illustrators of his time. Early in his career he had worked with the celebrated theatre designer William Pitcher before enrolling at the Central School of Arts and Crafts to study lithography with A S Hartrick who, on his retirement in 1929, was replaced by Hutton._

_He experimented in the auto-lithography process in which the artist’s designs drawn directly onto the plate are printed on a mechanical off-set litho press. His aim was to find a process for making high volume, affordable, colour illustrations for children’s books and he was instrumental in the establishment of the highly successful Puffin imprint for Penguin Books. He also wrote and illustrated the 1945 classic of children’s books A Picture History of Britain, which ranged from pre-history to the 1940s. The Oxford University Press issued a facsimile edition of this in 2007._

_Hutton also exhibited paintings at the Royal Academy, the London Group, the Royal Institute of Painters in Watercolours, the Redfern Gallery and elsewhere. The British Museum, the Tate Gallery, the Victoria & Albert Museum and National Gallery of Canada are among public collections which hold examples of his work.”_

But the full flavour of Hutton’s work can be seen in the excellent gallery provided at [Fishink](https://fishinkblog.com/2020/03/09/clarke-hutton-mid-century-illustration/)where the full splendour of the artist’s mid-century influences are dazzling.

In this edition he provides 15 full page, full colour illustrations and a host of part page drawings and vignettes.

By contrast with some of the hefty Victorian editions with their rather forbidding black/white/grey engravings, this book positively zings with colour and life – the quality of the art adding substantially to the text and bringing with it a new freshness in reading a story you’ll probably have some familiarity with. Bunyan’s allegory has given the English language so many phrases that we have absorbed into common usage and reading, Pilgrim’s story is a cultural must even if, like me, you’re not a believer in the Christian message.

Copies can be found on the second hand market and you'll pick up a good copy with a jacket for between £10 and £15.

Terry Potter

### **_The Pilgrim’s Progress_ by John Bunyan, illustrated by Clarke Hutton**

_The Pilgrim’s Progress: from this world to that which is to come delivered under the similitude of a dream_ by John Bunyan has never been out-of-print since its first publication in 1678 and is one of the most reprinted books ever. It has also been produced in a dizzying number of different editions. These multifarious reprints and different editions started multiplying almost immediately after the first publication.Wikipedia tells us:

_“There were**eleven editions**of the first part in John Bunyan's lifetime, published in successive years from 1678 to 1685 and in 1688, and there were two editions of the second part, published in 1684 and 1686.”_

Modern day rare book dealers, Adrian Harrington can update this to some extent:

_“The Pilgrim's Progress became one of the most published books in the English language; 1,300 editions having been printed by 1938, 250 years after the author's death.”_

It probably wouldn’t be an outlandish guess to think that by the time I sat down to start writing this short piece, the number of editions probably exceed 5,000.

It is, of course, a famous Christian allegory and its accessibility in dramatizing Biblical sermonizing probably accounts not just for the number of editions (it’s always been a favourite of prize giving, especially in Sunday Schools, for children) but also for the number that are illustrated editions. Illustrating the text expands the reading audience for those who rely on the illustrations to supplement some of the difficulties they may face with literacy skills.

But it’s not Bunyan’s text I’m interested in here but a very specific edition I have picked up, published by SCM Press Limited in 1947 and which is superbly illustrated by Clarke Hutton.

SCM Press is, of course, a specialist Christian publisher that appears to be still flourishing today. I love it when the publisher respects the reader and gives full details of the production values:

_“The lithographed illustrations were drawn direct on the plate by the artist. The type is Perpetua, designed by Eric Gill, printed on paper supplied by A. Archibald & Co., and bound by James Burn & Co. The book as a whole was designed by John R. Biggs. Printed in Great Britain by W.S. Cowell Limited at Butter Market, Ipswich in 1947.”_

Reference to the lithographed illustrations brings us on to the work of Clarke Hutton. The University of [Warwick Art Collection website](https://warwick.ac.uk/services/art/artist/clarkehutton/)gives us a useful potted biography:

_“Born: 1898. Died: 1966. Nationality: British._

_Hutton became one of the most eminent and influential book illustrators of his time. Early in his career he had worked with the celebrated theatre designer William Pitcher before enrolling at the Central School of Arts and Crafts to study lithography with A S Hartrick who, on his retirement in 1929, was replaced by Hutton._

_He experimented in the auto-lithography process in which the artist’s designs drawn directly onto the plate are printed on a mechanical off-set litho press. His aim was to find a process for making high volume, affordable, colour illustrations for children’s books and he was instrumental in the establishment of the highly successful Puffin imprint for Penguin Books. He also wrote and illustrated the 1945 classic of children’s books A Picture History of Britain, which ranged from pre-history to the 1940s. The Oxford University Press issued a facsimile edition of this in 2007._

_Hutton also exhibited paintings at the Royal Academy, the London Group, the Royal Institute of Painters in Watercolours, the Redfern Gallery and elsewhere. The British Museum, the Tate Gallery, the Victoria & Albert Museum and National Gallery of Canada are among public collections which hold examples of his work.”_

But the full flavour of Hutton’s work can be seen in the excellent gallery provided at [Fishink](https://fishinkblog.com/2020/03/09/clarke-hutton-mid-century-illustration/)where the full splendour of the artist’s mid-century influences are dazzling.

In this edition he provides 15 full page, full colour illustrations and a host of part page drawings and vignettes.

By contrast with some of the hefty Victorian editions with their rather forbidding black/white/grey engravings, this book positively zings with colour and life – the quality of the art adding substantially to the text and bringing with it a new freshness in reading a story you’ll probably have some familiarity with. Bunyan’s allegory has given the English language so many phrases that we have absorbed into common usage and reading, Pilgrim’s story is a cultural must even if, like me, you’re not a believer in the Christian message.

Copies can be found on the second hand market and you'll pick up a good copy with a jacket for between £10 and £15.

Terry Potter

March 2022

# The Pilgrim's Progress: The Second Part (eBook)

### ![Image 5](https://www.monergism.com/sites/default/files/content_images/2018/pilgrims_progress_second_part_john_bunyan800.jpg)Author: John Bunyan

### Available editions:  
[ePub](https://www.monergism.com/thethreshold/sdg/bunyan/Pilgrim's%20Progress_%20Part%20Two%20-%20John%20Bunyan.epub)|[.mobi](https://www.monergism.com/thethreshold/sdg/bunyan/Pilgrim's%20Progress_%20Part%20Two%20-%20John%20Bunyan.mobi)|[.pdf](https://www.monergism.com/thethreshold/sdg/bunyan/Pilgrim's%20Progress_Part%202_John%20Bunyan_crowdedship.pdf)

John Bunyan’s _The Pilgrim’s Progress: The Second Part_ is a masterful continuation of his iconic allegory, where the journey of Christian’s wife, Christiana, and their children unfolds in vivid and spiritually rich detail. First published in 1684, this work presents a heartfelt portrayal of grace and redemption as Christiana, once resistant to Christian's pilgrimage, embarks on her own journey to the Celestial City, accompanied by her sons and her faithful companion, Mercy.

This sequel not only mirrors the triumphs and struggles of Christian's path but also adds unique dimensions by emphasizing the communal and familial aspects of faith. Readers will be drawn to Christiana’s transformation—from guilt-stricken widow to determined pilgrim—as she navigates trials with courage and humility. Along the way, new characters such as Great-Heart, Mercy, and Mr. Ready-to-Halt illuminate the story with their unique virtues, each offering insights into the perseverance required of believers. The text intertwines action-packed encounters with powerful spiritual truths, making it both an engaging narrative and a profound devotional tool.

What sets _The Second Part_ apart is its rich portrayal of community, compassion, and the collective strength of believers united by faith. Through the lens of Christiana and her companions, Bunyan weaves themes of grace, forgiveness, and the joy of walking together toward the promise of eternal life. The story offers encouragement for families, highlighting how the faith of one can ripple out to transform others.

Readers will find themselves captivated not only by the compelling allegory but also by Bunyan’s ability to address deep theological truths with simplicity and emotional depth. This sequel stands as a timeless treasure, inviting individuals, families, and church communities to reflect on their journey of faith, the obstacles they face, and the hope that sustains them.

Whether you are a longtime admirer of Bunyan’s work or a new reader, _The Pilgrim’s Progress: The Second Part_ is a must-read for those seeking spiritual encouragement and inspiration. It reminds us that no pilgrim walks alone, and that every journey, no matter how challenging, is undergirded by the grace and mercy of God.

# The Pilgrim's Progress: The Second Part (eBook)

### ![Image 5](https://www.monergism.com/sites/default/files/content_images/2018/pilgrims_progress_second_part_john_bunyan800.jpg)Author: John Bunyan

### Available editions:  
[ePub](https://www.monergism.com/thethreshold/sdg/bunyan/Pilgrim's%20Progress_%20Part%20Two%20-%20John%20Bunyan.epub)|[.mobi](https://www.monergism.com/thethreshold/sdg/bunyan/Pilgrim's%20Progress_%20Part%20Two%20-%20John%20Bunyan.mobi)|[.pdf](https://www.monergism.com/thethreshold/sdg/bunyan/Pilgrim's%20Progress_Part%202_John%20Bunyan_crowdedship.pdf)

John Bunyan’s _The Pilgrim’s Progress: The Second Part_ is a masterful continuation of his iconic allegory, where the journey of Christian’s wife, Christiana, and their children unfolds in vivid and spiritually rich detail. First published in 1684, this work presents a heartfelt portrayal of grace and redemption as Christiana, once resistant to Christian's pilgrimage, embarks on her own journey to the Celestial City, accompanied by her sons and her faithful companion, Mercy.

This sequel not only mirrors the triumphs and struggles of Christian's path but also adds unique dimensions by emphasizing the communal and familial aspects of faith. Readers will be drawn to Christiana’s transformation—from guilt-stricken widow to determined pilgrim—as she navigates trials with courage and humility. Along the way, new characters such as Great-Heart, Mercy, and Mr. Ready-to-Halt illuminate the story with their unique virtues, each offering insights into the perseverance required of believers. The text intertwines action-packed encounters with powerful spiritual truths, making it both an engaging narrative and a profound devotional tool.

What sets _The Second Part_ apart is its rich portrayal of community, compassion, and the collective strength of believers united by faith. Through the lens of Christiana and her companions, Bunyan weaves themes of grace, forgiveness, and the joy of walking together toward the promise of eternal life. The story offers encouragement for families, highlighting how the faith of one can ripple out to transform others.

Readers will find themselves captivated not only by the compelling allegory but also by Bunyan’s ability to address deep theological truths with simplicity and emotional depth. This sequel stands as a timeless treasure, inviting individuals, families, and church communities to reflect on their journey of faith, the obstacles they face, and the hope that sustains them.

Whether you are a longtime admirer of Bunyan’s work or a new reader, _The Pilgrim’s Progress: The Second Part_ is a must-read for those seeking spiritual encouragement and inspiration. It reminds us that no pilgrim walks alone, and that every journey, no matter how challenging, is undergirded by the grace and mercy of God.

WHEN at the first I took my pen in hand Thus for to write, I did not understand That I at all should make a little book In such a mode: nay, I had undertook To make another, which when almost done, Before I was aware, I this begun. And thus it was: I, writing of the way And race of saints in this our gospel day, Fell suddenly into an allegory About their journey and the way to glory, In more than twenty things, which I set down. This done, I twenty more had in my crown; And they again began to multiply, Like sparks that from the coals of fire do fly. Nay, then, thought I, if that you breed so fast, I’ll put you by yourselves, lest you at last Should prove ad infinitum , and eat out The book that I already am about. Well, so I did: but yet I did not think To show to all the world my pen and ink. 8 The Pilgrim’s Progress 

This book it chalks out before thine eyes, The man that seeks the everlasting prize: It shows you whence he comes, whither he goes, What he leaves undone; also what he does. It also shows you how he runs, and runs Till he unto the gate of glory comes. It shows too who set out for life amain, As if the lasting crown they would attain: Here also you may see the reason why They lose their labor, and like fools do die. This book will make a traveler of thee, If by its counsel thou wilt ruled be. It will direct thee to the Holy Land, If thou wilt its directions understand. Yea, it will make the slothful active be; The blind also delightful things to see. Then read my fancies; they will stick like burrs And may be, to the helpless, comforters. This book is writ in such a dialect, As may the minds of listless men affect: It seems a novelty, and yet contains Nothing but sound and honest gospel strains. > 1

The jail. Mr. Bunyan wrote this precious book in Bedford jail, where he was impris-oned 12 years for preaching the gospel. His bonds were those of the gospel; and like Peter, he could sleep soundly in prison. Blessed be God for even the toleration and religious privileges we now enjoy in consequence of it. Our author, thus pre-vented from preaching, turned his thoughts to writing; and during his confine-ment, composed The Pilgrim’s Progress and many other useful works. Thus the Lord causes “the wrath of man to praise Him” (Psa 76:10). The servants of Christ, when restrained by wicked laws from publishing the Word of life from the pulpit, have become more abundantly useful by their writings—(G. Burder). 2 You will observe what honour, from his Pilgrim’s first setting out, Bunyan puts upon the Word of God. He would give to no inferior instrumentality, not even to one of God’s providences, the business of awakening his Pilgrim to a sense of his danger; but he places him before us reading his book, awakened by the Word. And he makes the first efficacious [i.e., effective] motive in the mind of this Pilgrim a salutary fear of the terrors of that Word, a sense of the wrath to come, beneath the burden of sin upon his soul—(Cheever, Lect. 6). The alarms of such an awakened soul are very different from the terrors of superstitious ignorance, which, arising from fright or danger, are easily quitted with the silly mummeries of priestcraft—(Andronicus). 3 “What shall I do?” This is his first exclamation. He has not as yet advanced so far as to say, What shall I do to be saved ? (Act 16:30)—(Cheever, Lect. 6).

We go about the world in the daytime and are absorbed in earthly schemes; the world is as bright as a rainbow, and it bears for us no marks or predictions of the Judg-ment, or of our sins; and conscience is retired, as it were, within a far inner circle of the soul. But when it comes night, and the pall of sleep is drawn over the senses, then conscience comes out solemnly, and walks about in the silent chambers of the soul. [It] makes her survey and her comments, and sometimes sits down and sternly reads the record of a life that the waking man would never look into, and the catalogue of crimes that are gathering for the Judgment. Imagination walks tremblingly behind her, and they pass through the open gate of the Scriptures into the eternal world—for thither all things in man’s being naturally and irresistibly tend. WHEN at the first I took my pen in hand Thus for to write, I did not understand That I at all should make a little book In such a mode: nay, I had undertook To make another, which when almost done, Before I was aware, I this begun. And thus it was: I, writing of the way And race of saints in this our gospel day, Fell suddenly into an allegory About their journey and the way to glory, In more than twenty things, which I set down. This done, I twenty more had in my crown; And they again began to multiply, Like sparks that from the coals of fire do fly. Nay, then, thought I, if that you breed so fast, I’ll put you by yourselves, lest you at last Should prove ad infinitum , and eat out The book that I already am about. Well, so I did: but yet I did not think To show to all the world my pen and ink. 8 The Pilgrim’s Progress 

This book it chalks out before thine eyes, The man that seeks the everlasting prize: It shows you whence he comes, whither he goes, What he leaves undone; also what he does. It also shows you how he runs, and runs Till he unto the gate of glory comes. It shows too who set out for life amain, As if the lasting crown they would attain: Here also you may see the reason why They lose their labor, and like fools do die. This book will make a traveler of thee, If by its counsel thou wilt ruled be. It will direct thee to the Holy Land, If thou wilt its directions understand. Yea, it will make the slothful active be; The blind also delightful things to see. Then read my fancies; they will stick like burrs And may be, to the helpless, comforters. This book is writ in such a dialect, As may the minds of listless men affect: It seems a novelty, and yet contains Nothing but sound and honest gospel strains. As I walked through the wilderness of this world, I lighted on a certain place where was a den; 1 and I laid me down in that place to sleep. And as I slept, I dreamed a dream. I dreamed, and behold, “I saw a man clothed with rags, standing in a certain place, with his face from his own house, a book in his hand, and a great burden upon his back” (Isa 64:6; Luk 14:33; Psa 38:4; Hab 2:2; Act 16:31). I looked, and saw him open the book 2 and read therein. And as he read, he wept and trembled; and not being able longer to contain, he brake out with a lamentable cry, saying, “What shall I do?” (Act 2:37). 3

> 1

The jail. Mr. Bunyan wrote this precious book in Bedford jail, where he was impris-oned 12 years for preaching the gospel. His bonds were those of the gospel; and like Peter, he could sleep soundly in prison. Blessed be God for even the toleration and religious privileges we now enjoy in consequence of it. Our author, thus pre-vented from preaching, turned his thoughts to writing; and during his confine-ment, composed The Pilgrim’s Progress and many other useful works. Thus the Lord causes “the wrath of man to praise Him” (Psa 76:10). The servants of Christ, when restrained by wicked laws from publishing the Word of life from the pulpit, have become more abundantly useful by their writings—(G. Burder). 2 You will observe what honour, from his Pilgrim’s first setting out, Bunyan puts upon the Word of God. He would give to no inferior instrumentality, not even to one of God’s providences, the business of awakening his Pilgrim to a sense of his danger; but he places him before us reading his book, awakened by the Word. And he makes the first efficacious [i.e., effective] motive in the mind of this Pilgrim a salutary fear of the terrors of that Word, a sense of the wrath to come, beneath the burden of sin upon his soul—(Cheever, Lect. 6). The alarms of such an awakened soul are very different from the terrors of superstitious ignorance, which, arising from fright or danger, are easily quitted with the silly mummeries of priestcraft—(Andronicus). 3 “What shall I do?” This is his first exclamation. He has not as yet advanced so far as to say, What shall I do to be saved ? (Act 16:30)—(Cheever, Lect. 6).

We go about the world in the daytime and are absorbed in earthly schemes; the world is as bright as a rainbow, and it bears for us no marks or predictions of the Judg-ment, or of our sins; and conscience is retired, as it were, within a far inner circle of the soul. But when it comes night, and the pall of sleep is drawn over the senses, then conscience comes out solemnly, and walks about in the silent chambers of the soul. [It] makes her survey and her comments, and sometimes sits down and sternly reads the record of a life that the waking man would never look into, and the catalogue of crimes that are gathering for the Judgment. Imagination walks tremblingly behind her, and they pass through the open gate of the Scriptures into the eternal world—for thither all things in man’s being naturally and irresistibly tend. Our dreams sometimes reveal our character, our sins, our destinies, more clearly than our waking thoughts; for by day the energies of our being are turned into artificial channels, by night our thoughts follow the bent that is most natural to them. # Pilgrim's Progress - What We Learn From It

[Zac Poonen](https://sermonindex.net/speakers/zac-poonen/)· 1:58:55 

**Zac Poonen's sermon explores the profound lessons from Pilgrim's Progress, emphasizing the journey of faith, the burden of sin, and the importance of the Holy Spirit in understanding salvation.**  
This sermon reflects on the timeless wisdom found in the Christian classic 'Pilgrim's Progress' by John Bunyan, highlighting the author's humility and God's honor upon his work. It emphasizes the importance of genuine fellowship with like-minded believers, the dangers of pride and taking shortcuts in the Christian journey, and the ultimate reward of enduring faith until the end to receive the crown of life.

## Full Transcript

One of the most popular Christian books that have ever been published is a book called Pilgrim's Progress. I think it's been translated into over 200 languages and next to the Bible is probably the most widely circulated Christian book. And I want to tell you a little bit about the author.

The reason why God allowed this book to remain for 350 years and to be so widely circulated was because God honored this man who wrote it. God sees where someone has known him and has written something that's really valuable. He makes sure it's circulated widely.

So his name was John Bunyan and even though he wrote a book which was the most widely circulated, he never made money from it. That's the best part of it. I don't know whether all of you realize that authors who write books get money for the books they write from their publishers.

Of course, CFC is different. We don't get anything. But almost all Christian authors, 99% of them, receive money and many of them become millionaires.

Many of the songs you sing here are written by Christian songwriters who have become millionaires just by selling those songs. And through my 55 years of being a Christian, I found that the best books are written by those who didn't make money from it. John Bunyan, Watchman Nee, A.W. Tozer, people like that.

And the best songs are written by those who didn't make money from it. Like Fanny Crosby, Charles Wesley and all the others. It's God and money that's always in competition with each other.

We are living in a world today where in Christianity people are trying to make money. And that's why I like to read those books written by people who wrote because they loved God, not because they wanted to make money. Who wrote songs because they loved God, not because they wanted to make money.

Now many of you probably don't have that discernment, but I do. And I know the songs I love to sing. Those which come from my heart who loved God because I'm not interested in the tune, I'm interested in the words.

In the same way in a book, I don't look at the cover. To look at the tune of a song is like looking at the cover of a book. The content.

And so here was a man and he was poor. It was not that he had so much money that he could live on. He was a poor man.

His job was repairing pots and pans in people's kitchens. He'd go house to house and repair pots and pans. That was his job.

He was a very poor man. His wife died when he was 30 years old, leaving four children, one of whom was blind. And he had this little meeting in a house, John Bunyan, where he would meet with people.

And in those days, the law in England was that if you're not ordained by a bishop of the Church of England, you cannot preach. And if you preach, you'll be imprisoned. That was the king's law.

And so you'd be in prison for three months, provided you don't preach again. So they imprisoned John Bunyan for three months. But he said, I'm going to preach.

As soon as you let me out, I'll preach again. So they locked him up. He was married a second time, and his poor wife was left outside with four children, one of them blind.

So poor that other believers had to give her money to support herself. This is the type of man who wrote this book. A man who suffered, and he ultimately stayed nearly 12 years in jail, in prison, just because he said, I want to preach the gospel.

And if you don't let me preach the gospel, you can lock me up. But, you know, here's another man who wrote something wonderful and didn't make money. The Apostle Paul, like all the other apostles.

Most widely circulated literature. The Bible is the most widely circulated book in the world, and these authors never made any money from it. Paul was locked up in prison, and that's why he wrote a number of his letters.

And John Bunyan was locked up in prison, and he wrote, more than once, he was in prison. And in one of those imprisons, he wrote Pilgrim's Progress. And it's been such a challenge to people throughout all these years.

Finally, after 12 years, the king let him go. So, let's turn to the first slide which begins the story. Here is a man with a Bible in his hand, with a burden on his back, and a Bible in his hand.

His name is Pilgrim. He read the Bible, and he felt the burden of his sin. Now, a lot of people don't feel the burden of their sin, even though they read the Bible.

Actually, we can feel the burden of our sin just with our conscience. So, he felt the burden of our sin, and how heavy that burden is depends on how sensitive your conscience is. If your conscience is not very sensitive, it's a little, small little bag on your back.

But this man's conscience was so sensitive that it was like a big burden he wanted to get rid of. Do you find a small sin like that, like a big burden? Then you're a true Christian. So, here was one, he had not yet become a Christian, but he had this tremendous burden of sin from his conscience, and he knew that the judgment of God would come upon sin.

That's the other thing people need to recognize, which they don't realize often. And he did not know how to escape. He did not know the Gospel.

So, when he heard this, he's the first people he wanted to save, warn rather, his own family. So, he goes home, and he tells his wife and children about this tremendous judgment of God that's going to come on sin, but they don't have a burden, as you can see. ### Sermon Outline

1.   **I points: - Introduction to Pilgrim's Progress - Significance of John Bunyan - Impact of the book over the years**
2.   **II points: - The burden of sin - Sensitivity of conscience - Importance of recognizing judgment**
3.   **III points: - The journey towards salvation - Opposition from family and friends - The role of Evangelist**
4.   **IV points: - The dangers of compromise - The swamp of discouragement - The importance of perseverance**
5.   **V points: - Misleading advice from worldly wise men - The futility of legalism - The true path to salvation**
6.   **VI points: - The role of the Holy Spirit as interpreter - Lessons from the house of the interpreter - The importance of anointed teachers**
7.   **VII points: - The battle against despair - The need for continuous renewal - The significance of fervent love**

### Frequently Asked Questions

What is the main theme of Pilgrim's Progress?

The main theme revolves around the journey of a Christian towards salvation and the challenges faced along the way.

Who was John Bunyan?

John Bunyan was a poor man and a preacher who authored Pilgrim's Progress while imprisoned for his faith.

What does the burden symbolize?

The burden symbolizes the weight of sin and the need for salvation that every individual must confront.

How does the sermon relate to modern Christianity?

The sermon highlights the ongoing struggle between true faith and the distractions of worldly desires in modern Christianity.

What role does the Holy Spirit play in understanding the Bible?

The Holy Spirit acts as an interpreter, helping believers understand the scriptures and apply them to their lives.

# Pilgrim's Progress - What We Learn From It

[Zac Poonen](https://sermonindex.net/speakers/zac-poonen/)· 1:58:55 

**Zac Poonen's sermon explores the profound lessons from Pilgrim's Progress, emphasizing the journey of faith, the burden of sin, and the importance of the Holy Spirit in understanding salvation.**  
This sermon reflects on the timeless wisdom found in the Christian classic 'Pilgrim's Progress' by John Bunyan, highlighting the author's humility and God's honor upon his work. It emphasizes the importance of genuine fellowship with like-minded believers, the dangers of pride and taking shortcuts in the Christian journey, and the ultimate reward of enduring faith until the end to receive the crown of life.

## Full Transcript

One of the most popular Christian books that have ever been published is a book called Pilgrim's Progress. I think it's been translated into over 200 languages and next to the Bible is probably the most widely circulated Christian book. And I want to tell you a little bit about the author.

The reason why God allowed this book to remain for 350 years and to be so widely circulated was because God honored this man who wrote it. God sees where someone has known him and has written something that's really valuable. He makes sure it's circulated widely.

So his name was John Bunyan and even though he wrote a book which was the most widely circulated, he never made money from it. That's the best part of it. I don't know whether all of you realize that authors who write books get money for the books they write from their publishers.

Of course, CFC is different. We don't get anything. But almost all Christian authors, 99% of them, receive money and many of them become millionaires.

Many of the songs you sing here are written by Christian songwriters who have become millionaires just by selling those songs. And through my 55 years of being a Christian, I found that the best books are written by those who didn't make money from it. John Bunyan, Watchman Nee, A.W. Tozer, people like that.

And the best songs are written by those who didn't make money from it. Like Fanny Crosby, Charles Wesley and all the others. It's God and money that's always in competition with each other.

We are living in a world today where in Christianity people are trying to make money. And that's why I like to read those books written by people who wrote because they loved God, not because they wanted to make money. Who wrote songs because they loved God, not because they wanted to make money.

Now many of you probably don't have that discernment, but I do. And I know the songs I love to sing. Those which come from my heart who loved God because I'm not interested in the tune, I'm interested in the words.

In the same way in a book, I don't look at the cover. To look at the tune of a song is like looking at the cover of a book. The content.

### Sermon Outline

1.   **I points: - Introduction to Pilgrim's Progress - Significance of John Bunyan - Impact of the book over the years**
2.   **II points: - The burden of sin - Sensitivity of conscience - Importance of recognizing judgment**
3.   **III points: - The journey towards salvation - Opposition from family and friends - The role of Evangelist**
4.   **IV points: - The dangers of compromise - The swamp of discouragement - The importance of perseverance**
5.   **V points: - Misleading advice from worldly wise men - The futility of legalism - The true path to salvation**
6.   **VI points: - The role of the Holy Spirit as interpreter - Lessons from the house of the interpreter - The importance of anointed teachers**
7.   **VII points: - The battle against despair - The need for continuous renewal - The significance of fervent love**

### Frequently Asked Questions

What is the main theme of Pilgrim's Progress?

The main theme revolves around the journey of a Christian towards salvation and the challenges faced along the way.

Who was John Bunyan?

John Bunyan was a poor man and a preacher who authored Pilgrim's Progress while imprisoned for his faith.

What does the burden symbolize?

The burden symbolizes the weight of sin and the need for salvation that every individual must confront.

How does the sermon relate to modern Christianity?

The sermon highlights the ongoing struggle between true faith and the distractions of worldly desires in modern Christianity.

What role does the Holy Spirit play in understanding the Bible?

The Holy Spirit acts as an interpreter, helping believers understand the scriptures and apply them to their lives.

# The Author’s Apology for His Book

_WHEN at the first I took my pen in hand_

_Thus for to write, I did not understand_

_That I at all should make a little book_

_In such a mode: nay, I had undertook_

_To make another, which when almost done,_

_Before I was aware, I this begun._

_And thus it was: I, writing of the way_

_And race of saints in this our gospel day,_

_Fell suddenly into an allegory_

_About their journey and the way to glory,_

_In more than twenty things, which I set down._

_This done, I twenty more had in my crown;_

_And they again began to multiply,_

_Like sparks that from the coals of fire do fly._

_Nay, then, thought I, if that you breed so fast,_

_I’ll put you by yourselves, lest you at last_

_Should prove_ ad infinitum _, and eat out_

_The book that I already am about._

_Well, so I did: but yet I did not think_

_To show to all the world my pen and ink._

_This book it chalks out before thine eyes,_

_The man that seeks the everlasting prize:_

_It shows you whence he comes,_

_whither he goes,_

_What he leaves undone; also what he does._

_It also shows you how he runs, and runs_

_Till he unto the gate of glory comes._

_It shows too who set out for life amain,_

_As if the lasting crown they would attain:_

_Here also you may see the reason why_

_They lose their labor, and like fools do die._

_This book will make a traveler of thee,_

_If by its counsel thou wilt ruled be._

_It will direct thee to the Holy Land,_

_If thou wilt its directions understand._

_Yea, it will make the slothful active be;_

_The blind also delightful things to see._

_Then read my fancies; they will stick like burrs_

_And may be, to the helpless, comforters._

_This book is writ in such a dialect,_

_As may the minds of listless men affect:_

_It seems a novelty, and yet contains_

_Nothing but sound and honest gospel strains._

The Pilgrim’s Progress

IN THE SIMILITUDE OF A DREAM

# Christian’s Pilgrimage

#### [The Jail.]

As I walked through the wilderness of this world, I lighted on a certain place where was a den;[[1]](https://johnbunyan.org/en/pilgrims-progress-part-1/#_ftn1) and I laid me down in that place to sleep. And as I slept, I dreamed a dream. I dreamed, and behold, “I saw a man clothed with rags, standing in a certain place, with his face from his own house, a book in his hand, and a great burden upon his back” (Isa 64:6; Luk 14:33; Psa 38:4; Hab 2:2; Act 16:31). I looked, and saw him open the book[[2]](https://johnbunyan.org/en/pilgrims-progress-part-1/#_ftn2) and read therein. And as he read, he wept and trembled; and not being able longer to contain, he brake out with a lamentable cry, saying, “What shall I do?” (Act 2:37).[[3]](https://johnbunyan.org/en/pilgrims-progress-part-1/#_ftn3)

#### [The World.]

In this plight, therefore, he went home, and refrained himself as long as he could, [so] that his wife and children should not perceive his distress. But he could not be silent long, because that his trouble increased. Wherefore at length he brake his mind to his wife and children; and thus he began to talk to them, “O my dear wife,” said he, “and you, the children of my bowels, I, your dear friend, am in myself undone by reason of a burden that lieth hard upon me. Moreover, I am for certain informed that this our city will be burned with fire from heaven; in which fearful overthrow, both myself with thee, my wife, and you, my sweet babes, shall miserably come to ruin—except (the which yet I see not) some way of escape can be found whereby we may be delivered.”

#### [Carnal physic for a sick soul.]

At this, his relations were sore amazed; not for that they believed that what he had said to them was true, but because they thought that some frenzy distemper had got into his head.[[4]](https://johnbunyan.org/en/pilgrims-progress-part-1/#_ftn4) Therefore, it drawing towards night, and they hoping that sleep might settle his brains, with all haste they got him to bed. But the night was as troublesome to him as the day; wherefore, instead of sleeping, he spent it in sighs and tears. So, when the morning was come, they would know how he did. He told them, worse and worse! He also set to talking to them again, but they began to be hardened. They also thought to drive away his distemper by harsh and surly carriages to[[5]](https://johnbunyan.org/en/pilgrims-progress-part-1/#_ftn5) him. Sometimes they would deride, sometimes they would chide, and sometimes they would quite neglect him. Wherefore he began to retire himself to his chamber to pray for and pity them, and also to console his own misery. He would also walk solitarily in the fields, sometimes reading and sometimes praying; and thus for some days he spent his time.[[6]](https://johnbunyan.org/en/pilgrims-progress-part-1/#_ftn6)

Now I saw upon a time, when he was walking in the fields, that he was, as he was wont, reading in his book and greatly distressed in his mind. And as he read, he burst out, as he had done before, crying, “What shall I do to be saved?” (Act 16:30-31).

I saw also that he looked this way and that way, as if he would run; yet he stood still, because, as I perceived, he could not tell which way to go.[[7]](https://johnbunyan.org/en/pilgrims-progress-part-1/#_ftn7) I looked then and saw a man named Evangelist coming to him, who asked, “Wherefore dost thou cry?”

He answered, Sir, I perceive, by the book in my hand, that I am condemned to die, and after that to come to judgment, (Heb 9:27); and I find that I am not willing to do the first (Job 16:21-22), nor able to do the second (Eze 22:14).

Then said Evangelist, Why not willing to die, since this life is attended with so many evils? The man answered, Because I fear that this burden that is upon my back will sink me lower than the grave; and I shall fall into Tophet (Isa 30:33). And, Sir, if I be not fit to go to prison, I am not fit, I am sure, to go to judgment, and from thence to execution; and the thoughts of these things make me cry.

Then said Evangelist, If this be thy condition, why standest thou still? He answered, Because I know not whither to go. Then he gave him a parchment roll, and there was written within, “Fly from the wrath to come” (Mat 3:7).

#### [Christ, and the way to Him, cannot be found without the Word.]

The man therefore, read it, and looking upon Evangelist very carefully, said, Whither must I fly? Then said Evangelist, pointing with his finger over a very wide field, Do you see yonder wicket gate (Mat 7:13)? The man said, No. Then said the other, Do you see yonder shining light (Psa 119:105; 2Pe 1:19)? He said, I think I do. Then said Evangelist, Keep that light in your eye, and go up directly thereto, so shalt thou see the gate; at which, when thou knockest, it shall be told thee what thou shalt do.[[8]](https://johnbunyan.org/en/pilgrims-progress-part-1/#_ftn8) So I saw in my dream that the man began to run. Now, he had not ran far from his own door, but his wife and children, perceiving it, began to cry after him to return (Luk 14:26). But the man put his fingers in his ears, and ran on, crying, Life! Life! Eternal life! So he looked not behind him (Gen 19:17), but fled towards the middle of the plain.[[9]](https://johnbunyan.org/en/pilgrims-progress-part-1/#_ftn9)

# An Unfriendly Neighbor (Obstinate and Pliable)

#### [They that fly from the wrath to come are a gazing-stock to the world.]

The neighbours also came out to see him run, and as he ran, some mocked, others threatened, and some cried after him to return. And among those that did so, there were two that were resolved to fetch him back by force (Jer 20:10). The name of the one was Obstinate, and the name of the other Pliable.[[10]](https://johnbunyan.org/en/pilgrims-progress-part-1/#_ftn10) Now by this time, the man was got a good distance from them. But, however, they were resolved to pursue him; which they did, and in a little time they overtook him. Then said the man, Neighbours, wherefore are ye come? They said, To persuade you to go back with us. But he said, That can by no means be. You dwell, said he, in the City of Destruction, the place also where I was born. I see it to be so; and dying there, sooner or later, you will sink lower than the grave, into a place that burns with fire and brimstone. Be content, good neighbours, and go along with me.

What, said Obstinate, and leave our friends and our comforts behind us?[[11]](https://johnbunyan.org/en/pilgrims-progress-part-1/#_ftn11)
