**Bunhill Fields** is a former burial ground in central London, in the [London Borough of Islington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Islington "London Borough of Islington"), just north of the [City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London "City of London"). What remains is about 1.6 hectares (4.0 acres) in extent[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-CityOfLondon-1) and the bulk of the site is a public garden maintained by the [City of London Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London_Corporation "City of London Corporation").

It was first in devoted use as a burial ground from 1665 until 1854, in which period approximately 123,000 interments were estimated to have taken place.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-nhle-2) Over 2,000 monuments remain, for the most part in concentrated blocks. It was a prototype of land-use protected, nondenominational grounds, and was particularly favoured by [nonconformists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") who passed their final years in the region. It contains the graves of many notable people, including [John Bunyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bunyan "John Bunyan") (died 1688), author of _[The Pilgrim's Progress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Pilgrim's\_Progress "The Pilgrim's Progress")_; [Daniel Defoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Defoe "Daniel Defoe") (died 1731), author of _[Robinson Crusoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinson\_Crusoe "Robinson Crusoe")_; [William Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Blake "William Blake") (died 1827), artist, poet, and mystic; [Susanna Wesley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susanna_Wesley "Susanna Wesley") (died 1742), known as the "Mother of Methodism" through her education of sons [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wesley "John Wesley") and [Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Wesley "Charles Wesley"); [Thomas Bayes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Bayes "Thomas Bayes") (died 1761), statistician and philosopher; [Isaac Watts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Watts "Isaac Watts") (died 1748), the "Father of English [Hymnody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymn "Hymn")"; and [Thomas Newcomen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Newcomen "Thomas Newcomen") (died 1729), steam engine pioneer.

[Video 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/80/Bunhill_Fields_hyperlapse_video.webm?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)

A hyperlapse video showing the paths around the cemetery

Bunhill Fields Burial Ground is listed Grade I on the [Register of Historic Parks and Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Register_of_Historic_Parks_and_Gardens_of_special_historic_interest_in_England "Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-nhle-2) It is now maintained by the Friends of City Gardens.

Nearby, on the west side of [Bunhill Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Row "Bunhill Row") and behind the residential tower Braithwaite House, is a former [Quaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers "Quakers") burial ground, in use from 1661 to 1855, at times also known as Bunhill Fields. [George Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Fox "George Fox") (died 1691), one of the founders of the movement, is among those buried there. Its remains are also a public garden, [Quaker Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaker_Gardens,_Islington "Quaker Gardens, Islington"), managed by the London Borough of Islington.

## Historical background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bunhill_Fields&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Historical background")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/3/36/Map_of_Bunhill_Fields_City_Road_London.jpg/250px-Map_of_Bunhill_Fields_City_Road_London.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map_of_Bunhill_Fields_City_Road_London.jpg)

Plan of the present Bunhill Fields public gardens (east at the top). Areas in green are fenced, and contain most of the surviving monuments. Areas in yellow and white have been largely cleared of monuments, and are fully accessible to the public.

Bunhill Fields was part of the Manor of [Finsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finsbury "Finsbury") (originally Fensbury), which has its origins as the [prebend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prebend "Prebend") of Halliwell and Finsbury, belonging to [St Paul's Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_St_Paul's_Cathedral "Old St Paul's Cathedral") and established in 1104. In 1315 the prebendary manor was granted by Archdeacon [Robert Baldock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Baldock "Robert Baldock") to the Mayor and Commonalty of London. This enabled more general public access to the semi-[fen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fen "Fen") or moor stretching from the City of London's boundary ([London Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Wall "London Wall")), to the village of [Hoxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoxton "Hoxton").

In 1498 part of the otherwise unenclosed landscape was set aside to form a large field for military exercises of archers and others. This part of the manor has sports and occasional military use: [Artillery Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artillery_Ground "Artillery Ground").

Next to this lies Bunhill Fields. The name derives from "Bone hill", likely linked to occasional burials from at least [Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxons "Anglo-Saxons") times, but more probably derives from the use for mass-deposit for human bones—amounting to over 1,000 cartloads—brought from St Paul's [charnel house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charnel_house "Charnel house") in 1549 (when that building was demolished).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-3) The dried bones were deposited on the moor and capped with a thin layer of soil. This built up a hill across the otherwise damp, flat fens, such that three windmills could safely be erected in a spot that came to be one of the many windmill hills.

## Opening as a burial ground

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bunhill_Fields&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Opening as a burial ground")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Mary_Page_monument_2.JPG/250px-Mary_Page_monument_2.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mary_Page_monument_2.JPG)

Monument of [Dame Mary Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Gregory_Page,_1st_Baronet "Sir Gregory Page, 1st Baronet") (died 1729). The inscription reads in part: "In 67 months she was tap'd [tapped] 66 times, Had taken away 240 gallons of water without ever repining at her case or ever fearing the operation."

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Monument_To_Theophilus_Gale%2C_South_Enclosure.jpg/250px-Monument_To_Theophilus_Gale%2C_South_Enclosure.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Monument_To_Theophilus_Gale,_South_Enclosure.jpg)

Monument to Theophilus Gale, South Enclosure.

In keeping with this tradition, in 1665 the City of London Corporation decided to use some of the land as a common burial ground for the interment of bodies of inhabitants who had died of the [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Plague_of_London "Great Plague of London") and could not be accommodated in the churchyards. Outer walls were completed but Church of England officials never consecrated the ground nor used it for burials. A Mr. Tindal took over the lease.

He allowed extramural graveyard burials in what was unconsecrated soil, thus popular with [nonconformists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)")—those [Protestant Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism "Protestantism") who practised their faiths outside the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"); unlike [Anglican churchyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England_parish_church "Church of England parish church") it was open for interment to anyone who could afford the fees. It appears on [Rocque's Map of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rocque's_Map_of_London,_1746 "John Rocque's Map of London, 1746") of 1746, and elsewhere, as "Tindal's Burying Ground".

An inscription at the eastern entrance gate to the burial ground reads:

> This church-yard was inclosed with a brick wall at the sole charges of the City of London, in the mayoralty of [Sir John Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lawrence_(Lord_Mayor) "John Lawrence (Lord Mayor)"), Knt., Anno Domini 1665; and afterwards the gates thereof were built and finished in the mayoralty of [Sir Thomas Bloudworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Bloodworth "Thomas Bloodworth"), Knt., Anno Domini, 1666.

The present gates and inscription date from 1868, but the wording follows that of an original 17th-century inscription at the western entrance, now lost.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-nhle-2)

The earliest recorded monumental inscription was that to "Grace, daughter of T. Cloudesly, of Leeds. February 1666".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-4) The earliest surviving monument is believed to be the [headstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headstone "Headstone") to [Theophilus Gale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theophilus_Gale "Theophilus Gale"): the inscription reads "Theophilus Gale MA / Born 1628 / Died 1678".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-5)

In 1769 an act of Parliament, the **Prebendary of St. Paul London (Leasing) Act 1769** ([9 Geo. 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9_Geo._3 "9 Geo. 3"). c. _61_ Pr.), gave the corporation the right to continue the lease for 99 years. The City authorities continued to let the ground to their tenant as a burial ground; in 1781 the corporation decided to take over management of the burial ground.

So many historically important Protestant nonconformists chose this as their place of interment that the 19th-century poet and writer [Robert Southey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Southey "Robert Southey") characterised Bunhill Fields in 1830 as the ground "which the Dissenters regard as their [Campo Santo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campo_Santo_(disambiguation) "Campo Santo (disambiguation)")".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-6) This term was applied to its "daughter", [Abney Park Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abney_Park_Cemetery "Abney Park Cemetery") in [Stoke Newington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoke_Newington "Stoke Newington").

## Closure as a burial ground

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bunhill_Fields&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Closure as a burial ground")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Bunhill_Fields_Act.jpg/250px-Bunhill_Fields_Act.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bunhill_Fields_Act.jpg)

Act of Parliament of 1867 for the Preservation of Bunhill fields as an Open Space

The [Burial Act 1852](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burial_Act_1852 "Burial Act 1852") was passed which enabled grounds to be closed once they became full. An Order for Closure for Bunhill Fields was made in December 1853, and the final burial (that of Elizabeth Howell Oliver) took place on 5 January 1854. Occasional interments continued to be permitted in existing vaults or graves: the final burial of this kind is believed to have been that of a Mrs. Gabriel of [Brixton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brixton "Brixton") in February 1860.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-Corporation_of_London_1991,_p._8-7) By this date approximately 123,000 interments had taken place in the burial ground.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-8)

Two decades before, a group of City nonconformists led by [George Collison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Collison "George Collison") bought a site for a new landscaped alternative, at part of [Abney Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abney_Park "Abney Park") in Stoke Newington. This was named [Abney Park Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abney_Park_Cemetery "Abney Park Cemetery") and opened in 1840. All parts were available for the burial of any person, regardless of religious creed. It preceded [Brookwood Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery "Brookwood Cemetery") as the prototype of many cemeteries to come nationally with "no invidious dividing lines". It has a unique nondenominational chapel, designed by [William Hosking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hosking "William Hosking").

## Community garden

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bunhill_Fields&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Community garden")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/1830londonNN.png/3840px-1830londonNN.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1830londonNN.png)

[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1830londonNN.png "File:1830londonNN.png")

Crop of Christopher and John Greenwood's 8 inch-to-mile map published in 1827 from an 1830 republication (click to view all).

Upon closure of the Bunhill Fields Burial Ground, its future was uncertain as its lessee, the City of London Corporation, was close to expiry of its lease, scheduled for Christmas 1867.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-9) To prevent the land from being redeveloped by the [Ecclesiastical Commissioners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecclesiastical_Commissioners "Ecclesiastical Commissioners") (who controlled the freehold) at this expiry, the Corporation formed the Special Bunhill Fields Burial Ground Committee in 1865. This became formally known as the Bunhill Fields Preservation Committee.

Appointed by the corporation, it consisted of twelve advisors under the chairmanship of [Charles Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Reed_(British_politician) "Charles Reed (British politician)"), [FSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Antiquaries_of_London "Society of Antiquaries of London") (son of the Congregational philanthropist Dr. Andrew Reed). He later rose to prominence as the first [Member of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) "Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)") (MP) for [Hackney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hackney_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Hackney (UK Parliament constituency)") and chairman of the first School Board for London before being knighted. Along with his interest in making it into a parkland landscape, he was similarly interested in the wider educational and public benefits of [Abney Park Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abney_Park_Cemetery "Abney Park Cemetery"), of which he was a prominent director.

To corroborate the committee's work, the corporation obtained an act of Parliament, the [Bunhill Fields Burial Ground Act 1867](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields_Burial_Ground_Act_1867?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bunhill Fields Burial Ground Act 1867 (page does not exist)") ([30 & 31 Vict.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/30_&_31_Vict. "30 & 31 Vict.") c. 38),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-CityOfLondon-1) "for the Preservation of Bunhill Fields Burial Ground... as an open space". The legislation enabled them to continue to maintain the site when [possession would have otherwise reverted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reversion_(law) "Reversion (law)") to the [Ecclesiastical Commissioners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecclesiastical_Commissioners "Ecclesiastical Commissioners"), provided it was laid out as a public open space with seating, gardens, and some of its most worthy monuments were restored. The improvements, which included the laying out of walks and paths, cost an estimated £3,500. The new park was opened by the [Lord Mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Mayor_of_London "Lord Mayor of London"), [James Clarke Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_James_Lawrence,_1st_Baronet "Sir James Lawrence, 1st Baronet"), on 14 October 1869.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-Corporation_of_London_1991,_p._8-7)

The ground was severely damaged by [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") bombing during World War II; it is believed to have hosted an [anti-aircraft gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-aircraft_warfare "Anti-aircraft warfare") during the [Blitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blitz "The Blitz").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-nhle-2) In the 1950s, after some debate, the City ordered: to clear the northern third (the projection) of the site of most of its monuments to open it as a public garden; and to preserve and protect the rest behind railings. Legislation in 1960 gave the freehold to the city (the corporation), which continues to maintain the grounds. Landscaping was designed and overseen by the architect and landscape architect [Peter Shepheard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Shepheard "Peter Shepheard") in 1964–65.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-nhle-2)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-10)

## Bunyan, Defoe and Blake

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bunhill_Fields&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Bunyan, Defoe and Blake")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Finsbury_bunyan_defoe_blake_1.jpg/250px-Finsbury_bunyan_defoe_blake_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Finsbury_bunyan_defoe_blake_1.jpg)

The broadwalk, looking north. John Bunyan's monument is in the foreground, with memorials to Daniel Defoe (obelisk, left) and Willam Blake (headstone, right) in the background.

The best-known monuments are those to the three literary and artistic figures [John Bunyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bunyan "John Bunyan"), [Daniel Defoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Defoe "Daniel Defoe") and [William Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Blake "William Blake"). Their graves have long been sites of cultural pilgrimage: Isabella Holmes stated in 1896 that the "most frequented paths" in the burial ground were those leading to the monuments of Bunyan and Defoe.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-11) In their present form, all these monuments post-date the closure of the burial ground. Their settings were further radically modified by the landscaping of 1964–65, when a paved north–south "broadwalk" was created in the middle of the burial ground to display them—outside the railed-off areas, accessible to visitors, and cleared of other monuments. Bunyan's monument lies at the broadwalk's southern end, and that to Defoe at its northern end, while Blake's headstone was moved from the site of his grave and repositioned next to Defoe, alongside the headstone to the lesser-known [Joseph Swain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Swain_(poet) "Joseph Swain (poet)") (died 1796). This arrangement survives, but in 2018 a second monument to Blake was placed on the actual site of his grave.

### John Bunyan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bunhill_Fields&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: John Bunyan")]

[John Bunyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bunyan "John Bunyan"), author of _[Pilgrim's Progress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Pilgrim's\_Progress "The Pilgrim's Progress")_, died in August 1688. He was initially buried in the "[Baptist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptists "Baptists") Corner" at the back of the burial ground, on the understanding that his remains would be moved into the [family vault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burial_vault_(tomb) "Burial vault (tomb)") of his friend John Strudwick when that was next opened for a burial. There is no certain evidence as to when (or even if) this was done: the probability, however, is that it occurred when Strudwick himself died in 1695, and certainly Bunyan's name was inscribed on the side of the monument.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-12) The Strudwick monument took the form of a large [Baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque_architecture "Baroque architecture") stone chest. By the 19th century, this had fallen into decay, but in the period following the closure of the burial ground a public appeal for its restoration was launched under the presidency of the [7th Earl of Shaftesbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Ashley-Cooper,_7th_Earl_of_Shaftesbury "Anthony Ashley-Cooper, 7th Earl of Shaftesbury"). This work was completed in May 1862, and comprised a complete reconstruction of the monument, undertaken by the sculptor [Edgar George Papworth Senior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_George_Papworth_Senior "Edgar George Papworth Senior") (1809–1866).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-13) Although Papworth retained the basic form of the tomb-chest, he added a [recumbent effigy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_effigy "Tomb effigy") of Bunyan to the top of it, and two [relief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relief "Relief") panels to its sides depicting scenes from _Pilgrim's Progress_. The monument was further restored in 1928 (the tercentenary of Bunyan's birth), and again after World War II (following serious wartime damage to the effigy's face).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-15)

### Daniel Defoe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bunhill_Fields&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Daniel Defoe")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Daniel_Defoe_monument_Bunhill_Fields.jpg/250px-Daniel_Defoe_monument_Bunhill_Fields.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Daniel_Defoe_monument_Bunhill_Fields.jpg)

1870 obelisk to Daniel Defoe

[Daniel Defoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Defoe "Daniel Defoe"), author of _[Robinson Crusoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinson\_Crusoe "Robinson Crusoe")_, died in April 1731 and was buried in Bunhill Fields: his wife, Mary, died in December 1732 and was laid to rest beside him. His daughter-in-law was also buried in the same grave. Defoe died in poverty, and the grave was marked with a simple headstone. In the winter of 1857/8 – at a time when the burial ground was closed and neglected—the grave was struck by lightning and the headstone broken. In 1869, James Clarke, editor of the _Christian World_ children's newspaper, launched an appeal for subscriptions to place a more suitable memorial on the grave. He encouraged his readers to make donations of [sixpence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixpence_(British_coin) "Sixpence (British coin)") each; and to stimulate enthusiasm opened two lists, one for boys and one for girls, to encourage a spirit of competition between them. Many adults also made donations. In the end, some 1,700 subscriptions raised a total of about £200. A design for a marble [obelisk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk "Obelisk") (or "Cleopatric pillar") was commissioned from C. C. Creeke; and the sculptor [Samuel Horner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Horner_(sculptor)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Samuel Horner (sculptor) (page does not exist)") of [Bournemouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bournemouth "Bournemouth") was commissioned to execute it. In late 1869, when the foundations were being dug, skeletons were disinterred, and there was an unseemly rush for souvenirs by the crowd of onlookers: the police had to be called before calm was restored. The monument was unveiled at a ceremony attended by three of Defoe's great-granddaughters on 16 September 1870.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-17)

### William Blake

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bunhill_Fields&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: William Blake")]

[William Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Blake "William Blake") died in August 1827 and was buried in the northern part of the burial ground. His wife, [Catherine Sophia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Blake "Catherine Blake"), died in October 1831 and was buried in a separate grave on the south side of the ground. By the 20th century, Blake's grave was in disrepair; and in 1927, for the centenary of his death and at a time when his reputation was on the rise, a new headstone was commissioned. As it had been decided to commemorate both William and Catherine, despite the fact that the headstone would stand at some distance from Catherine's grave, the inscription was phrased as "Near by lie the remains of ...". When Bunhill Fields was relandscaped in the 1960s, Blake's grave lay in the area that was to be cleared of monuments. The headstone was therefore moved approximately 20 metres (yards) to its present location, next to the monument to Daniel Defoe. It was also rotated through 90°, so that it now faces south rather than west.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-18)[Joseph Swain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Swain_(poet) "Joseph Swain (poet)")'s headstone was added to the grouping at the same time, although that faces west.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-nhle-2) Flowers, coins and other [tokens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Votive_offering "Votive offering") are regularly left by visitors to Blake's headstone.

In 2006–07, members of the group The Friends of William Blake established the original location of his grave, and proposed placing a new memorial there.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-19) In the form of a [ledger stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ledger_stone "Ledger stone"), with lettering by [Lida Cardozo Kindersley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lida_Lopes_Cardozo_Kindersley "Lida Lopes Cardozo Kindersley"), this was finally unveiled on 12 August 2018 by [Philip Pullman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Pullman "Philip Pullman"), President of the Blake Society.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-21)

## Records

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bunhill_Fields&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Records")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Grave_of_John_Rippon%2C_Bunhill_Fields.jpg/250px-Grave_of_John_Rippon%2C_Bunhill_Fields.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Grave_of_John_Rippon,_Bunhill_Fields.jpg)

Tomb of [John Rippon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rippon "John Rippon") (died 1836)

Burial ground registers, from 1713 to 1854, are held at [The National Archives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_National_Archives_(United_Kingdom) "The National Archives (United Kingdom)") at [Kew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kew "Kew").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-22) Other records, including interment order books dating from 1789 to 1854, and a list of the legible monument/headstone inscriptions in 1869, are held at [The London Archives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_London_Archives "The London Archives").

[Baptist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptist "Baptist") minister [John Rippon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rippon "John Rippon")—who was himself buried at the site in 1836—made transcripts of its monumental inscriptions in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, some copied while "laying on his side". In 1803 he issued a prospectus for a six-volume publication on Bunhill Fields, but this never came to fruition. The [British Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Library "British Library") now holds 14 manuscript volumes of his transcripts; a further six volumes are held in the [College of Arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Arms "College of Arms").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-25)

**Bunhill Fields** is a former burial ground in central London, in the [London Borough of Islington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Islington "London Borough of Islington"), just north of the [City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London "City of London"). What remains is about 1.6 hectares (4.0 acres) in extent[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-CityOfLondon-1) and the bulk of the site is a public garden maintained by the [City of London Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London_Corporation "City of London Corporation").

It was first in devoted use as a burial ground from 1665 until 1854, in which period approximately 123,000 interments were estimated to have taken place.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-nhle-2) Over 2,000 monuments remain, for the most part in concentrated blocks. It was a prototype of land-use protected, nondenominational grounds, and was particularly favoured by [nonconformists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") who passed their final years in the region. It contains the graves of many notable people, including [John Bunyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bunyan "John Bunyan") (died 1688), author of _[The Pilgrim's Progress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Pilgrim's\_Progress "The Pilgrim's Progress")_; [Daniel Defoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Defoe "Daniel Defoe") (died 1731), author of _[Robinson Crusoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinson\_Crusoe "Robinson Crusoe")_; [William Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Blake "William Blake") (died 1827), artist, poet, and mystic; [Susanna Wesley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susanna_Wesley "Susanna Wesley") (died 1742), known as the "Mother of Methodism" through her education of sons [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wesley "John Wesley") and [Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Wesley "Charles Wesley"); [Thomas Bayes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Bayes "Thomas Bayes") (died 1761), statistician and philosopher; [Isaac Watts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Watts "Isaac Watts") (died 1748), the "Father of English [Hymnody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymn "Hymn")"; and [Thomas Newcomen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Newcomen "Thomas Newcomen") (died 1729), steam engine pioneer.

[Video 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/80/Bunhill_Fields_hyperlapse_video.webm?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)

A hyperlapse video showing the paths around the cemetery

Bunhill Fields Burial Ground is listed Grade I on the [Register of Historic Parks and Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Register_of_Historic_Parks_and_Gardens_of_special_historic_interest_in_England "Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-nhle-2) It is now maintained by the Friends of City Gardens.

Nearby, on the west side of [Bunhill Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Row "Bunhill Row") and behind the residential tower Braithwaite House, is a former [Quaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers "Quakers") burial ground, in use from 1661 to 1855, at times also known as Bunhill Fields. [George Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Fox "George Fox") (died 1691), one of the founders of the movement, is among those buried there. Its remains are also a public garden, [Quaker Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaker_Gardens,_Islington "Quaker Gardens, Islington"), managed by the London Borough of Islington.

## Historical background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bunhill_Fields&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Historical background")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/3/36/Map_of_Bunhill_Fields_City_Road_London.jpg/250px-Map_of_Bunhill_Fields_City_Road_London.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map_of_Bunhill_Fields_City_Road_London.jpg)

Plan of the present Bunhill Fields public gardens (east at the top). Areas in green are fenced, and contain most of the surviving monuments. Areas in yellow and white have been largely cleared of monuments, and are fully accessible to the public.

Bunhill Fields was part of the Manor of [Finsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finsbury "Finsbury") (originally Fensbury), which has its origins as the [prebend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prebend "Prebend") of Halliwell and Finsbury, belonging to [St Paul's Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_St_Paul's_Cathedral "Old St Paul's Cathedral") and established in 1104. In 1315 the prebendary manor was granted by Archdeacon [Robert Baldock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Baldock "Robert Baldock") to the Mayor and Commonalty of London. This enabled more general public access to the semi-[fen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fen "Fen") or moor stretching from the City of London's boundary ([London Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Wall "London Wall")), to the village of [Hoxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoxton "Hoxton").

In 1498 part of the otherwise unenclosed landscape was set aside to form a large field for military exercises of archers and others. This part of the manor has sports and occasional military use: [Artillery Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artillery_Ground "Artillery Ground").

Next to this lies Bunhill Fields. The name derives from "Bone hill", likely linked to occasional burials from at least [Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxons "Anglo-Saxons") times, but more probably derives from the use for mass-deposit for human bones—amounting to over 1,000 cartloads—brought from St Paul's [charnel house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charnel_house "Charnel house") in 1549 (when that building was demolished).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-3) The dried bones were deposited on the moor and capped with a thin layer of soil. This built up a hill across the otherwise damp, flat fens, such that three windmills could safely be erected in a spot that came to be one of the many windmill hills.

## Opening as a burial ground

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bunhill_Fields&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Opening as a burial ground")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Mary_Page_monument_2.JPG/250px-Mary_Page_monument_2.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mary_Page_monument_2.JPG)

Monument of [Dame Mary Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Gregory_Page,_1st_Baronet "Sir Gregory Page, 1st Baronet") (died 1729). The inscription reads in part: "In 67 months she was tap'd [tapped] 66 times, Had taken away 240 gallons of water without ever repining at her case or ever fearing the operation."

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Monument_To_Theophilus_Gale%2C_South_Enclosure.jpg/250px-Monument_To_Theophilus_Gale%2C_South_Enclosure.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Monument_To_Theophilus_Gale,_South_Enclosure.jpg)

Monument to Theophilus Gale, South Enclosure.

In keeping with this tradition, in 1665 the City of London Corporation decided to use some of the land as a common burial ground for the interment of bodies of inhabitants who had died of the [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Plague_of_London "Great Plague of London") and could not be accommodated in the churchyards. Outer walls were completed but Church of England officials never consecrated the ground nor used it for burials. A Mr. Tindal took over the lease.

He allowed extramural graveyard burials in what was unconsecrated soil, thus popular with [nonconformists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)")—those [Protestant Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism "Protestantism") who practised their faiths outside the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"); unlike [Anglican churchyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England_parish_church "Church of England parish church") it was open for interment to anyone who could afford the fees. It appears on [Rocque's Map of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rocque's_Map_of_London,_1746 "John Rocque's Map of London, 1746") of 1746, and elsewhere, as "Tindal's Burying Ground".

An inscription at the eastern entrance gate to the burial ground reads:

> This church-yard was inclosed with a brick wall at the sole charges of the City of London, in the mayoralty of [Sir John Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lawrence_(Lord_Mayor) "John Lawrence (Lord Mayor)"), Knt., Anno Domini 1665; and afterwards the gates thereof were built and finished in the mayoralty of [Sir Thomas Bloudworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Bloodworth "Thomas Bloodworth"), Knt., Anno Domini, 1666.

The present gates and inscription date from 1868, but the wording follows that of an original 17th-century inscription at the western entrance, now lost.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-nhle-2)

The earliest recorded monumental inscription was that to "Grace, daughter of T. Cloudesly, of Leeds. February 1666".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-4) The earliest surviving monument is believed to be the [headstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headstone "Headstone") to [Theophilus Gale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theophilus_Gale "Theophilus Gale"): the inscription reads "Theophilus Gale MA / Born 1628 / Died 1678".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-5)

In 1769 an act of Parliament, the **Prebendary of St. Paul London (Leasing) Act 1769** ([9 Geo. 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9_Geo._3 "9 Geo. 3"). c. _61_ Pr.), gave the corporation the right to continue the lease for 99 years. The City authorities continued to let the ground to their tenant as a burial ground; in 1781 the corporation decided to take over management of the burial ground.

So many historically important Protestant nonconformists chose this as their place of interment that the 19th-century poet and writer [Robert Southey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Southey "Robert Southey") characterised Bunhill Fields in 1830 as the ground "which the Dissenters regard as their [Campo Santo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campo_Santo_(disambiguation) "Campo Santo (disambiguation)")".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-6) This term was applied to its "daughter", [Abney Park Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abney_Park_Cemetery "Abney Park Cemetery") in [Stoke Newington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoke_Newington "Stoke Newington").

## Closure as a burial ground

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bunhill_Fields&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Closure as a burial ground")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Bunhill_Fields_Act.jpg/250px-Bunhill_Fields_Act.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bunhill_Fields_Act.jpg)

Act of Parliament of 1867 for the Preservation of Bunhill fields as an Open Space

The [Burial Act 1852](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burial_Act_1852 "Burial Act 1852") was passed which enabled grounds to be closed once they became full. An Order for Closure for Bunhill Fields was made in December 1853, and the final burial (that of Elizabeth Howell Oliver) took place on 5 January 1854. Occasional interments continued to be permitted in existing vaults or graves: the final burial of this kind is believed to have been that of a Mrs. Gabriel of [Brixton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brixton "Brixton") in February 1860.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-Corporation_of_London_1991,_p._8-7) By this date approximately 123,000 interments had taken place in the burial ground.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-8)

Two decades before, a group of City nonconformists led by [George Collison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Collison "George Collison") bought a site for a new landscaped alternative, at part of [Abney Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abney_Park "Abney Park") in Stoke Newington. This was named [Abney Park Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abney_Park_Cemetery "Abney Park Cemetery") and opened in 1840. All parts were available for the burial of any person, regardless of religious creed. It preceded [Brookwood Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_Cemetery "Brookwood Cemetery") as the prototype of many cemeteries to come nationally with "no invidious dividing lines". It has a unique nondenominational chapel, designed by [William Hosking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hosking "William Hosking").

## Community garden

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bunhill_Fields&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Community garden")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/1830londonNN.png/3840px-1830londonNN.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1830londonNN.png "Crop of Christopher and John Greenwood's 8 inch-to-mile map published in 1827 from an 1830 republication (click to view all).")

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/1830londonNN.png/3840px-1830londonNN.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1830londonNN.png)

[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1830londonNN.png "File:1830londonNN.png")

Crop of Christopher and John Greenwood's 8 inch-to-mile map published in 1827 from an 1830 republication (click to view all).

Upon closure of the Bunhill Fields Burial Ground, its future was uncertain as its lessee, the City of London Corporation, was close to expiry of its lease, scheduled for Christmas 1867.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-9) To prevent the land from being redeveloped by the [Ecclesiastical Commissioners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecclesiastical_Commissioners "Ecclesiastical Commissioners") (who controlled the freehold) at this expiry, the Corporation formed the Special Bunhill Fields Burial Ground Committee in 1865. This became formally known as the Bunhill Fields Preservation Committee.

Appointed by the corporation, it consisted of twelve advisors under the chairmanship of [Charles Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Reed_(British_politician) "Charles Reed (British politician)"), [FSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Antiquaries_of_London "Society of Antiquaries of London") (son of the Congregational philanthropist Dr. Andrew Reed). He later rose to prominence as the first [Member of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) "Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)") (MP) for [Hackney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hackney_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Hackney (UK Parliament constituency)") and chairman of the first School Board for London before being knighted. Along with his interest in making it into a parkland landscape, he was similarly interested in the wider educational and public benefits of [Abney Park Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abney_Park_Cemetery "Abney Park Cemetery"), of which he was a prominent director.

To corroborate the committee's work, the corporation obtained an act of Parliament, the [Bunhill Fields Burial Ground Act 1867](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields_Burial_Ground_Act_1867?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bunhill Fields Burial Ground Act 1867 (page does not exist)") ([30 & 31 Vict.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/30_&_31_Vict. "30 & 31 Vict.") c. 38),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-CityOfLondon-1) "for the Preservation of Bunhill Fields Burial Ground... as an open space". The legislation enabled them to continue to maintain the site when [possession would have otherwise reverted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reversion_(law) "Reversion (law)") to the [Ecclesiastical Commissioners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecclesiastical_Commissioners "Ecclesiastical Commissioners"), provided it was laid out as a public open space with seating, gardens, and some of its most worthy monuments were restored. The improvements, which included the laying out of walks and paths, cost an estimated £3,500. The new park was opened by the [Lord Mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Mayor_of_London "Lord Mayor of London"), [James Clarke Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_James_Lawrence,_1st_Baronet "Sir James Lawrence, 1st Baronet"), on 14 October 1869.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-Corporation_of_London_1991,_p._8-7)

The ground was severely damaged by [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") bombing during World War II; it is believed to have hosted an [anti-aircraft gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-aircraft_warfare "Anti-aircraft warfare") during the [Blitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blitz "The Blitz").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-nhle-2) In the 1950s, after some debate, the City ordered: to clear the northern third (the projection) of the site of most of its monuments to open it as a public garden; and to preserve and protect the rest behind railings. Legislation in 1960 gave the freehold to the city (the corporation), which continues to maintain the grounds. Landscaping was designed and overseen by the architect and landscape architect [Peter Shepheard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Shepheard "Peter Shepheard") in 1964–65.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-nhle-2)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-10)

## Bunyan, Defoe and Blake

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bunhill_Fields&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Bunyan, Defoe and Blake")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Finsbury_bunyan_defoe_blake_1.jpg/250px-Finsbury_bunyan_defoe_blake_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Finsbury_bunyan_defoe_blake_1.jpg)

The broadwalk, looking north. John Bunyan's monument is in the foreground, with memorials to Daniel Defoe (obelisk, left) and Willam Blake (headstone, right) in the background.

The best-known monuments are those to the three literary and artistic figures [John Bunyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bunyan "John Bunyan"), [Daniel Defoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Defoe "Daniel Defoe") and [William Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Blake "William Blake"). Their graves have long been sites of cultural pilgrimage: Isabella Holmes stated in 1896 that the "most frequented paths" in the burial ground were those leading to the monuments of Bunyan and Defoe.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-11) In their present form, all these monuments post-date the closure of the burial ground. Their settings were further radically modified by the landscaping of 1964–65, when a paved north–south "broadwalk" was created in the middle of the burial ground to display them—outside the railed-off areas, accessible to visitors, and cleared of other monuments. Bunyan's monument lies at the broadwalk's southern end, and that to Defoe at its northern end, while Blake's headstone was moved from the site of his grave and repositioned next to Defoe, alongside the headstone to the lesser-known [Joseph Swain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Swain_(poet) "Joseph Swain (poet)") (died 1796). This arrangement survives, but in 2018 a second monument to Blake was placed on the actual site of his grave.

### John Bunyan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bunhill_Fields&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: John Bunyan")]

[John Bunyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bunyan "John Bunyan"), author of _[Pilgrim's Progress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Pilgrim's\_Progress "The Pilgrim's Progress")_, died in August 1688. He was initially buried in the "[Baptist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptists "Baptists") Corner" at the back of the burial ground, on the understanding that his remains would be moved into the [family vault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burial_vault_(tomb) "Burial vault (tomb)") of his friend John Strudwick when that was next opened for a burial. There is no certain evidence as to when (or even if) this was done: the probability, however, is that it occurred when Strudwick himself died in 1695, and certainly Bunyan's name was inscribed on the side of the monument.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-12) The Strudwick monument took the form of a large [Baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque_architecture "Baroque architecture") stone chest. By the 19th century, this had fallen into decay, but in the period following the closure of the burial ground a public appeal for its restoration was launched under the presidency of the [7th Earl of Shaftesbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Ashley-Cooper,_7th_Earl_of_Shaftesbury "Anthony Ashley-Cooper, 7th Earl of Shaftesbury"). This work was completed in May 1862, and comprised a complete reconstruction of the monument, undertaken by the sculptor [Edgar George Papworth Senior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_George_Papworth_Senior "Edgar George Papworth Senior") (1809–1866).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-13) Although Papworth retained the basic form of the tomb-chest, he added a [recumbent effigy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_effigy "Tomb effigy") of Bunyan to the top of it, and two [relief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relief "Relief") panels to its sides depicting scenes from _Pilgrim's Progress_. The monument was further restored in 1928 (the tercentenary of Bunyan's birth), and again after World War II (following serious wartime damage to the effigy's face).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-15)

### Daniel Defoe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bunhill_Fields&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Daniel Defoe")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Daniel_Defoe_monument_Bunhill_Fields.jpg/250px-Daniel_Defoe_monument_Bunhill_Fields.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Daniel_Defoe_monument_Bunhill_Fields.jpg)

1870 obelisk to Daniel Defoe

[Daniel Defoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Defoe "Daniel Defoe"), author of _[Robinson Crusoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinson\_Crusoe "Robinson Crusoe")_, died in April 1731 and was buried in Bunhill Fields: his wife, Mary, died in December 1732 and was laid to rest beside him. His daughter-in-law was also buried in the same grave. Defoe died in poverty, and the grave was marked with a simple headstone. In the winter of 1857/8 – at a time when the burial ground was closed and neglected—the grave was struck by lightning and the headstone broken. In 1869, James Clarke, editor of the _Christian World_ children's newspaper, launched an appeal for subscriptions to place a more suitable memorial on the grave. He encouraged his readers to make donations of [sixpence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixpence_(British_coin) "Sixpence (British coin)") each; and to stimulate enthusiasm opened two lists, one for boys and one for girls, to encourage a spirit of competition between them. Many adults also made donations. In the end, some 1,700 subscriptions raised a total of about £200. A design for a marble [obelisk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk "Obelisk") (or "Cleopatric pillar") was commissioned from C. C. Creeke; and the sculptor [Samuel Horner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Horner_(sculptor)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Samuel Horner (sculptor) (page does not exist)") of [Bournemouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bournemouth "Bournemouth") was commissioned to execute it. In late 1869, when the foundations were being dug, skeletons were disinterred, and there was an unseemly rush for souvenirs by the crowd of onlookers: the police had to be called before calm was restored. The monument was unveiled at a ceremony attended by three of Defoe's great-granddaughters on 16 September 1870.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-17)

### William Blake

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bunhill_Fields&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: William Blake")]

[William Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Blake "William Blake") died in August 1827 and was buried in the northern part of the burial ground. His wife, [Catherine Sophia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Blake "Catherine Blake"), died in October 1831 and was buried in a separate grave on the south side of the ground. By the 20th century, Blake's grave was in disrepair; and in 1927, for the centenary of his death and at a time when his reputation was on the rise, a new headstone was commissioned. As it had been decided to commemorate both William and Catherine, despite the fact that the headstone would stand at some distance from Catherine's grave, the inscription was phrased as "Near by lie the remains of ...". When Bunhill Fields was relandscaped in the 1960s, Blake's grave lay in the area that was to be cleared of monuments. The headstone was therefore moved approximately 20 metres (yards) to its present location, next to the monument to Daniel Defoe. It was also rotated through 90°, so that it now faces south rather than west.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-18)[Joseph Swain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Swain_(poet) "Joseph Swain (poet)")'s headstone was added to the grouping at the same time, although that faces west.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-nhle-2) Flowers, coins and other [tokens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Votive_offering "Votive offering") are regularly left by visitors to Blake's headstone.

In 2006–07, members of the group The Friends of William Blake established the original location of his grave, and proposed placing a new memorial there.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-19) In the form of a [ledger stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ledger_stone "Ledger stone"), with lettering by [Lida Cardozo Kindersley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lida_Lopes_Cardozo_Kindersley "Lida Lopes Cardozo Kindersley"), this was finally unveiled on 12 August 2018 by [Philip Pullman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Pullman "Philip Pullman"), President of the Blake Society.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-21)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bunhill_Fields&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Records")]

Tomb of [John Rippon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rippon "John Rippon") (died 1836)

Burial ground registers, from 1713 to 1854, are held at [The National Archives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_National_Archives_(United_Kingdom) "The National Archives (United Kingdom)") at [Kew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kew "Kew").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-22) Other records, including interment order books dating from 1789 to 1854, and a list of the legible monument/headstone inscriptions in 1869, are held at [The London Archives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_London_Archives "The London Archives").

[Baptist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptist "Baptist") minister [John Rippon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rippon "John Rippon")—who was himself buried at the site in 1836—made transcripts of its monumental inscriptions in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, some copied while "laying on his side". In 1803 he issued a prospectus for a six-volume publication on Bunhill Fields, but this never came to fruition. The [British Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Library "British Library") now holds 14 manuscript volumes of his transcripts; a further six volumes are held in the [College of Arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Arms "College of Arms").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunhill_Fields#cite_note-25)

## Abstract

Printers in the ancien regime were primarily driven by economic motifs, they had to make money in order to ensure the survival of the firm. This article investigates how one particular printing house, that of the Antwerp based Verdussen family, exploited several networks to safeguard en expand their business in the seventeenth century.

Books and prints became a major resource of cultural exchange in XVIth century Europe. At that time Paris and London were among the most important centers of printing and were inevitably involved in book and print trading and exchange. One example of a successful career made between two European capitals was examined by Marianne Grivel in her article on Gilles Godet – a French engraver and editor working in London. There are many other examples of that kind. The testament of a London bookseller Nicolas Fichard who died in Paris in 1554 in the house of an editor and bookseller Oudin Petit shows that he was in constant connection with the French book market. The interest of London editors in Parisian printing presses is revealed by a contract made in 1564 between Fleury Prevost and Richard Tottel for the print of a book of laws of England. Thomas Vatroullier was a French huguenot refugee who moved to London but his connection with France was never lost. The first book he has published was decorated by the copies of plates by French painter Baptiste Pellerin for the Parisian music printers Robert Ballard and Adrien Le Roy. The plates of Le Roy and Ballard were very close to those used by Gilles Godet as frames for his popular prints. Vatroullier knew Godet as well as some other Parisian book traders and we can see that a social milieux formed by booksellers, printers and editors wasn’t limited by international frontiers. They were all collaborating in different ways: trade, duplication of editions and their decoration, association in book production etc. Personal or common acquaintances as well as origins helped to establish this network. The detailed examination of their collaboration as well as depiction of the complexity of this network is the aim of this paper.

The project "Communities of Print" explores early modern books not just as a medium for distributing information, but as material objects of Renaissance visual culture and art. It focuses on the visual and social impact of the books on various communities and examines their usage in communal settings. The paper also briefly outlines the presentations made at the first conference organised within the project in June 2016 in Manchester. This article uses space syntax analysis to explore the relationship between the spatial configuration of the city of Antwerp and the organisation of its trades and occupations in the early 19th century. A cadastral map from 1835 and a commercial almanac for 1838 were used to map the occupations held by the inhabitants of some 10,667 plots. Antwerp maintained a medieval spatial configuration at this time, with a strong ‘background network’ of distributed streets and continuous public spaces that privileged movement and encounter. However a ‘foreground network’ of streets was still found to be more accessible to global through movement. The spatial analysis of economic activity found a low level of clustering of different trades and occupations in particular parts of the city. Economic activities were rather broadly distributed throughout the background network of the street system. However, some trades and occupations took advantage of the foreground network of accessible streets more than others, and this was found to be statistically significant. Those occupations with high accessibility at all scales included retailers, wholesalers and artisans. While retailers would have prioritised access to passing trade, the latter two groups may have valued the circulation of goods, products and knowledge as much as the circulation of people.

[Natalie Lussey Seale](https://edinburgh.academia.edu/NatalieLussey)

In the increasingly polarized historiography of the printing industry of Venice, the workshop established by Giovanni Andrea Vavassore around 1515 offers a refreshing perspective on the role of the minor publisher in the Renaissance lagoon. Neither focused on a specific genre or format of book, nor interested in employing innovatory techniques of production, Vavassore instead emerges as a printing poligrafo: a man willing to turn his hand to the production of printed wares of every kind; a maker of prints and maps, as well as a publisher, printer, and seller of all types of edition. Beginning with the formation of his press, this article follows Vavassore’s journey to the lagoon and charts the establishment of his workshop. It also examines the process by which a new artisan might learn skills and amass contacts from other members of the printing trade. Rather than an inherently competitive trade, Vavassore’s experience of printing in Venice stresses the importance of collaboration, cooperation, and networking. Working with other publishers, printers, mapmakers, and itinerant performers, he was able to establish an extensive and vibrant market for his printed wares both in Venice and beyond. The printing policy of the workshop chiefly, to print what sold, and make the largest profits in doing so – emerges as key to the success of the Vavassore over the course of eight decades. Through the examination of a series of graphic prints, maps, pamphlets, and editions, this article questions the contemporary outreach and lasting influence of one of Venice’s many minor publishers in the Renaissance.

This book discusses the production and consumption of printed images in an urban environment in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, up to 1585. The story begins in the fifteenth century. At some point - no one knows exactly when - prints were suddenly being offered for sale in Antwerp. Initially they may have been brought from other cities by merchants and travellers, but at length the first printmaker established himself in the city. In the sixteenth century Antwerp fast developed into one of the main centres of printmaking in the western world. The author explores the complex way in which the printed image secured a place for itself in the urban fabric. He reconstructs the different traditions from which the print producers evolved, and explains how existing institutions in the city related to the new medium. He traces the way in which the traditional guilds tried to bring practitioners of this ‘singular skill’, as it was labelled in 1452, into their ranks, and shows how the government tried to gain control of the new medium. He discusses the interplay between printmakers seeking strategies to market their wares, and a public confronted with an interesting array of cheap new products.The reader is given an impression of the variety of prints produced, which have thus far received little attention in art history. Archival research has generated a good deal of detailed new information on the prices of prints, the numbers of impressions made, the costs of printing and colouring, and so forth.

## Abstract

Printers in the ancien regime were primarily driven by economic motifs, they had to make money in order to ensure the survival of the firm. This article investigates how one particular printing house, that of the Antwerp based Verdussen family, exploited several networks to safeguard en expand their business in the seventeenth century.

At the end of the sixteenth century the Duarte family, who were of Jewish origin, moved from Portugal to Antwerp and it was here that Diego (I) Duarte laid the foundations for a particularly lucrative business in gemstones and jewellery. His son Gaspar (I) and grandson Gaspar (II) were also very successful professionally and became purveyors of fine jewellery to the courts in (among other places) England, France, the Dutch Republic and the Habsburg Empire. Their wealth enabled the Duartes to collect art and make music in their "palace" on the Meir. Their artistic taste and discernment was such that the mansion became a magnet for visitors from all over Western Europe. The arts were a catalyst for the Duartes' business, but also constituted a universal language that permitted the family to transcend religious and geographical borders. The death of Diego (II) Duarte in 1691 brought to an end the story of the Duartes in Antwerp. The Duartes were possibly the foremost dealers in jewellery and gemstones in Antwerp in the seventeenth century, but they did not achieve that position without a great deal of effort. Thanks to hard work, determination, a love of the arts and a widespread family network, plus the advantage of Antwerp's geographically central position, these enterprising cosmopolitans managed to overcome religious discrimination and a succession of setbacks. And in the intimacy of their home they brought together the world of business, the arts and diplomacy in an environment that welcomed every discerning visitor, irrespective of his or her religious background. Books and prints became a major resource of cultural exchange in XVIth century Europe. At that time Paris and London were among the most important centers of printing and were inevitably involved in book and print trading and exchange. One example of a successful career made between two European capitals was examined by Marianne Grivel in her article on Gilles Godet – a French engraver and editor working in London. There are many other examples of that kind. The testament of a London bookseller Nicolas Fichard who died in Paris in 1554 in the house of an editor and bookseller Oudin Petit shows that he was in constant connection with the French book market. The interest of London editors in Parisian printing presses is revealed by a contract made in 1564 between Fleury Prevost and Richard Tottel for the print of a book of laws of England. Thomas Vatroullier was a French huguenot refugee who moved to London but his connection with France was never lost. The first book he has published was decorated by the copies of plates by French painter Baptiste Pellerin for the Parisian music printers Robert Ballard and Adrien Le Roy. The plates of Le Roy and Ballard were very close to those used by Gilles Godet as frames for his popular prints. Vatroullier knew Godet as well as some other Parisian book traders and we can see that a social milieux formed by booksellers, printers and editors wasn’t limited by international frontiers. They were all collaborating in different ways: trade, duplication of editions and their decoration, association in book production etc. Personal or common acquaintances as well as origins helped to establish this network. The detailed examination of their collaboration as well as depiction of the complexity of this network is the aim of this paper.

The paper discusses the international multidisciplinary research project "Communities of Print: Using Books in Early Modern Europe", launched by Manchester Metropolitan University (UK) in 2016. The project united the leading scholars specialising in art history, early modern history and literary studies, as well as librarians and archivists. The project "Communities of Print" explores early modern books not just as a medium for distributing information, but as material objects of Renaissance visual culture and art. It focuses on the visual and social impact of the books on various communities and examines their usage in communal settings. The paper also briefly outlines the presentations made at the first conference organised within the project in June 2016 in Manchester. They concerned such topics as the public availability of monastic and private libraries in early modern culture, book trading networks in Europe, the attribution of ownership marks and annotations, usage of medieval manuscripts and their role in early modern book collections, reading practices and access to printed material, and the evolution of anti-Catholic imagery in the early modern Protestant print. Finally, the paper observes some implications of the project, which stem from the close cooperation of researchers of art, history, literature and practitioners-librarians and archivists,-such as refining the knowledge and understanding of early modern books as the objects of visual culture.

[Francesca Froy](https://ucl.academia.edu/FrancescaFroy)

This article uses space syntax analysis to explore the relationship between the spatial configuration of the city of Antwerp and the organisation of its trades and occupations in the early 19th century. A cadastral map from 1835 and a commercial almanac for 1838 were used to map the occupations held by the inhabitants of some 10,667 plots. Antwerp maintained a medieval spatial configuration at this time, with a strong ‘background network’ of distributed streets and continuous public spaces that privileged movement and encounter. However a ‘foreground network’ of streets was still found to be more accessible to global through movement. The spatial analysis of economic activity found a low level of clustering of different trades and occupations in particular parts of the city. Economic activities were rather broadly distributed throughout the background network of the street system. However, some trades and occupations took advantage of the foreground network of accessible streets more than others, and this was found to be statistically significant. Those occupations with high accessibility at all scales included retailers, wholesalers and artisans. While retailers would have prioritised access to passing trade, the latter two groups may have valued the circulation of goods, products and knowledge as much as the circulation of people.

[Staying Afloat: The Vavassore Workshop and The Role of the Minor Publisher in Sixteenth Century Venice](https://www.academia.edu/33966034/Staying_Afloat_The_Vavassore_Workshop_and_The_Role_of_the_Minor_Publisher_in_Sixteenth_Century_Venice)

[Natalie Lussey Seale](https://edinburgh.academia.edu/NatalieLussey)

In the increasingly polarized historiography of the printing industry of Venice, the workshop established by Giovanni Andrea Vavassore around 1515 offers a refreshing perspective on the role of the minor publisher in the Renaissance lagoon. Neither focused on a specific genre or format of book, nor interested in employing innovatory techniques of production, Vavassore instead emerges as a printing poligrafo: a man willing to turn his hand to the production of printed wares of every kind; a maker of prints and maps, as well as a publisher, printer, and seller of all types of edition. Beginning with the formation of his press, this article follows Vavassore’s journey to the lagoon and charts the establishment of his workshop. It also examines the process by which a new artisan might learn skills and amass contacts from other members of the printing trade. Rather than an inherently competitive trade, Vavassore’s experience of printing in Venice stresses the importance of collaboration, cooperation, and networking. Working with other publishers, printers, mapmakers, and itinerant performers, he was able to establish an extensive and vibrant market for his printed wares both in Venice and beyond. The printing policy of the workshop chiefly, to print what sold, and make the largest profits in doing so – emerges as key to the success of the Vavassore over the course of eight decades. Through the examination of a series of graphic prints, maps, pamphlets, and editions, this article questions the contemporary outreach and lasting influence of one of Venice’s many minor publishers in the Renaissance.

This book discusses the production and consumption of printed images in an urban environment in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, up to 1585. The story begins in the fifteenth century. At some point - no one knows exactly when - prints were suddenly being offered for sale in Antwerp. Initially they may have been brought from other cities by merchants and travellers, but at length the first printmaker established himself in the city. In the sixteenth century Antwerp fast developed into one of the main centres of printmaking in the western world. The author explores the complex way in which the printed image secured a place for itself in the urban fabric. He reconstructs the different traditions from which the print producers evolved, and explains how existing institutions in the city related to the new medium. He traces the way in which the traditional guilds tried to bring practitioners of this ‘singular skill’, as it was labelled in 1452, into their ranks, and shows how the government tried to gain control of the new medium. He discusses the interplay between printmakers seeking strategies to market their wares, and a public confronted with an interesting array of cheap new products.The reader is given an impression of the variety of prints produced, which have thus far received little attention in art history. Archival research has generated a good deal of detailed new information on the prices of prints, the numbers of impressions made, the costs of printing and colouring, and so forth.

ISING from a prolonged study of the Marian
and Elizabethan period of our Literature, we
are oppressed with a sense of its magnitude
and manysidedness, and of the utter impos­
sibility of mentioning here even a tithe of the
interesting facts that have been met with in
the search.
There is also the clear conviction that nothing
in it is worthless : but that everything—even a
Ballad, a Proclamation, or a Sermon—may in
some way or other be turned to good account.
Further there is the most distinct percep­
tion of the growth of English Mind all through
the long reign of the Virgin Queen.
In its earlier years, our Scholars and Poets were busy with translations from
the great Classical Authors, and our Divines were even busier with translations of
the Works of the Protestant Theologians on the Continent. Original English work
was then relatively poor. Theatres did not exist in this country. But few Interludes
were written, and still fewer were printed. There was then in our language but
little food for the Imagination.
A TRANSCRIPT dc, U V, xxv.

Gradually however Prose Fiction came into our Literature in the shape of
translations of ancient Writers like APULEIUS and HELIODORUS, and of modern Writers
like BOCCACCIO and BANDELLO.
It was in the year 1579 that JOHN LYLY broke new ground with his EUPHUES
and founded our modern Prose Fiction. ROBERT GREENE and THOMAS LODGE were his
disciples.
Soon after this, our Poetry distinctly improves, and becomes more original.
Plays are now constantly acted, and in increasing numbers come into print. So,
at length, when the men born or bred in the Queen's reign have come to their
maturity, we have that magnificent outburst of our Literature in the last years of her
reign, the like of which the World has never seen elsewhere in so few years of human
history.
It is the Imaginative Literature that is the everlasting glory of a nation. Its
Politics, its Science, and its Philosophy serve their day, and then become mere matters
of history : but its Poetry, its Drama, and its Fiction never grow old. They shine on,
in undying freshness and beauty, through all the Ages.
Want of space however prevents any further consideration of this noble theme.
We can here only offer a few brief observations upon the more salient points in this
Volume.

of the Printers and Publishers. The distracting ways in which these names are spelt in

Age is that which appears upon his printed books: and even in that there is often
variation in the spellipg.
Stationers sometimes changed the printed form of their name out of mere
caprice. Thomas East took it into his head to adopt the ducal spelling of Este. His
widow however had more sense, and printed as Lucretia East: and his apprentice to
whom he left his business, though he, out of gratitude, assumed his old master's name,
still it was as Thomas Snodham alias East.
So likewise Richard Olifife changed his name to Olive, and James Bowler to Boler.
The Jaggard family had also an alternative form, Jagger.
Again, father and son often spelt their names differently; as John AUde and his
son Edward AU-de, JOHN KINGSTON and his son Felix Kyngston, John Waley and his
son Robert Walley. The first Three John Harisons have only one '' r " in their names ;
John Harrison, (4), has two.
One great advantage of this List of London Publishers is that it makes us
independent of all this erratic spelling. Every man can now be identified.
Before passing from the subject of Names, we may point out what a remark­
able confirmation the mass of names in this Volume gives of the well known
fact, that down to the time of the Commonwealth Englishmen had only one
Christian name.
How persistent was this national habit when foreigners had several Christian
names besides a surname of three or more words. For example, compare EDMUND
SPENSER with PHILIPP AUREOL THEOPHRAST BOMBAST VON HOHENHEIM,
called Paracelsus; or FRANCIS BACON with PHILIP VAN MARNIX VAN SANT
